title: Spotify tracks
text:
Source
Collected from the Spotify Web API by Kaylin Pavlik and published as a TidyTuesday dataset (21 January 2020). The course file is a random sample of 10,000 of its tracks. Spotify’s terms restrict commercial use.


Rows
One row per track and playlist (11,554 rows): 1,101 tracks are in more than one playlist. For one row per track, use distinct(track_id, .keep_all = TRUE), as the loader below does.


Columns
track_id, track_name, track_artist, track_popularity (0 to 100), release_date, release_year, playlist_genre, playlist_subgenre, and the audio features danceability, energy, key, loudness, mode, speechiness, acousticness, instrumentalness, liveness, valence, tempo, duration_ms.


Target
track_popularity, Spotify’s score in January 2020. It rewards recent plays, so release_year carries recency as well as era. A tenth of the tracks score exactly 0.


Notes
The genre is the playlist’s, not the track’s. No missing values in the features; one track has no name. Six genres, no lyrics, no artist history, no play counts.

title: Spotify tracks
text:
Loader
library(tidyverse)
sp <- read_csv("https://ml4ds.com/files/spotify_tracks.csv") |>
  distinct(track_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>          # one row per track
  mutate(duration_min = duration_ms / 60000)

title: Health system patients (synthetic)
text:
Source
Obermeyer, Z., Powers, B., Vogeli, C. and Mullainathan, S. (2019), “Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations”, Science 366(6464), 447–453, doi:10.1126/science.aax2342. The authors released a synthetic version of their data, with a data dictionary and their code: gitlab.com/labsysmed/dissecting-bias. The course reads the file from there and does not host it.


Rows
48,784 patient-years, each one row: 5,582 of Black and 43,202 of White patients. The rows were generated with the R package synthpop from the study’s data, so no row is a real patient, and, unlike the original data, the rows are not grouped by patient.


Columns
160. Measured in the year before (names ending _tm1): age band, sex, 34 chronic conditions and their count gagne_sum_tm1, 13 kinds of cost, and 94 indicators of test results and medications. Measured in the year itself (names ending _t): cost_t (total cost, rounded to $100), cost_avoidable_t (emergency and inpatient), gagne_sum_t (number of active chronic conditions), five test results, program_enrolled_t, and risk_score_t, the commercial algorithm’s score. Also race.


Targets
Whether cost_t is in the top quarter; cost_t; gagne_sum_t.


Notes
Claims about these rows are claims about the synthetic data, which mimic the study’s data in their moments and covariances. The commercial algorithm did not use race, and the course’s models do not either.

title: Health system patients (synthetic)
text:
Loader
library(tidyverse)
hs <- read_csv("https://gitlab.com/labsysmed/dissecting-bias/-/raw/master/data/data_new.csv")
outcomes_t <- c("risk_score_t", "program_enrolled_t", "gagne_sum_t", "cost_t", "cost_avoidable_t",
                "bps_mean_t", "ghba1c_mean_t", "hct_mean_t", "cre_mean_t", "ldl_mean_t")
inputs <- setdiff(names(hs), c(outcomes_t, "race"))   # the year before, without race

title: Movies
text:
Source
IMDb data extracted by Hadley Wickham, shipped in the R package ggplot2movies (GPL-3). IMDb’s terms restrict commercial use.


Rows
One row per film (58,788 rows), films with a known length and at least five user votes, 1893 to 2005.


Columns
title, year, length (minutes), budget (91% missing), rating (average user rating, 1 to 10), votes, r1 to r10 (the share of users giving each rating, in coarse bands, so a row need not sum to 100), mpaa (mostly blank), and seven genre indicators (Action, Animation, Comedy, Drama, Documentary, Romance, Short).


Target
rating. The ratings come from people who chose to watch a film and then to rate it.


Notes
votes and r1 to r10 are computed from the same users’ ratings as rating, so they are not used as inputs. Lengths are as reported to IMDb; there is no director, cast, language or country. The course uses the 33,287 films from 1919 on that run 11 to 200 minutes and have at least 20 votes (the loader below).

title: Movies
text:
Loader
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2movies)
mv <- movies |>
  filter(length <= 200, length > 10, year > 1918, votes >= 20)

title: Machine learning
text:
Where we left off

Prediction competition: curated data, the same for every competitor; a task; an agreed score; an evaluation dataset the competitors cannot see. Winning model chosen by best score

The Netflix prize went to a blend that was never put into production

Winning a competition is not always useful

Today, what a winning score does and does not tell us:

how variable the leaderboard is
what happens when the data the model meets are not like the data it was scored on
what the score leaves out

title: Machine learning
section: Data: patients of a health system
text:
Data: patients of a health system
Obermeyer et al. (2019) studied a commercial algorithm that a US health system used to predict patients’ costs, and released synthetic rows that mimic their data: 48,784 patient-years (5,582 Black, 43,202 White)

Inputs, from the year before: age band, sex, 34 chronic conditions, 13 kinds of cost, 94 test results and medications (149 columns)
Outcomes, the year after: cost, number of active chronic conditions, test results
Task: predict whether next year’s cost will be in the top quarter (above $6,800 on the training rows), as a probability \(\hat p(x)\)
Score: the Brier score, squared error for a probability, \(\ell(y, \hat p) = (y - \hat p)^2\), between 0 and 1

Split once at random: 16,000 training, 8,000 tuning, 12,000 test, 12,784 kept back for later

title: Machine learning
text:
CTF competition: the tuning leaderboard









The four models with any structure are within 0.014 of each other, and every bar is about 0.010 wide

title: Machine learning
section: Can the same rows separate two models?
text:
Can the same rows separate two models?

The two leaders’ bars overlap. Their scores come from the same 8,000 patients. Can those patients still tell the two models apart?


Score each patient twice and take the difference, \(\Delta_j = \ell\big(y_j, \hat p_A(x_j)\big) - \ell\big(y_j, \hat p_B(x_j)\big)\)

The difference of the two scores is \(\bar\Delta\), with standard error \(\mathrm{sd}(\Delta)/\sqrt m\)
\(\mathrm{Var}(\ell_A - \ell_B) = \mathrm{Var}(\ell_A) + \mathrm{Var}(\ell_B) - 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(\ell_A, \ell_B)\): the models err on mostly the same patients, so the covariance is large

boosted trees minus lasso: \(\bar\Delta = -0.0021\), standard error 0.0008, against 0.0025 for one score alone
The pair to compare on the test rows: boosted trees against lasso, chosen now

title: Machine learning
text:
A score and its risk
A score is a mean of \(m\) losses, \(\hat R = \frac1m\sum_j \ell_j\), with mean \(R\), the risk

A loss between 0 and 1 has variance at most \(\frac14\), so \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat R) \le \frac{1}{4m}\)

If \(\hat R\) were normal with that variance: \(P\big(|\hat R - R| \ge t\big) \le 2e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}\) with \(\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{4m}\), which is \(2e^{-2mt^2}\)












\(m = 50\) losses of 0 or 1
The central limit theorem makes the normal shape plausible, but does not control the far tail at a fixed \(m\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Hoeffding’s inequality

Hoeffding’s inequality (stated). If \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_m\) are independent with \(0 \le Z_i \le 1\) and \(\bar Z\) is their mean, then for every \(t > 0\) and every \(m\), \(P\big(|\bar Z - \mathbb E\bar Z| \ge t\big) \le 2e^{-2mt^2}\)

Why it holds for every \(m\):

Markov’s inequality on \(e^{\lambda D}\), \(D = \bar Z - \mathbb E\bar Z\); by independence, \(\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda D}\big]\) is a product of \(m\) factors
Hoeffding’s lemma (stated): each factor is at most what a normal with variance \(\frac14\) would give; then choose \(\lambda\)


\(K\) models fixed in advance, by the union bound: every score within \(t_K = \sqrt{\log(2K/\delta)/(2m)}\) of its risk, with probability \(1 - \delta\). Here \(t_K = 0.018\): gaps above \(2t_K\) are resolved for 1 of the 10 pairs, against a paired standard error of 0.0008

title: Machine learning
text:
Resampling the test rows
A program can enroll only the 3% with the highest scores. Of those 360 test patients, the share with top-quarter cost is 84.7% for boosted trees and 82.5% for lasso

Which patients are in the top 3% depends on every patient’s score. This number is not an average of per-patient losses. What replaces \(\mathrm{sd}/\sqrt m\)?


Bootstrap the test rows: draw \(m\) rows with replacement, recompute the difference, repeat \(B\) times, and read off the spread. Each drawn row keeps both models’ predictions, so the comparison stays paired
90% bootstrap interval for the difference: -0.6 to 5.3 percentage points, so this number does not separate them. The models are held fixed: the interval says nothing about refitting, and nothing about how the pair was chosen

title: Machine learning
text:
Scores that move
Adaptive drift (stated). If the candidates depend on earlier scores on the same rows (tune, look, tune again), the union bound no longer covers them, and the score can be driven away from the risk. A test set scored once, for models fixed before, does not move
Recht et al. (2019) built new test sets for CIFAR-10 and ImageNet to the original recipe. Accuracy fell for every model, many by about 10 percentage points (the best ImageNet model in their Table 1 from 82.9% to 72.2%), with the order of the models almost unchanged. They split the drop into three gaps:
\[
\hat R_{\text{old}} - \hat R_{\text{new}} = \underbrace{\hat R_{\text{old}} - R_{\text{old}}}_{\text{adaptivity}} \;+\; \underbrace{R_{\text{old}} - R_{\text{new}}}_{\text{distribution}} \;+\; \underbrace{R_{\text{new}} - \hat R_{\text{new}}}_{\text{sampling}}
\]
and found it was mostly the distribution: slightly harder images. On 120 Kaggle competitions, public and private leaderboards agreed closely (Roelofs et al. 2019)

title: Machine learning
section: When the function itself has moved
text:
When the function itself has moved
If \(p(y \mid x)\) changes (a new payment rule, a new treatment, a change in who gets care), neither fix applies: the old rows contain no information about the new relation, and only new outcomes reveal it
Deploying a model can be what moves it: a program that enrolls the predicted high-cost patients changes their costs, and next year’s training rows record a world the model helped make

title: Machine learning
text:
Causes and effects as inputs
Theory: the distribution of \(Y\) given all its causes is unchanged by interventions that leave \(Y\)’s own mechanism alone, so a model on the causes should travel
Nastl and Hardt (2024), 16 tabular tasks with several domains each (income by region, voting by region, hospital mortality by insurance type, …): models on all features beat models on causal features in and out of domain in every task. Their advice: approximate the best predictor on all the features available
The invariance holds for the true conditional distribution, not for the risk of a model fitted to a few features

title: Machine learning
text: Part 3: scores and decisions

title: Machine learning
section: An absurdly abbreviated history of optics
text:
An absurdly abbreviated history of optics

Ptolemy (100-170) measured refraction of light passing from air to water, altering measurements so they would fit to a quadratic curve (ancient “machine learning” or curve fitting)
Ibn Sahl (940-1000) described the correct law, which English speakers refer to as Snell’s law
Fermat (1607-1665) proposed the more general “principle of least time” which can be used to derive Snell’s law and solve other optical problems – predict values in different settings

title: Machine learning
text:
Ptolemy’s curve in glass












Points: Ptolemy’s table, air to water, within 2.2 degrees of Snell’s law, \(\sin i = n \sin r\) with \(n = 1.33\)
In glass the same curve is off by 1.4 degrees at 10 and 9.0 at 80. Snell’s law changes one number, \(n = 1.5\)
Refitted to new measurements, a quadratic would fit glass too. It could not say anything before them

title: Machine learning
text:
Put the “science” back in “data science”!
Feynman, Lectures on Physics, Vol. 1:

Now in the further development of science, we want more than just a formula. First we have an observation, then we have numbers that we measure, then we have a law which summarizes all the numbers. But the real glory of science is that we can find a way of thinking such that the law is evident.

And from “Cargo Cult Science”:

When you have put a lot of ideas together to make an elaborate theory, you want to make sure, when explaining what it fits, that those things it fits are not just the things that gave you the idea for the theory; but that the finished theory makes something else come out right, in addition.

title: Machine learning
text:
CTF competition: what it delivered
Donoho (2017) called prediction plus the common task framework machine learning’s “secret sauce”:

training data shared by everyone, competitors, and a referee who scores each submitted rule on data hidden from them
effort goes to measured performance; many groups compete; judging is impartial and automatic
winners arrive already tested, so they look close to deployable


The Netflix prize: the winning blend was never put into production

title: Machine learning
text:
Outcome reasoning and model reasoning
Rodu and Baiocchi (2023): a competition justifies “Algorithm A performs better than Algorithm B”, not deployment


Two ways to trust a prediction:

outcome reasoning: measured performance
model reasoning: the model’s structure, checked against what we know

Only the second can be argued before use

Outcome reasoning is enough only if:

measurement: future outcomes can be scored
adaptability: the model can be updated in time
resilience: accumulated errors are tolerable
agnosis: conflict with beliefs is tolerable


Each depends on who is asking, the stakeholders

title: Machine learning
text:
The winner, deployed
The health system uses a cost score to choose who gets extra care: the 3% with the highest scores are enrolled in a program for patients with complex needs
Use the competition’s winner, boosted trees. On the test patients at or above the 97th percentile of its score, the share with top-quarter cost is 81.8% for Black and 85.4% for White patients

The score predicts cost well, and about equally well in both groups. What could still be wrong?

text:
The same score, by health









Left: what the score was trained for, similar in both groups. Right: at the same score, Black patients are sicker. Enrolled: 6.4 active chronic conditions for Black, 4.6 for White patients
Why, in the study: at the same number of chronic illnesses, $1,801 a year less was spent on Black patients (in these rows, $320), so cost understates their need

title: Machine learning
section: Should this be predicted at all?
text:
Should this be predicted at all?

For which of these tasks would a model with a better score make things better?

which patients will cost the most next year, to offer them extra care
which defendants will be re-arrested before trial, to decide who is released
which applicants will stay in a job for two years, to decide who is hired
which drivers will claim on their insurance, to set the price they pay

title: Machine learning
text:
Limits of predictive optimization
The case for prediction: decisions that are consistent, cheap, auditable, and often more accurate than unaided judgment (Wang et al. 2024). Questions a score does not answer:

Acting on it: does acting on the prediction help? A decision can change the outcome it was predicted from
The target: is it what we care about? Re-arrest is not offending, and cost is not need
Predictability: in a mass competition on life outcomes, 160 teams’ best predictions were only slightly better than a simple benchmark (Salganik et al. 2020)
Contesting: can the person decided about get an explanation, their data, and a way to correct the decision?

Some predictions are objected to even when they are accurate: pricing car insurance by credit score holds people accountable for things that are not their fault (Kiviat 2019)

title: Machine learning
section: More warnings for data about humans
text:
More warnings for data about humans
Social science is hard! Health is also (at least partially) social. It is very difficult to predict life outcomes, even with machine learning models and big data
Strategic/adversarial/adaptive behavior: Goodhart’s law / Campbell’s law / Lucas critique / Friedman’s thermostat / Washback effect / Performativity / Reflexivity / Hammer’s law
For these reasons, when dealing with human data:

Almost all variables correlate
Unconfoundedness assumptions are always wrong
Can’t separate “normative vs scientific” (ethics always important)

Remember: focus on what is importantly wrong

title: Machine learning
text:
Recap








The loss and the target define the problem
optimal model theorem; optimal threshold theorem; quantile optimality


Training error underestimates the risk
optimism theorem; the selected candidate’s score is biased low


Faster rates need assumptions
no free lunch; the k-NN rate


Shrinkage and averaging trade bias for variance
bias–variance decompositions; ridge; the correlated-average variance


Prediction is not intervention
adjustment theorem; inverse propensity weighting; partial dependence and causal effects


A score is evidence about one target on one distribution, not a license to deploy
Hoeffding’s inequality; covariate and label shift; another target

title: Machine learning

Before the seminar

Do the exercises at the top of the seminar notebook before the seminar

title: Machine learning
text:
Conclusion
The leaderboard
Compare two models on the same rows, paired. Hoeffding’s inequality bounds every score at once for models fixed in advance. Choose the comparison before opening the test rows; resample the rows for anything that is not a mean
When the data move
Covariate shift: reweight by \(p_{\text{test}}/p_{\text{train}}\), where the supports overlap. Label shift: move the intercept. Neither repairs a change in \(p(y \mid x)\)
Scores and decisions
That one model beats another, on one target and one distribution. Whether to deploy it, and whether the target is the right one, are questions the score does not answer

title: Week 9 seminar
text:
Before the seminar

The lecture stated two results without proof: exercise 1 proves quantile optimality, and exercise 2 proves the coverage of a split conformal interval. Exercise 3 computes partial dependence and individual curves by hand. Do all three on paper before the seminar. You may use, without proof: differentiation under the integral sign (if \(G(a) = \int_{-\infty}^a h(y, a)\,dy\), then \(G'(a) = h(a, a) + \int_{-\infty}^a \partial_a h(y, a)\,dy\), and similarly for \(\int_a^\infty\), where the boundary term changes sign); and that if \(V_1, \ldots, V_{m+1}\) are independent draws from one continuous distribution, every ordering of them is equally likely.






WarningHints



Each exercise has hints, collapsed below it. Do not open a hint unless you have been stuck for at least a few minutes, and open them in order. Solutions are shown in the seminar if you ask.


Exercise 1 (quantile optimality). \(Y\) has a continuous distribution function \(F\) with a density \(f\) and a finite mean, and \(0 < \tau < 1\). The pinball loss of a prediction \(\hat y\) is \(\rho_\tau(y - \hat y) = (y - \hat y)\big(\tau - \mathbf 1\{y < \hat y\}\big)\). Let \(G(\hat y) = \mathbb E[\rho_\tau(Y - \hat y)]\).

Before any calculus: move the prediction from \(\hat y\) up to \(\hat y + \delta\), with \(\delta > 0\) small. How does the loss change for an outcome below \(\hat y\)? For an outcome above \(\hat y + \delta\)? Use this to guess at which \(\hat y\) the expected loss stops falling.
Write \(G(\hat y)\) as two integrals, one over \(y < \hat y\) and one over \(y \ge \hat y\), and show that \(G'(\hat y) = F(\hat y) - \tau\).
Show that \(G\) is convex, and conclude that a \(\tau\)-quantile, a value \(q_\tau\) with \(F(q_\tau) = \tau\), minimizes \(G\). When is the minimizer not unique?
Suppose that, for each \(x\), \(Y\) given \(X = x\) has a continuous distribution function with a density and a finite mean. Explain why the same argument shows that the conditional \(\tau\)-quantile \(q_\tau(x)\) is the best prediction at \(x\), and why the function \(x \mapsto q_\tau(x)\) minimizes \(\mathbb E[\rho_\tau(Y - h(X))]\) over functions \(h\).







NoteHint 1






Below the prediction the loss is \((1 - \tau)(\hat y - y)\); above it, \(\tau(y - \hat y)\). Which outcomes are below \(\hat y\), and with what probability?










NoteHint 2






The boundary terms from differentiating under the integral sign are zero: at \(y = \hat y\) both integrands vanish.










NoteHint 3






A differentiable function whose derivative is nondecreasing is convex. (d) \(\mathbb E[\rho_\tau(Y - h(X))] = \mathbb E\big[\mathbb E[\rho_\tau(Y - h(X)) \mid X]\big]\).




Exercise 2 (coverage of a split conformal interval; Lei et al. 2018). A model \(\hat f\) has been fitted on training rows. Then \(m\) held-out rows \((X_1, Y_1), \ldots, (X_m, Y_m)\) and a new row \((X, Y)\) are independent draws from one distribution, independent of the training rows. Write \(R_i = |Y_i - \hat f(X_i)|\) and \(R = |Y - \hat f(X)|\), and assume these have a continuous distribution, so that there are no ties. Let \(k = \lceil 0.9(m + 1)\rceil\), assume \(k \le m\), and let \(C\) be the \(k\)th smallest of \(R_1, \ldots, R_m\). The interval is \(\hat f(X) \pm C\).

Explain why, given the training rows, \(R_1, \ldots, R_m, R\) are independent and identically distributed. Show that the interval covers \(Y\) exactly when \(R\) is among the \(k\) smallest of all \(m + 1\) values, and conclude that \(P\big(Y \in \hat f(X) \pm C\big) = k/(m + 1) \ge 0.9\). What does this probability average over?
Compute \(k\) and the coverage for \(m = 9\), \(19\) and \(1{,}000\). What happens when \(m = 5\)?
Suppose \(C\) is computed the same way from the training rows’ residuals instead. Which step of (a) fails, and in which direction does the coverage usually move?
Suppose the held-out rows were also used to choose between several models before \(C\) was computed. Which step of (a) fails?







NoteHint 1






Given the training rows, \(\hat f\) is a fixed function.










NoteHint 2






The interval covers \(Y\) when \(R \le C\). If \(R \le C\), how many of \(R_1, \ldots, R_m\) can be smaller than \(R\)?




Exercise 3 (partial dependence by hand). A fitted model is \(\hat f(x_1, x_2) = x_1x_2\), and the data are four units:

Evaluate each unit’s ICE curve for \(x_1\) at \(t = -1, 0, 1\), and sketch the four curves.
Compute \(\mathrm{PDP}_1(t)\). Does the PDP say that \(\hat f\) uses \(x_1\)? Does it?

Now \(\hat f(x_1, x_2) = g_1(x_1) + g_2(x_2)\) for any functions \(g_1\) and \(g_2\). Show that the ICE curves for \(x_1\) are parallel and that \(\mathrm{PDP}_1(t) = g_1(t) + c\) for a constant \(c\).

title: Week 9 seminar
text:
Problems

Problems 1 and 2 use the normal distribution function \(\Phi\); for a 90% interval, \(\Phi(1.645) = 0.95\). If \(W \sim N(\mu, s^2)\), then \(P(|W| \le c) = \Phi\big((c - \mu)/s\big) - \Phi\big((-c - \mu)/s\big)\).
Problem 1 (the residuals of a nearest-neighbor fit).  The inputs come in groups of \(k\) rows that share the same \(x\), and \(Y = f^\star(x) + \varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\), independent across rows. The \(k\)-nearest-neighbor fit predicts, at the \(x\) of a group, the mean \(\bar y\) of that group’s \(k\) outcomes \(y_1, \ldots, y_k\). A training row’s residual is \(y_i - \bar y\). A new outcome at that \(x\) is \(Y_0 = f^\star(x) + \varepsilon_0\), independent of the group’s outcomes.

Find the distribution of a training residual \(y_i - \bar y\), and of the new residual \(Y_0 - \bar y\).
There are many groups, and \(C\) is the 90th percentile of the absolute training residuals over all of them, so \(C\) is close to the 90th percentile of the distribution of \(|y_i - \bar y|\). Find it. Find the coverage \(P(|Y_0 - \bar y| \le C)\) as a function of \(k\), and evaluate it at \(k = 1, 2, 5, 10\) and \(50\).
Instead, \(C\) comes from held-out rows: one more row in each group, not used in the fit. What is \(C\) now, and the coverage? How much wider is the interval than \(f^\star(x) \pm 1.645\sigma\), which needs the truth?
In this setting, larger \(k\) gives a narrower interval with the right coverage. What does the setting leave out that stops us from taking \(k\) as large as we like?

Problem 2 (smoothing bias and the confidence interval).  One input. The rows are spread evenly in \(x\), \(n\) of them per unit of \(x\), and \(Y = f^\star(x) + \varepsilon\) with independent \(N(0, \sigma^2)\) errors, \(\sigma\) known. At a point \(x_0\) the fit \(\hat f(x_0)\) averages the \(k = 2nh\) outcomes with \(|x_i - x_0| \le h\). \(f^\star\) is twice differentiable, with \(f^{\star\prime\prime}(x_0) = a \ne 0\). For small \(h\), use \(f^\star(x_i) \approx f^\star(x_0) + f^{\star\prime}(x_0)(x_i - x_0) + \frac a2(x_i - x_0)^2\), and treat the \(x_i\) in the window as spread evenly over it, so that the average of \(x_i - x_0\) is 0 and the average of \((x_i - x_0)^2\) is \(h^2/3\).

Show that the bias \(\mathbb E\hat f(x_0) - f^\star(x_0)\) is about \(ah^2/6\), and that the variance of \(\hat f(x_0)\) is \(\sigma^2/(2nh)\).
Find the \(h\) that minimizes the mean squared error, bias\(^2\) + variance, and show that, to the order of these approximations, at that \(h\) the size of the bias is half the standard deviation of \(\hat f(x_0)\), \(|\text{bias}|/\mathrm{sd} = 1/2\), whatever \(n\), \(\sigma\) and \(a\).
The confidence interval \(\hat f(x_0) \pm 1.645\,\mathrm{sd}\) for \(f^\star(x_0)\), with \(\mathrm{sd} = \sigma/\sqrt k\), ignores the bias. What is its coverage at the \(h\) of (b)? Does more data help?
With \(d\) inputs and a window of half-width \(h\) in each, the bias is still proportional to \(h^2\) and the variance to \(1/(nh^d)\). Show that at the \(h\) that minimizes the mean squared error, \(|\text{bias}|/\mathrm{sd} = \sqrt d/2\), and find the coverage for \(d = 4\) and \(d = 9\).
The prediction interval \(\hat f(x_0) \pm 1.645\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \mathrm{sd}^2}\) for a new outcome \(Y_0 = f^\star(x_0) + \varepsilon_0\). With one input, the \(h\) of (b) and \(k = 90\), what is its coverage?
How would you change the fit used for the confidence interval to bring its coverage back to 90%, and what does that cost?

Problem 3 (calibration in two groups).  A score takes the values 0.2 and 0.8. In two groups of 100 people:

Score

With the condition

50

0.8
20
16


B
0.2

Find each group’s base rate. Is the score calibrated within each group? Overall?
Predict 1 when the score is above 0.5. In each group, find the true positive rate (the share of people with the condition who are predicted 1), the false positive rate (the share of people without it who are predicted 1) and the positive predictive value (the share of people predicted 1 who have it).
In each group, find the average score among people with the condition and among people without it.
Let \(S\) be any score that is calibrated in a group with base rate \(p\), so \(P(Y = 1 \mid S) = S\). Show that \(\mathbb E S = p\), and so \(p\,\mathbb E[S \mid Y = 1] + (1 - p)\,\mathbb E[S \mid Y = 0] = p\). Use this to show that two groups with different base rates cannot have the same \(\mathbb E[S \mid Y = 1]\) and the same \(\mathbb E[S \mid Y = 0]\), unless \(\mathbb E[S \mid Y = 1] = 1\) and \(\mathbb E[S \mid Y = 0] = 0\).

title: Week 9 seminar
text:
Coding

Two simulations, where the truth is known: part 1 checks intervals at one point, and part 2 asks a fitted model a causal question. The optional item at the end recalibrates a score on the NHANES adults, with the lecture’s split, which is made here so that the seed is set once, before every random step below.

nh <- NHANESraw |>
  filter(Age >= 20) |>
  select(Diabetes, Gender, Age, Race1, Poverty, Weight, Height, BMI, Pulse, BPSysAve, TotChol, DirectChol, PhysActive) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(diabetes = as.numeric(Diabetes == "Yes"), male = as.numeric(Gender == "male"),
         active = as.numeric(PhysActive == "Yes"))
set.seed(310)   # change this number: a different split, and different numbers below
nh_id <- sample(nrow(nh))
nh_train <- nh[nh_id[1:4000], ]
nh_tune <- nh[nh_id[4001:7000], ]
nh_test <- nh[nh_id[7001:nrow(nh)], ]


1. Intervals at one point

One input, uniform on \([0, 1]\); \(f^\star(x) = \sin(2\pi x)\); noise \(N(0, 1)\); 500 training rows. At \(x_0 = 0.25\), \(f^\star\) is at its peak, \(f^\star(x_0) = 1\). The \(k\)-nearest-neighbor fit at \(x_0\) averages the outcomes of the \(k\) rows whose \(x\) is closest to \(x_0\). With \(\sigma = 1\) known, the usual intervals, which ignore any bias, are: for \(f^\star(x_0)\), the confidence interval \(\hat f(x_0) \pm 1.645/\sqrt k\); for a new outcome \(Y_0\) at \(x_0\), the prediction interval \(\hat f(x_0) \pm 1.645\sqrt{1 + 1/k}\).

f_star <- function(x) sin(2 * pi * x)
sim <- function(n) tibble(x = runif(n), y = f_star(x) + rnorm(n))
x0 <- 0.25
ks <- c(5, 10, 25, 50, 90, 150, 250)

Question 1. Complete knn_at(x0, k, d), which returns the mean outcome of the k rows of d whose x is closest to x0. On one sample of 500 rows, compute the fit at \(x_0\) for each k in ks. Then look at the plot of the fits for \(k = 10\) and \(k = 150\) across \(x\). What goes wrong for small \(k\), and for large \(k\)?

# knn_at <- function(x0, k, d) ____
d <- sim(500)
# round(sapply(ks, function(k) knn_at(x0, k, d)), 3)


x_grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.005)
curves <- expand_grid(k = c(10, 150), x = x_grid) |>
  mutate(fit = map2_dbl(x, k, function(x, k) knn_at(x, k, d)), k = paste("k =", k))
ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = tibble(x = x_grid, y = f_star(x_grid)), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(x, fit, colour = k), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = x0, colour = "grey50") +
  labs(colour = NULL, title = "Dashed: f*. Grey line: x0 = 0.25")

Question 2. Repeat on 2,000 samples of 500 rows (the chunk below, about 3 seconds). For each k, estimate the bias and the standard deviation of \(\hat f(x_0)\), its mean squared error, and how often each interval covers: the confidence interval covers \(f^\star(x_0)\), and the prediction interval covers a new outcome \(Y_0\). At which k is the mean squared error smallest? How often does each interval cover there?

fits <- replicate(2000, { d_s <- sim(500); sapply(ks, function(k) knn_at(x0, k, d_s)) })   # one row per k, one column per sample
y0 <- f_star(x0) + rnorm(2000)                                                            # a new outcome for each sample


# q2 <- tibble(k = ks,
#              bias = rowMeans(fits) - f_star(x0),
#              sd = apply(fits, 1, sd),
#              mse = ____,
#              ci_covers = ____,
#              pi_covers = ____)
# q2

Checkpoint (run it; if it stops, fix question 2 before going on): for small k the bias is negligible, so the confidence interval should cover about 90%.

stopifnot(abs(q2$ci_covers[q2$k == 10] - 0.9) < 0.03)

Question 3. Using question 2’s table: which k would you use for a confidence interval for \(f^\star(x_0)\) that covers about 90%, and what does it cost? Why does the prediction interval keep its coverage at \(k = 150\)?
Question 4. Now an interval at every \(x\): \(\hat f(x) \pm C\), with one \(C\). For \(k\) = 1, 5 and 25 and the sample d from question 1, compute \(C\) two ways: as the 90th percentile of the absolute training residuals (each training row’s fit uses that row too), and from 500 held-out rows, as the \(\lceil 0.9 \times 501 \rceil = 451\)st smallest of their absolute residuals. Check each on 2,000 fresh rows. Compare with problem 1, which predicted 0%, 82% and 89% for training residuals when \(f^\star\) is flat.

hold <- sim(500)
fresh <- sim(2000)
# q4 <- map_dfr(c(1, 5, 25), function(k) {
#   fit_train <- sapply(d$x, function(x) knn_at(x, k, d))
#   pred_hold <- sapply(hold$x, function(x) knn_at(x, k, d))
#   pred_fresh <- sapply(fresh$x, function(x) knn_at(x, k, d))
#   C_train <- ____
#   C_hold <- ____
#   tibble(k, C_train, C_hold,
#          covers_train = mean(____),
#          covers_hold = mean(____))
# })
# q4



2. Every tool, one causal question

A simulated world with three inputs. \(x_1\) causes \(x_2\); \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) cause \(y\); \(x_3\) is caused by \(y\) and by \(x_1\): \[
x_1 \sim \mathrm{Unif}[-2, 2], \quad x_2 = x_1 + \varepsilon_2, \quad y = \tfrac12 x_1 + \tfrac32\sin x_2 + \varepsilon_y, \quad x_3 = y + x_1 + \varepsilon_3,
\] with independent normal noises of standard deviations 0.8, 0.5 and 0.3. The question: which input should we set, and how, to raise \(y\), and by how much? A forest fitted on all three inputs predicts \(y\) well. Apply every interpretation tool from the lecture, write down what they suggest, then intervene in the simulator and compare.

draw_world <- function(n) {
  x1 <- runif(n, -2, 2)
  x2 <- x1 + rnorm(n, 0, 0.8)
  y <- 0.5 * x1 + 1.5 * sin(x2) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
  x3 <- y + x1 + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)
  tibble(x1, x2, x3, y)
}
world <- draw_world(2000)
world_fresh <- draw_world(2000)
fit_all <- randomForest(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = world, ntree = 300, mtry = 3, nodesize = 20)

Question 5. Compute the forest’s MSE on the fresh rows, and compare it with the variance of \(y\).

# base <- mse(world_fresh$y, ____)
# c(mse = base, var_y = var(world_fresh$y))

Question 6. Importance, four ways. Split importance and Shapley values are computed in the chunk after this one. Write the other two: permutation importance (shuffle one input in the fresh rows and score again), and leave-one-covariate-out (LOCO: refit the forest without the input, with mtry = 2 and the other settings unchanged, and score it on the fresh rows), each as the rise in fresh MSE over base. Which input does each measure rank first, and with what share of its total?

# perm_imp <- sapply(c("x1", "x2", "x3"), function(j) {
#   d_perm <- world_fresh
#   d_perm[[j]] <- ____
#   ____ - base
# })
# fit_no_x1 <- randomForest(____, data = world, ntree = 300, mtry = 2, nodesize = 20)
# fit_no_x2 <- ____
# fit_no_x3 <- ____
# loco_imp <- c(x1 = ____, x2 = ____, x3 = ____)


split_imp <- importance(fit_all)[, "IncNodePurity"]
shap <- permshap(fit_all, X = select(world_fresh[1:200, ], x1, x2, x3),
                 bg_X = select(world[1:200, ], x1, x2, x3), verbose = FALSE)   # about 5 seconds
shap_imp <- colMeans(abs(shap$S))
imp <- rbind(split = split_imp, permutation = perm_imp, LOCO = loco_imp, `mean |Shapley|` = shap_imp)
round(imp / rowSums(imp), 2)   # each measure as a share of its total

Question 7. Partial dependence by hand. Complete pdp_curve(): for each value t in grid, set the input to t for every row of d and average the forest’s predictions. The chunk after it draws the three curves, and 100 of the 500 ICE curves for \(x_1\). According to the PDP, what happens to \(y\) when \(x_1\) goes from \(-1\) to \(1\)? What share of all 500 ICE curves for \(x_1\) end lower at \(1\) than at \(-1\)?

# pdp_curve <- function(fit, d, input, grid) sapply(grid, function(t) {
#   d[[input]] <- ____
#   ____
# })


grid <- seq(-2, 2, by = 0.25)
d_pd <- world_fresh[1:500, ]
pd <- tibble(t = grid, x1 = pdp_curve(fit_all, d_pd, "x1", grid), x2 = pdp_curve(fit_all, d_pd, "x2", grid),
             x3 = pdp_curve(fit_all, d_pd, "x3", grid))
ice <- d_pd[rep(1:100, each = length(grid)), ] |> mutate(unit = rep(1:100, each = length(grid)), t = rep(grid, 100), x1 = t)
ice$pred <- predict(fit_all, ice)                                                    # one ICE curve per unit, the first 100 units
slope_ice <- (predict(fit_all, mutate(d_pd, x1 = 1)) - predict(fit_all, mutate(d_pd, x1 = -1))) / 2   # each unit's ICE slope from -1 to 1
p_pd <- pd |> pivot_longer(-t, names_to = "input", values_to = "pdp") |>
  ggplot(aes(t, pdp, colour = input)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + labs(x = "value set", y = "PDP", title = "Partial dependence")
p_ice <- ggplot(ice, aes(t, pred, group = unit)) + geom_line(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = pd, aes(t, x1, group = NULL), colour = "black", linewidth = 1.4) +
  labs(x = "x1 set to", y = "prediction", title = "ICE curves for x1 (100 of 500), and the PDP")
p_pd | p_ice
c(pdp_x1_at_minus1 = pd$x1[pd$t == -1], pdp_x1_at_1 = pd$x1[pd$t == 1], share_ice_down = mean(slope_ice < 0))

Question 8. Before you run anything else, write down two answers. (a) From questions 6 and 7: which input gives the largest rise in the forest’s average prediction when it is moved from \(-1\) to \(1\), and how large is the rise? (b) From the equations above: what would setting each input from \(-1\) to \(1\) do to the mean of \(y\)? The sign is enough.
Question 9. Intervene in the simulator. \(do(x_1 = t)\) replaces \(x_1\)’s line with \(x_1 = t\) for everyone and leaves the other equations alone. Complete world_do_x1(n, t) and world_do_x2(n, t), each returning the mean of \(y\) over n draws. Setting \(x_3\) leaves the mean of \(y\) at \(\mathbb E[y] = 0\), as question 8 found from the equations. The chunk after it plots each input’s effect against its PDP. Compare with your answers to question 8.

# world_do_x1 <- function(n, t) {
#   x1 <- ____
#   x2 <- ____
#   y <- ____
#   mean(y)
# }
# world_do_x2 <- function(n, t) {
#   ____
# }


truth <- tibble(t = grid, x1 = sapply(grid, function(t) world_do_x1(1e5, t)),
                x2 = sapply(grid, function(t) world_do_x2(1e5, t)), x3 = 0)
bind_rows(pivot_longer(pd, -t, names_to = "input") |> mutate(curve = "PDP of the forest"),
          pivot_longer(truth, -t, names_to = "input") |> mutate(curve = "effect of setting it")) |>
  ggplot(aes(t, value, linetype = curve)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + facet_wrap(~ input) +
  labs(x = "value set", y = NULL, linetype = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Question 10. Fit two more models: a forest on \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) only (the forest fit_no_x3 from question 6), and a smooth of \(x_1\) alone, gam(y ~ s(x1), data = world). Compute each model’s PDP for \(x_1\) and its fresh MSE. Which PDP matches the effect of setting \(x_1\), and which model predicts best? To read the effect of \(x_2\) from a PDP, which inputs should the model include? Which of the tools in questions 6 and 7 could have told you which model to read?

Optional, can be done at home: recalibrating a score
Boosted trees with xgboost’s defaults predict diabetes from nine measurements, fitted on the lecture’s training adults (data note).

Fitting several curves

Could we fit this model one curve at a time?

title: Machine learning
text:
Backfitting algorithm
Model: \(\hat f(x_1, \ldots, x_p) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat f_1(x_1) + \cdots + \hat f_p(x_p)\). Columns \(\mathbf x_1, \ldots, \mathbf x_p\); \(\hat f_k(\mathbf x_k)\) is the vector of fitted values of curve \(k\)

Initialize: \(\hat\beta_0 = \bar y\), and \(\hat f_j^{(0)} = 0\) for every \(j\)
For iteration \(t = 1, 2, \ldots\):

for \(j = 1, \ldots, p\):

partial residual \(\mathbf r_j^{(t)} = \mathbf y - \hat\beta_0 - \sum_{k < j} \hat f_k^{(t)}(\mathbf x_k) - \sum_{k > j} \hat f_k^{(t-1)}(\mathbf x_k)\)
\(\hat f_j^{(t)}\): a one-input smoother (e.g. a spline) of \(\mathbf r_j^{(t)}\) on \(\mathbf x_j\), centered to mean zero

stop when iteration \(t\) barely changes the fitted values

title: Machine learning
text:
Backfitting and partialling out
Two centered inputs, and a line for each component: \(\hat f_j(x) = \hat\beta_j x\). Start at \(\hat\beta_2^{(0)} = 0\). Iteration \(t\) fits each slope to its partial residual: \[
\hat\beta_1^{(t)} = \frac{\mathbf x_1^T\big(\mathbf y - \hat\beta_2^{(t-1)} \mathbf x_2\big)}{\mathbf x_1^T \mathbf x_1}, \qquad
\hat\beta_2^{(t)} = \frac{\mathbf x_2^T\big(\mathbf y - \hat\beta_1^{(t)} \mathbf x_1\big)}{\mathbf x_2^T \mathbf x_2}
\]

The slopes stop changing only where both hold: \(\mathbf x_j^T(\mathbf y - \hat\beta_1 \mathbf x_1 - \hat\beta_2 \mathbf x_2) = 0\) for \(j = 1, 2\). These are the normal equations: the fixed point is least squares

Partialling-out theorem: the coefficient on \(\mathbf x_2\) is \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \mathbf y / \tilde{\mathbf x}_2^T \tilde{\mathbf x}_2\), the slope on what is left of \(\mathbf x_2\) after \(\mathbf x_1\) has explained what it can.

Backfitting does this with smooth curves instead of lines

title: Machine learning
text:
Backfitting on the films









Length, year and Short on the training films, starting from zero. Length and Short are closely related: each iteration moves a little more of the shorts’ higher ratings from the length curve to the Short coefficient, which settles after about 70 iterations

title: Machine learning
text:
Backfitting, more generally
Any number of inputs. With one coefficient per input, each update minimizes the RSS over that coefficient with the others held fixed: coordinate descent (Gauss–Seidel, in numerical linear algebra). A spline gives each input a block of coefficients, updated together: block coordinate descent. Fast for unrelated inputs, slow for strongly related ones
Gram–Schmidt residualizes each input (predictor) on the ones before it, once. Backfitting leaves the inputs alone and residualizes \(\mathbf y\) iteratively
Partialling out with flexible fits. Residualize both \(\mathbf y\) and \(\mathbf x_j\) on the other inputs, with any regression method, then regress residual on residual: double machine learning, later in the course

text:
Partial dependence plots for a GAM
These univariate plots for GAMs are called partial dependence plots (PDPs), each up to a constant: for an additive fit, the partial dependence on \(x_j\) is \(\hat f_j\) plus a constant. They show how the GAM depends on each feature: a simple one-dimensional dependence, because of the additivity assumption









But what if additivity is wrong?

title: Machine learning
text:
Growing a tree

Recursive: split the data by the most discriminating single-variable question; then do the same inside each leaf, and so on
Greedy: each split is the best now. A weak split that would enable a strong one below it can be missed, so stopping early is risky: grow a large tree, then prune (next slide)
When to stop: a leaf too small to split (rpart’s minsplit), or no split that improves the fit enough (cp)
Grown until no leaf can split, a tree is like 1-nearest neighbors: on the training films, year and length alone give 2,670 leaves


\(k\) nearest neighbors average the \(k\) training points closest to \(x_0\); a tree averages those in \(x_0\)’s leaf, a neighborhood chosen by subsets of features

Pruning
For each \(\alpha \geq 0\), the sub-tree minimizing \(\text{RSS} + \alpha \times (\text{number of leaves})\). The Star Wars tree, as \(\alpha\) increases from 0:

title: Machine learning

Trees and missing inputs
The films’ budget is missing for 87%: a film with no budget cannot answer “budget < c?”

Missingness as information: a split also chooses which side the films with no budget go to, like its cutoff, to lower the RSS (xgboost’s default direction); or a budget missing indicator that the tree can split on
Missingness as a nuisance: rpart’s surrogate splits, backup questions on other inputs that send the training films the same way; a film missing the split’s input follows the best backup it can answer
Informative here: budgets were recorded mostly for widely rated films (median 1,238 votes, against 71). Potentially useful for prediction

title: Machine learning
text:
Part 4: three model improvement strategies
Sacrifice simplicity/interpretability for prediction accuracy
Bagging*: bootstrap aggregating

Resample training data, average resulting models

Random forest

Randomly drop predictors at each split

Boosting*

Successively add simple models to improve the aggregate

* Can be used with other models too, not just trees

title: Machine learning
text:
Bagging: bootstrap aggregating
Problem: a single tree model can have high variance (like many non-smooth or non-regularized models)

Bootstrap: for each \(b = 1, \ldots, B\) resamples (with replacement) of the training data, fit \(\hat f^b\) on bootstrap sample \(b\)
Aggregate: combine the \(B\) models, using majority vote for classification or mean for regression

\[\hat f_\text{bag} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B \hat f^b\]
(“Smoothing” useful for high-variance models)

title: Machine learning
text:
Averaging \(B\) trees
Average \(B\) trees’ predictions at one input \(x\) (variance over the draw of the training data, and of the resampling)

What is the variance of their average if the \(B\) trees are

copies of the same tree, with variance \(\tau^2\)?
independent, each with variance \(\tau^2\)?
each with variance \(\tau^2\), every pair with correlation \(\rho\)?

title: Machine learning
text:
Recall: variance of a sum
For random variables \(V_1, \ldots, V_n\) and constants \(a_1, \ldots, a_n\), every variance plus every covariance: \[
\mathrm{Var}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i V_i\Big) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\, \mathrm{Var}(V_i) + \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j \neq i} a_i a_j\, \mathrm{Cov}(V_i, V_j)}_{n(n-1) \text{ terms; } \binom{n}{2} \text{ distinct}}
\]

title: Machine learning
text:
Correlated-average variance
With \(n = B\) and every \(a_i = 1\): \(B\) terms \(\tau^2\) and \(B(B - 1)\) terms \(\rho\tau^2\), \(\;\mathrm{Var}\big(\sum_{b} V_b\big) = B\tau^2 + B(B - 1)\rho\tau^2\)


Correlated-average variance. \(V_1, \ldots, V_B\), each with variance \(\tau^2\), every pair with correlation \(\rho\): \[
\mathrm{Var}\Big(\frac1B \sum_{b=1}^B V_b\Big) = \rho\,\tau^2 + (1 - \rho)\,\frac{\tau^2}{B}
\]

Proof: divide by \(B^2\) and regroup, \(\frac{\tau^2}{B} + \frac{B - 1}{B}\rho\tau^2 = \rho\tau^2 + (1 - \rho)\frac{\tau^2}{B}\). Bagging shrinks the second term; \(\rho\tau^2\) stays, since bootstrap trees grown from one sample are alike

title: Machine learning
text:
Random forest: dropping predictors

Suppose \(B\) is large, say 300. Which term of the correlated-average variance is left, and how could we make it smaller?


Problem: aggregation does not increase information if the aggregates are highly correlated, e.g. averaging 1000 trees but each one uses the same small set of predictor variables

Drop predictors randomly, at every split
e.g. each split chooses among a random \(\sqrt{p}\) of the \(p\) predictors
Aggregate models which are now (typically) less correlated, achieving greater variance reduction

title: Machine learning
text:
Out-of-bag predictions

Each bootstrap sample contains some subset of the training data
Roughly \(1/e \approx 0.37\) portion of the training samples will be left out of each bootstrap sample
Can use these to estimate test error (e.g. instead of \(K\)-fold cross-validation)

Software implementations may do this automatically

title: Machine learning
text:
Adding trees
A forest grows its trees separately and averages them. Now grow them one after another and add them up: after \(b\) trees the fit is \(\hat f^{(b)}\), the sum so far

We may add one small tree to \(\hat f^{(b)}\). What should it predict?


The residual from the existing fit: \(y - \hat f^{(b)}(x)\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Boosting: iterated fitting on residuals
Idea: train models sequentially, decreasing residuals by a small amount each time. Each model contributes something different
Can use “weak learners” (e.g. trees with one split, “stumps”) to grow an ensemble model gradually fitting closer to the training data

Relationship with gradient descent
Gradient descent: small step in direction of negative gradient
Boosting: small step in direction of weak learner approximating the negative gradient
Instead of taking an unrestricted gradient step, we reduce the loss by taking a small step in the direction of a weak learner: a simple, low-cost model
Optional additional reading: ESL sections 10.10–10.12 (gradient boosting, tree size, regularization)

title: Machine learning
text:
Boosting as approximate gradient descent
The training loss depends on a model only through its \(n\) fitted values \(\mathbf f = (f_1, \ldots, f_n)\), \(f_i = f(x_i)\): a function of \(n\) numbers \[
L(\mathbf f) = \sum_{i=1}^n \tfrac12 (y_i - f_i)^2, \qquad -\frac{\partial L}{\partial f_i} = y_i - f_i
\] The negative gradient is the residual vector

A gradient step, \(\mathbf f^{(b)} = \mathbf f^{(b-1)} + \gamma\,(\mathbf y - \mathbf f^{(b-1)})\), changes only those \(n\) values. Boosting trees fits a small tree approximating the negative gradient (the residuals) and steps along it, with learning rate \(\gamma\): \[
\hat f^{(0)} = \bar y, \qquad \hat f^{(b)} = \hat f^{(b-1)} + \gamma\, \hat t_b, \qquad \hat t_b \text{ a small tree fitted to } y_i - \hat f^{(b-1)}(x_i)
\]

title: Machine learning
text:
Boosting in practice
More tuning parameters
Number of trees/steps \(B\), complexity of each tree/model \(d\), regularization/learning rate \(\gamma\). Warning: can now overfit with large \(B\) (unlike bagging/r.f.)
Software may choose them automatically. No guarantee it’s reasonable!
Bagging and boosting
Bagging and forests start with large trees, which have high variance individually, and average them to lower the variance. Boosting starts with weak learners like tree stumps, which have high bias individually, and fits iteratively on residuals to lower the bias

title: Machine learning
text:
Iterations and learning rate












Iterations \(B\). Training error keeps falling; tuning error turns. Stopping there is early stopping, as for gradient descent
Learning rate \(\gamma\). Smaller steps
Depth. How many inputs one tree can combine (next)

title: Machine learning
text:
Tree depth and interactions

Can a tree with one split fit \(f(x_1, x_2) = x_1 x_2\) well? Hint: assume the inputs are independent, both \(\mathrm{Unif}[-1, 1]\)
How many splits would we want for \(f(x_1, \ldots, x_p) = x_1 \cdots x_p\)?


A stump asks one question, so a sum of stumps is a sum of one-input functions: an additive model. Depth \(d\): interactions of up to \(d\) inputs
A boosted model is additive in trees, not in the predictors

title: Machine learning
text:
We’re in dangerous territory

Less interpretable methods/models
Many tuning parameters
Increasingly sophisticated software with many defaults and/or automatically optimized tuning parameters


But consider, Alfred North Whitehead wrote (1911; emphasis added):

It is a profoundly erroneous truism, repeated by all copy-books and by eminent people when they are making speeches, that we should cultivate the habit of thinking of what we are doing. The precise opposite is the case. Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them.

title: Machine learning
text:
Conclusion
Additive models
One curve per input, each fitted to what the others leave: partialling out, one input at a time
Additivity vs interactions
A plot of one input at a time works most naturally for additive models, and can be importantly wrong when the truth has interactions
Trees and ensembles
Greedy questions, pruned by validation. Bagging and forests average trees to lower variance; boosting adds small trees, gradient descent on the fitted values

title: Machine learning
text: Part 1: cross-validation

title: Machine learning
text:
Cross-validation
We chose the knob on the selection set, \(D'\): fit \(\hat f_\lambda\) on \(D\) for a grid of \(\lambda\), score each on \(D'\), keep the best, refit on \(D \cup D'\). Common when one fit is expensive

When one fit is cheap:
Idea: swap \(D\) and \(D'\) and get two estimates, \(\hat R(\hat f_\lambda)\) and \(\hat R(\hat f'_\lambda)\). Average these and choose \(\hat\lambda\) using the average
Idea: apply the same process with several “folds” of data
\(K\)-fold cross-validation
Each subset used once as the held-out set, and \(K - 1\) times for training

title: Machine learning
text:
Cross-validation cartoon





Gives \(K\) estimates of the held-out error at each \(\lambda\). Credit: Wikipedia

title: Machine learning
text:
\(K\)-fold cross-validation
Each subset used once as the held-out set, and \(K - 1\) times for training
Choose \(\hat\lambda\) to minimize \[
\hat R_{K\text{-cv}}(\lambda) = \frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K \hat R_k\big(\hat f^{(k)}_\lambda\big)
\] where \(\hat f^{(k)}_\lambda\) is fitted on the data that “holds out” the \(k\)th fold, and \(\hat R_k\) is its error on that fold
Then refit the model \(\hat f_{\hat\lambda}\) at that value \(\hat\lambda\) on the entire dataset

The CV curve on the Spotify tracks









The 5,000 training tracks, \(K = 10\). One curve per family, the knob where each is lowest (orange). Every fold’s fit standardizes on its own training rows. The selection set was not used: each track was fitted on nine times and scored once

title: Machine learning
section: Standard errors: held out, and the CV bars
text:
Standard errors: held out, and the CV bars











A flat bottom: \(k = 50\) to \(200\) are within one bar of each other

A held-out score is a mean of \(m\) losses \(L_j = \ell(y_j, \hat f(x_j))\), independent with \(\hat f\) fixed: \[
\widehat{\text{Err}} = \frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m L_j, \qquad \text{SE} = \frac{\text{sd}(L)}{\sqrt m}
\] The structures lecture’s bars: \(m = 2{,}000\) selection tracks. Software’s CV bars: the same formula on the \(K\) fold scores, \(m = K\); a heuristic, since the folds share fitting rows

title: Machine learning
text:
Lessons about cross-validation

Think of it as a way to choose model complexity, not the model itself
Beware common cross-validation errors! From Duda and Hart quoted in MLstory


… the same data were often used for designing and testing the classifier. This mistake is frequently referred to as “testing on the training data.” A related but less obvious problem arises when a classifier undergoes a long series of refinements guided by the results of repeated testing on the same data. This form of “training on the testing data” often escapes attention until new test samples are obtained.

title: Machine learning
text:
Lessons about cross-validation

Beware common cross-validation errors! From ESL:


Ideally, the test set should be kept in a “vault,” and be brought out only at the end of the data analysis. Suppose instead that we use the test-set repeatedly, choosing the model with smallest test-set error. Then the test set error of the final chosen model will underestimate the true test error, sometimes substantially.


Cross-validate the entire model-building pipeline (not just one step), and only do it once – or at least not many times
Choosing \(K\): larger \(\to\) \(\hat R_{K\text{-cv}}\) has lower bias, more variance. Often use \(K = 5\) or \(10\)

title: Machine learning
text: Part 2: the nearest-neighbor rate

title: Machine learning
text:
Why care about rates?
Over a trillion dollars is going into scaling up AI models. What if this is mathematically guaranteed to fail?
Data Centers Are Burning Fossil Fuels. It’s Destroying Big Tech’s Climate Goals

title: Machine learning
text:
The best \(k\) as \(n\) and \(p\) grow
The CV curve put \(k\) at 100 on 5,000 tracks and \(p = 11\) inputs. Where would the minimum be with 50,000 tracks? With 110 inputs?

Bias–variance decomposition, \(k\)-NN form: inputs fixed, \(y_i = f^\star(x_i) + \varepsilon_i\), \(\varepsilon_i\) independent, mean \(0\), variance \(\sigma^2\); \(\hat f_k(x_0)\) the mean of the \(k\) nearest \(y_i\): \[
\mathbb E\big[(Y_0 - \hat f_k(x_0))^2\big] = \sigma^2 + \Big[f^\star(x_0) - \tfrac1k\textstyle\sum_l f^\star(x_{(l)})\Big]^2 + \sigma^2/k
\]

The variance term is explicit, \(\sigma^2/k\). The bias term depends on \(f^\star\) at the \(k\) nearest inputs, and can be bounded only by an assumption on \(f^\star\)

What assumption on \(f^\star\) makes the bias term a number? Write it down.

title: Machine learning
text:
\(k\)-NN rate: bounding the bias












\(r_k(x_0)\): the distance from \(x_0\) to its \(k\)th nearest training input. Every neighbor is within it
Assume \(f^\star\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz: \(|f^\star(x) - f^\star(x')| \le L\,\|x - x'\|\). Then each neighbor’s \(f^\star\) is within \(L\,r_k\) of \(f^\star(x_0)\), so their average is too


\(k\)-NN rate. Inputs fixed, \(f^\star\) \(L\)-Lipschitz, noise variance \(\sigma^2\): \(\;\mathbb E\big[(\hat f_k(x_0) - f^\star(x_0))^2 \,\big|\, \text{inputs}\big] \;\le\; L^2\, r_k(x_0)^2 + \sigma^2/k\)

Proof. “Inputs fixed”: given the training inputs \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\), the neighbors are fixed and only the noise is random. The bias \(\frac1k\sum_l [f^\star(x_{(l)}) - f^\star(x_0)]\) has each term at most \(L\,r_k\) in size, so its square is at most \(L^2 r_k^2\); the variance is \(\sigma^2/k\). \(\blacksquare\)

title: Machine learning
text:
The nearest-neighbor distance lemma
How far away is the \(k\)th neighbor? Inputs i.i.d. uniform on \([0, 1]^p\). A ball around \(x_0\) holding \(k\) of the \(n\) points has volume about \(k/n\), so its radius is about \((k/n)^{1/p}\)



Nearest-neighbor distance lemma (stated). For \(x_0\) away from the boundary, \(\mathbb E\big[r_k(x_0)^2\big] \le C_p\,(k/n)^{2/p}\), with \(C_p\) depending on \(p\) only.

In one dimension the \(k\)th neighbor is about \(k/2n\) away on each side. In \(p = 10\) the radius is about \((k/n)^{1/10}\): with \(k/n = 1/100\), \(0.63\) of the side of the cube












Curse of dimensionality: in many dimensions, the nearest \(1\%\) of the data is not near.

title: Machine learning
text:
The rate
Put the two together and choose \(k\): \[
\mathbb E\big[(\hat f_k(x_0) - f^\star(x_0))^2\big] \;\le\; C_p L^2 (k/n)^{2/p} + \sigma^2/k
\] The first term grows with \(k\), the second shrinks. They balance at \(k = c\,n^{2/(p+2)}\), and there \[
\text{error} \le C\, n^{-2/(p+2)}, \qquad c, C \text{ constants not depending on } n
\]
To halve the bound, \(2^{(p+2)/2}\) times the data: \(2.8\times\) in \(p = 1\), \(4\times\) in \(p = 2\), \(64\times\) in \(p = 10\)

Minimax rate (stated). Over all \(L\)-Lipschitz \(f^\star\) in \(p\) dimensions no estimator beats \(n^{-2/(p+2)}\) for every \(f^\star\) (Stone 1980, 1982); a particular \(f^\star\), a constant say, does better.

title: Machine learning
section: The cost of a non-free lunch
text:
The cost of a non-free lunch









Assumption on \(f^\star\)
Squared error (up to constants; rows 1 and 2 minimax)
The family




\(L\)-Lipschitz in \(p\) inputs
\(n^{-2/(p+2)}\)
nearest neighbors, a tree, a network: smoothness only


a sum of a fixed number of Lipschitz one-input curves (additivity, plus design conditions)
\(n^{-2/3}\), the one-input rate (Stone 1985)
additive splines: no interactions


linear with \(s\) nonzero coefficients among \(p\) (sparsity, plus design and noise conditions)
about \(s\log p/n\), an upper bound (Hastie et al. 2015, Theorem 11.2)
the lasso: a sparse plane




Smoothness alone: \(p\) in the exponent. Additivity: the one-input exponent. Sparsity: \(p\) out of the exponent, into a \(\log p\). Rows 2 and 3 are stated, not derived

No free lunch theorem, with numbers. A faster rate needs a stronger assumption.

title: Machine learning
text:
Part 3: ridge and the lasso side by side
Assumptions \(\leftrightarrow\) biases?

title: Machine learning
text:
History: Stein’s paradox
Estimating \(\mu \in \mathbb R^p\) from an i.i.d. sample \(\mathbf Y_1, \ldots, \mathbf Y_n \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2 I)\). The MLE is \(\bar{\mathbf Y}\) (obvious and best, right?)
Charles Stein discovered in the 1950’s that the MLE is inadmissible if \(p > 2\) 🤯
The James–Stein estimator shrinks \(\bar{\mathbf Y}\) toward some other point, any other point, chosen a priori, e.g. 0: \[
\hat\mu_{\text{JS}} = \Big(1 - \frac{(p-2)\sigma^2/n}{\|\bar{\mathbf Y}\|^2}\Big)\bar{\mathbf Y}, \qquad \text{MSE}(\hat\mu_{\text{JS}}) < \text{MSE}(\bar{\mathbf Y}) \text{ for all } \mu, \text{ if } p > 2
\]

title: Machine learning
text:
Shrinkage: less variance, more bias
James–Stein shrinkage demo
Statisticians emphasized unbiasedness. After Stein’s example, bias is not always bad. Most ML methods use bias this way

title: Machine learning
text:
Ridge and the lasso, again


\[
\text{ridge: } \min_\beta\ \|\mathbf y - \mathbf X\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda\|\beta\|_2^2
\] \[
\|\beta\|_2^2 = \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^2
\]

\[
\text{lasso: } \min_\beta\ \|\mathbf y - \mathbf X\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda\|\beta\|_1
\] \[
\|\beta\|_1 = \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j|
\]

Ridge’s estimates are dense: every coefficient nonzero, in general; the lasso’s are exactly zero over whole ranges of \(\lambda\). What \(\lambda\) does to one coefficient is hidden in general, because the coefficients interact; in the simplest design they do not

title: Machine learning
text:
The identity design
\(\mathbf X = I\) (\(n = p\)), so \(\mathbf y = \beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon\): one observation per coefficient, least squares \(\hat\beta = \mathbf y\). A penalty that adds up over coefficients, as ridge’s and the lasso’s do, splits the objective: \(\|\mathbf y - \beta\|_2^2 + \mathcal P_\lambda(\beta) = \sum_j \big[(y_j - \beta_j)^2 + \mathcal P_\lambda(\beta_j)\big]\), one problem per coefficient

Ridge: \(\hat\beta_{\lambda, j} = \dfrac{y_j}{1 + \lambda}\), every coefficient shrunk by the same factor, zero only if \(y_j = 0\)


Lasso: \(\hat\beta_{\lambda, j} = \mathrm{sign}(y_j)\,\big(|y_j| - \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\big)_+\), each \(y_j\) moved toward zero by \(\lambda/2\), stopping at zero: exactly zero whenever \(|y_j| \le \lambda/2\)



Soft thresholding. \(\arg\min_b\ (y - b)^2 + \lambda|b| = \mathrm{sign}(y)\,(|y| - \lambda/2)_+\). Deriving both minimizers: an exercise in the notebook.

title: Machine learning
text:
Bias–variance decomposition, ridge form
Same design, noise variance \(\sigma^2\). Least squares, \(\hat\beta = \mathbf y\): unbiased, variance \(\sigma^2\) per coefficient. Divide by \(1 + \lambda\): \[
\text{bias}_j = -\frac{\lambda}{1 + \lambda}\,\beta_j, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_{\lambda,j}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{(1 + \lambda)^2}
\]

Bias–variance decomposition, ridge form. \(\mathbf X = I\), \(\mathbf y = \beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon\), noise independent, mean \(0\), variance \(\sigma^2 > 0\): \(\;\mathrm{MSE}(\lambda) = \mathbb E\|\hat\beta_\lambda - \beta\|^2 = \sum_{j=1}^p (\lambda^2\beta_j^2 + \sigma^2)/(1 + \lambda)^2\), with slope \(-2p\sigma^2 < 0\) at \(\lambda = 0\): for every \(\beta\), some \(\lambda > 0\) beats least squares.

Proof: an exercise in the notebook. Which \(\lambda\)? The best is \(\sigma^2\) over the mean of \(\beta_j^2\), noise over signal: unknown

\(n = 100\) observations, \(p = 200\) inputs, \(\mathbf y = \mathbf X\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon\) with only 16 nonzero coefficients. Lasso and ridge at the \(\lambda\) cross-validation chooses

The ten models cross-validation fit, each on nine folds, at lambda.min: the kept inputs change from fold to fold. The same instability as a tree’s cutoffs. At the one-SE \(\lambda\) the ten sets agree

title: Machine learning
text:
A fixed \(\lambda\) and a data-chosen \(\hat\lambda\)


\(\hat\beta_{\text{lasso}}(\lambda)\) at a fixed \(\lambda\)

\(\hat\beta_{\text{lasso}}(\hat\lambda)\) at a data-chosen \(\hat\lambda\)

Different in general! Theoretical results about the first (the rate, the ridge-form decomposition at a fixed \(\lambda\)) may not apply to the second

Choosing on a dataset is empirical risk minimization over a finite class: the winner’s score on the rows it was chosen on is biased low.

title: Machine learning
text:
A penalty on wiggliness
The spline of the structures lecture: \(f(x) = \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^J \beta_j b_j(x)\), \(J\) the knob. Instead: take a large \(J\) as a ceiling, and penalize wiggliness


\[
\min_f\; \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i - f(x_i)\big)^2 + \lambda\int f''(x)^2\,dx
\] \(\lambda = 0\): the \(J\)-basis fit. \(\lambda \to \infty\): \(f'' = 0\), a straight line. In between: \(\lambda\) chosen by generalized cross-validation (GCV, mgcv’s default)

The bias–variance trade-off









Expected test error = noise + bias\(^2\) + variance. More flexibility: less bias, more variance; the sum is a U

title: Machine learning
section: Does statistics apply to deep learning?
text:
Does statistics apply to deep learning?
The bias–variance trade-off is one of the most important pillars of statistical wisdom. If we make a model too complex, it overfits to the training data… or does it?





Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal (2019). Does zero training error necessarily mean the model is overfit? No.

title: Machine learning
section: Zero training error: what does it mean?
text:
Zero training error: what does it mean?









\(n = 20\) points, natural splines with \(J\) basis functions: least squares up to \(J = n\); beyond, of the many fits with zero training error, the one with the smallest \(\|\beta\|\) (ridge’s limit as \(\lambda \to 0\)). Zero training error does not say which fit you have

title: Machine learning
text:
Double descent, demonstrated









Test MSE against \(J\), averaged over 50 draws of 20 points: a U up to \(J = n\), a spike at \(J = n\) (interpolation threshold), a second descent beyond it (Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal 2019). Ridge on same basis, \(\lambda\) by cross-validation: never interpolates, no spike. Dashed: noise variance

title: Machine learning
text:
Double descent: takeaways
It can happen for some models (large neural networks) on some data (high signal-to-noise: images, translation). So zero training error does not necessarily mean overfit, and a test error that has started rising might fall again later: we don’t know
It does not contradict the bias–variance trade-off. The horizontal axis may not accurately indicate model complexity
For most methods in this course, expect a U: \(k\)-NN, trees, ridge, the lasso. Regularized fits do not interpolate, and have no second descent (the ridge curve)
ISLR section 10.8, pp. 441–443

title: Machine learning
text:
Conclusion

Cross-validation: the standard for tuning when model fits are less expensive and/or datasets aren’t extremely large. The minimum CV-error underestimates risk of the chosen model
Modeling assumptions (smoothness, additivity, sparsity, wiggliness) make different types of models work well. We generally don’t know if assumptions are true
Most ML models are optimized (in the bias–variance trade-off) with nonzero bias. Achieving zero training error without overfitting is not a new discovery of the AI community and does not contradict the trade-off

title: James-Stein shrinkage: a picture
text:
One observation \(\mathbf Y \sim N(\mu, I_p)\), or equivalently the sample mean of \(n\) draws with \(\sigma^2/n = 1\). The natural estimate of \(\mu\) is \(\mathbf Y\) itself. The James-Stein estimator pulls it toward a point chosen in advance, here \(\mathbf 0\): \[
\hat\mu_c = \Big(1 - \frac{c}{\|\mathbf Y\|^2}\Big)_+ \mathbf Y, \qquad c = p - 2 .
\] The subscript \(+\) is the positive part, so a \(\mathbf Y\) with \(\|\mathbf Y\|^2 \le c\) is shrunk all the way to \(\mathbf 0\) instead of past it. James and Stein (1961) proved that for \(p \ge 3\) the version without the positive part has smaller mean squared error than \(\mathbf Y\) for every \(\mu\); the positive part, a later refinement, is better still.
The pictures below draw many \(\mathbf Y\) around one fixed truth \(\mu\) (the diamond), shrink each one, and color it by whether it ended up closer to \(\mu\) (blue) or farther away (orange, hollow). The grey segment is the move. Hover over a point for its numbers; drag the three-dimensional picture to rotate it.
Show the setup code
library(dplyr); library(plotly)

# Course palette (theme/st310.scss): viridis for the primary scale, magma for the second.
v_dark <- "#440154"; v_blue <- "#31688e"; m_orange <- "#fc8961"; m_black <- "#000004"
help_col <- v_blue; hurt_col <- m_orange
hurt_line <- "rgba(252,137,97,0.8)"; hurt_wire <- "rgba(252,137,97,0.95)"

set.seed(310)

# Shrink every row of Y toward 0 with its own factor (1 - c / |y|^2)_+ and record the squared errors.
shrink <- function(Y, mu, c) {
  d2 <- rowSums(Y^2)
  f <- pmax(1 - c / d2, 0)
  Yhat <- Y * f
  tibble(d2 = d2, f = f,
         se = rowSums(sweep(Y, 2, mu)^2),
         newse = rowSums(sweep(Yhat, 2, mu)^2)) |>
    mutate(worse = newse > se, to_zero = f == 0)
}

# Interleave start, end, NA so one plotly line trace draws every segment.
segments_xy <- function(a, b) {
  n <- nrow(a); out <- matrix(NA_real_, 3 * n, ncol(a))
  out[seq(1, 3 * n, 3), ] <- a; out[seq(2, 3 * n, 3), ] <- b
  out
}

hover_text <- function(s) {
  sprintf("|y|<sup>2</sup> = %.2f<br>factor = %.2f<br>squared error before = %.2f<br>squared error after = %.2f", s$d2, s$f, s$se, s$newse)
}

title: James-Stein shrinkage: a picture
text:
Two dimensions, as a heuristic
In two dimensions the James-Stein constant is \(c = p - 2 = 0\): no shrinkage at all, which agrees with the theorem’s condition \(p \ge 3\) (the sample mean cannot be beaten for every \(\mu\) in one or two dimensions). So this picture borrows the three-dimensional constant, \(c = 1\), to show the geometry on a page. Truth \(\mu = (2.4, 1.8)\), \(\|\mu\| = 3\), 150 draws.


Show the code
mu2 <- c(2.4, 1.8); c2 <- 1; n2 <- 150
Y2 <- matrix(rnorm(n2 * 2), ncol = 2) + rep(mu2, each = n2)
s2 <- shrink(Y2, mu2, c2) |> mutate(x = Y2[, 1], y = Y2[, 2], nx = x * f, ny = y * f)

th <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200)
circle <- function(center, r) tibble(x = center[1] + r * cos(th), y = center[2] + r * sin(th))
zero_disk2 <- circle(c(0, 0), sqrt(c2))                              # inside: shrunk all the way to 0
hurt2 <- circle(mu2 / 2, sqrt(sum(mu2^2) / 4 + c2 / 2))              # inside: shrinking hurts (see below)
seg2 <- segments_xy(cbind(s2$x, s2$y), cbind(s2$nx, s2$ny))
hover2 <- hover_text(s2)

plot_ly() |>
  # background layers: the two circles, then 0 and mu
  add_trace(x = hurt2$x, y = hurt2$y, type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
            line = list(color = hurt_line, dash = "dot", width = 1.8),
            name = "inside: shrinking hurts, if not sent to 0", hoverinfo = "name") |>
  add_trace(x = zero_disk2$x, y = zero_disk2$y, type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
            line = list(color = "#8c8c8c", dash = "dash", width = 1.2),
            name = "inside: shrunk to 0", hoverinfo = "name") |>
  add_trace(x = 0, y = 0, type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
            marker = list(color = m_black, size = 11, symbol = "x"), name = "0 (shrink toward)", hoverinfo = "name") |>
  add_trace(x = mu2[1], y = mu2[2], type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
            marker = list(color = v_dark, size = 12, symbol = "diamond"), name = "truth mu", hoverinfo = "name") |>
  # data layers on top: the segments, then the points
  add_trace(x = seg2[, 1], y = seg2[, 2], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
            line = list(color = "rgba(80,80,80,0.35)", width = 1), hoverinfo = "none", showlegend = FALSE) |>
  add_trace(data = filter(s2, !worse), x = ~x, y = ~y, type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
            marker = list(color = help_col, size = 7, opacity = 0.8),
            text = hover2[!s2$worse], hoverinfo = "text", name = "shrinking helps") |>
  add_trace(data = filter(s2, worse), x = ~x, y = ~y, type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
            marker = list(color = hurt_col, size = 8, symbol = "circle-open", line = list(width = 2.2)),
            text = hover2[s2$worse], hoverinfo = "text", name = "shrinking hurts") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "", zeroline = FALSE, range = c(-1.6, 5.6)),
         yaxis = list(title = "", zeroline = FALSE, scaleanchor = "x", scaleratio = 1, range = c(-2.2, 5)),
         legend = list(x = 0.01, y = 0.99, bgcolor = "rgba(255,255,255,0.7)"),
         margin = list(l = 30, r = 10, t = 10, b = 30))






Every point moves along the line from itself to \(\mathbf 0\). The closer it starts to \(\mathbf 0\), the larger the fraction it is shrunk by, reaching 100% inside the dashed circle; the longest moves start at that circle. The ones that get worse are the ones that were already “between” \(\mu\) and \(\mathbf 0\); the dotted circle, centered halfway between them, is the exact boundary for every point not shrunk all the way to \(\mathbf 0\). In this run 82 of 150 draws improve and 2 land on \(\mathbf 0\).

title: James-Stein shrinkage: a picture
section: Three dimensions, the theorem’s smallest case
text:
Three dimensions, the theorem’s smallest case
Here \(c = p - 2 = 1\) is the James-Stein constant itself. Truth \(\mu = (2, 2, 1)\), again \(\|\mu\| = 3\), 300 draws. The dotted circle has become a sphere, drawn as a wireframe.


Show the code
mu3 <- c(2, 2, 1); c3 <- 1; n3 <- 300
Y3 <- matrix(rnorm(n3 * 3), ncol = 3) + rep(mu3, each = n3)
s3 <- shrink(Y3, mu3, c3) |> mutate(x = Y3[, 1], y = Y3[, 2], z = Y3[, 3], nx = x * f, ny = y * f, nz = z * f)
seg3 <- segments_xy(cbind(s3$x, s3$y, s3$z), cbind(s3$nx, s3$ny, s3$nz))
hover3 <- hover_text(s3)

# the sphere inside which shrinking hurts: center mu/2, radius sqrt(|mu|^2/4 + c/2), as a wireframe
wire <- function(center, r, n_mer = 8, n_par = 4, m = 60) {
  t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = m); pieces <- list()
  for (a in seq(0, pi, length.out = n_mer + 1)[-(n_mer + 1)])                   # meridians
    pieces[[length(pieces) + 1]] <- cbind(r * cos(t) * cos(a), r * cos(t) * sin(a), r * sin(t))
  for (ph in seq(-pi / 2, pi / 2, length.out = n_par + 2)[-c(1, n_par + 2)])   # parallels
    pieces[[length(pieces) + 1]] <- cbind(r * cos(ph) * cos(t), r * cos(ph) * sin(t), rep(r * sin(ph), m))
  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(pieces, function(P) rbind(P, NA)))
  sweep(out, 2, center, "+")
}
W <- wire(mu3 / 2, sqrt(sum(mu3^2) / 4 + c3 / 2))

plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(x = W[, 1], y = W[, 2], z = W[, 3], type = "scatter3d", mode = "lines",
            line = list(color = hurt_wire, width = 3.5), hoverinfo = "none", name = "inside: shrinking hurts, if not sent to 0") |>
  add_trace(x = seg3[, 1], y = seg3[, 2], z = seg3[, 3], type = "scatter3d", mode = "lines",
            line = list(color = "rgba(50,50,50,0.5)", width = 2.5), hoverinfo = "none", showlegend = FALSE) |>
  add_trace(data = filter(s3, !worse), x = ~x, y = ~y, z = ~z, type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers",
            marker = list(color = help_col, size = 3.5, opacity = 0.85),
            text = hover3[!s3$worse], hoverinfo = "text", name = "shrinking helps") |>
  add_trace(data = filter(s3, worse), x = ~x, y = ~y, z = ~z, type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers",
            marker = list(color = hurt_col, size = 4.5, symbol = "circle-open", line = list(color = hurt_col, width = 2)),
            text = hover3[s3$worse], hoverinfo = "text", name = "shrinking hurts") |>
  add_trace(x = 0, y = 0, z = 0, type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers",
            marker = list(color = m_black, size = 4, symbol = "x"), name = "0 (shrink toward)", hoverinfo = "name") |>
  add_trace(x = mu3[1], y = mu3[2], z = mu3[3], type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers",
            marker = list(color = v_dark, size = 5, symbol = "diamond"), name = "truth mu", hoverinfo = "name") |>
  layout(scene = list(aspectmode = "data",
                      xaxis = list(title = "", showticklabels = FALSE), yaxis = list(title = "", showticklabels = FALSE),
                      zaxis = list(title = "", showticklabels = FALSE),
                      camera = list(eye = list(x = 1.6, y = -1.5, z = 0.9))),
         legend = list(x = 0.01, y = 0.99, bgcolor = "rgba(255,255,255,0.7)"),
         margin = list(l = 0, r = 0, t = 0, b = 0))






In this run 198 of 300 draws improve and 4 land on \(\mathbf 0\). Rotate the picture so that \(\mathbf 0\) and \(\mu\) line up: the sphere covers a smaller share of the cloud than the circle did, because the cloud now has a third direction to spread into.
Counting improved draws is not the theorem’s criterion: mean squared error averages the squared errors, so the size of each gain and loss counts. Here 82 of 150 two-dimensional draws improve, yet the average squared error rises from 2.21 to 2.35; in three dimensions it falls from 3.08 to 2.98.

title: James-Stein shrinkage: a picture
text:
The same three-dimensional draws, flattened
The 300 draws of the picture above with their third coordinate dropped, so \(\mathbf 0\) stays at the origin, \(\mu = (2, 2, 1)\) goes to \((2, 2)\), and the sphere’s outline is the dotted circle. Each point keeps the color it earned in three dimensions.


Show the code
seg3f <- segments_xy(cbind(s3$x, s3$y), cbind(s3$nx, s3$ny))
sph_c3 <- mu3 / 2; sph_r3 <- sqrt(sum(mu3^2) / 4 + c3 / 2)
hurt3f <- circle(sph_c3[1:2], sph_r3)
# helped in 3D, but the flattened point falls inside the circle: above or below the sphere
s3 <- s3 |> mutate(in_circle = (x - sph_c3[1])^2 + (y - sph_c3[2])^2 < sph_r3^2,
                   above_below = !worse & in_circle,
                   in_sphere = (x - sph_c3[1])^2 + (y - sph_c3[2])^2 + (z - sph_c3[3])^2 < sph_r3^2)
n_ab <- sum(s3$above_below); n_ab_out <- sum(s3$above_below & !s3$in_sphere)

plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(x = hurt3f$x, y = hurt3f$y, type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
            line = list(color = hurt_line, dash = "dot", width = 1.8),
            name = "the sphere's outline", hoverinfo = "name") |>
  add_trace(x = 0, y = 0, type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
            marker = list(color = m_black, size = 11, symbol = "x"), name = "0 (shrink toward)", hoverinfo = "name") |>
  add_trace(x = mu3[1], y = mu3[2], type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
            marker = list(color = v_dark, size = 12, symbol = "diamond"), name = "truth mu", hoverinfo = "name") |>
  add_trace(x = seg3f[, 1], y = seg3f[, 2], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
            line = list(color = "rgba(80,80,80,0.35)", width = 1), hoverinfo = "none", showlegend = FALSE) |>
  add_trace(data = filter(s3, !worse), x = ~x, y = ~y, type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
            marker = list(color = help_col, size = 7, opacity = 0.8),
            text = hover3[!s3$worse], hoverinfo = "text", name = "shrinking helps") |>
  add_trace(data = filter(s3, worse), x = ~x, y = ~y, type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
            marker = list(color = hurt_col, size = 8, symbol = "circle-open", line = list(width = 2.2)),
            text = hover3[s3$worse], hoverinfo = "text", name = "shrinking hurts") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "", zeroline = FALSE, range = c(-1.6, 5.6)),
         yaxis = list(title = "", zeroline = FALSE, scaleanchor = "x", scaleratio = 1, range = c(-1.8, 5.4)),
         legend = list(x = 0.01, y = 0.99, bgcolor = "rgba(255,255,255,0.7)"),

Some blue points now appear inside the circle: 55 of them in this run, and all 55 are outside the sphere. They were above or below it, and dropping the third coordinate moved them onto the disk. Compare with the first picture, where nothing blue can be inside the circle except a point shrunk all the way to \(\mathbf 0\).

knn_predict <- function(Xnew, Xtrain, ytrain, k) {
