title: Machine learning
text:
Where we left the fitting
Least squares has a formula for \(\hat\beta\), and \(\hat\beta\) solves the normal equations. Logistic regression is fitted by maximum likelihood, and glm did it for us
Today: what did glm do? How can we tell whether fitting is working? Should we let it finish?

Write down the normal equations from memory. Then guess: how is it different for logistic regression?

title: Machine learning
text:
Model fitting: maximum likelihood
How do we estimate \(\beta\)? Maximum likelihood:
\[
\text{maximize } L(\beta ; \mathbf y | \mathbf X) = \prod_{i=1}^n L(\beta ; y_i | \mathbf x_i)
\] (assuming the data is i.i.d.)

Maximum likelihood (Fisher, 1912–1922): choose the parameter that makes the observed data most probable. We maximize the log-likelihood because a product of \(n\) small numbers underflows and a sum differentiates term by term; log is increasing, so the maximizer is the same. Least squares is a log-likelihood: for \(y_i \sim N(\mathbf x_i^T\beta, \sigma^2)\) it is \(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i (y_i - \mathbf x_i^T\beta)^2 + \text{const}\). In glm, family names the distribution whose likelihood is maximized: gaussian is lm, binomial is logistic regression.

Next slide: a bit of mathematics

title: Machine learning
text:
MLE for logistic regression
Each factor is a Bernoulli (binomial, one trial) probability, \(P(y_i \mid \mathbf x_i) = p_i^{y_i}(1 - p_i)^{1 - y_i}\) with \(p_i = p(\mathbf x_i^T\beta) = 1/(1 + e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta})\):
\[
L(\beta ; \mathbf y | \mathbf X) = \prod_{i=1}^n \left( \frac{1}{1+e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta}} \right)^{y_i} \left(1- \frac{1}{1+e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta}} \right)^{1-y_i}
\]

\[
\ell(\beta ; \mathbf y | \mathbf X) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i \log \left( \frac{1}{1+e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta}} \right) + (1-y_i) \log \left(1- \frac{1}{1+e^{- \mathbf x_i^T\beta}} \right) \right]
\]

title: Machine learning
text:
MLE: the derivative
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ell(\beta ; \mathbf y | \mathbf X) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i  \left( \frac{\mathbf x_i e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta}}{1+e^{-\mathbf x_i^T\beta}} \right) + (1-y_i) \left(\frac{-\mathbf x_i}{1+e^{- \mathbf x_i^T\beta}} \right) \right]
\]
\[= \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf x_i \left[ y_i - \left(\frac{1}{1+e^{- \mathbf x_i^T\beta}} \right) \right] = \color{#b73779}{\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf x_i [y_i - \hat p_i(\beta)]}\]
Set this equal to 0 and solve for \(\beta\)

title: Machine learning
section: The score equations, read as orthogonality
text:
The score equations, read as orthogonality

Least squares, the normal equations: \(\mathbf X^T(\mathbf y - \mathbf X\hat\beta) = \mathbf 0\). The residual is orthogonal to every column of \(\mathbf X\).

Logistic score equations. Stack the last slide’s rows: writing \(\mathbf p(\beta) = (\hat p_1(\beta), \ldots, \hat p_n(\beta))^T\), the MLE \(\hat\beta\) solves \[
\mathbf X^T\big(\mathbf y - \mathbf p(\hat\beta)\big) = \mathbf 0
\]
Same shape as least squares, with \(\mathbf X\hat\beta\) replaced by the fitted probabilities: the residual \(\mathbf y - \hat{\mathbf p}\) is orthogonal to every column of \(\mathbf X\)
No closed form, because \(\mathbf p(\beta)\) is not linear in \(\beta\)

title: Machine learning
section: Two things the score equations say
text:
Two things the score equations say
Row one is the intercept. \(\sum_i (y_i - \hat p_i) = 0\): the fitted probabilities average to the observed proportion of 1s on the training rows.
The log-likelihood is concave. Differentiating once more, \[
\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial\beta\,\partial\beta^T} = -\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\, \mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^T, \qquad w_i = \hat p_i(\beta)\,\big(1 - \hat p_i(\beta)\big) > 0
\] Each term is \(-w_i\, \mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^T\) with \(w_i > 0\). In any direction \(v\), \(v^T \mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^T v = (\mathbf x_i^T v)^2 \ge 0\), so the sum curves downward, or is flat, in every direction: the log-likelihood is concave, and any finite solution of the score equations is its global maximum
What concavity does not give: existence (the separable case has no finite solution). So how do we solve the score equations?

title: Machine learning
text:
Newton-Raphson

Find the roots of a function
Iteratively approximating the function by its tangent
Root of the tangent line is used as starting point for next approximation
See the animation on Wikipedia

Exercise: using the gradient and the Hessian from the previous slides, derive the Newton-Raphson update for \(\beta\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Logistic regression fitting: multivariate case
Newton-IRLS (equivalent) steps, \(g\) the logit link. Each iteration is a weighted least-squares fit around the current fit
\[
\begin{eqnarray}
\hat{\mathbf p}_t & \gets & g^{-1}(\mathbf X \hat \beta_t)
& \ \text{ update probs.} \\
\mathbf W_t & \gets & \text{diag}[\hat{\mathbf p}_t (1 - \hat{\mathbf p}_t)]
& \ \text{ update weights} \\
\hat{\mathbf{y}}_t & \gets & g(\hat{\mathbf p}_t) + \mathbf W_t^{-1}(\mathbf y - \hat{\mathbf p}_t)
& \ \text{ update response}
\end{eqnarray}
\]
and then update parameter estimate (LS sub-problem) \[\hat{\beta}_{t+1} \gets \arg \min_{\beta} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_t - \mathbf X \beta)^T \mathbf W_t (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_t - \mathbf X \beta)\]

Note: larger weights on observations with \(\hat p\) closer to 1/2, i.e. the most difficult to classify (look for variations of this theme) See Section 4.4.1 of ESL

title: Machine learning
text:
GLMs in R
Does glm use Newton-Raphson for every family? Its fitter is IRLS, which is Fisher scoring: Newton with the expected Hessian in place of the actual one. For the default links (binomial-logit, poisson-log, gaussian-identity) the two coincide; for other links it is a close relative. lm is the one-step case
How many iterations? Usually under ten. summary() prints Number of Fisher Scoring iterations
When does it fail? Mostly when there is no finite MLE, the separable case, with coefficients growing at every iteration. The warning fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred is a symptom to investigate, not a diagnosis: a finite MLE with a steep slope triggers it too
Why does the rest of machine learning not do this? Each step solves a \(p \times p\) system. For \(p\) in the millions that is the cost that matters; the next part avoids it

title: Machine learning
text:
Part 2: gradient descent
ML \(\approx\) ERM \(+\) SGD

title: Machine learning
text:
ML tasks as optimization problems
For a given loss function \(\ell(y, f(x))\) and probability model \((X,Y) \sim P\), we want to find a function \(f\) to minimize risk:
\[
\underset{f}{\text{minimize }}\ R(f) = \mathbb E_P[\ell(Y, f(X))]
\]

Math model \(\leftrightarrow\) Statistical model
Assume an i.i.d. sample from \(P\), focus on empirical risk minimization (ERM)
\[
\underset{f \in \mathcal F}{\text{minimize }}\ \hat R_n(f) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(y_i, f(x_i))
\]

We also choose a function class \(\mathcal F\) (or parameter set), i.e. a class of functions \(f\), determining the domain of the optimization

title: Machine learning
text:
Examples: linear regression, GLM
Linear regression. Probability model: errors \(\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\). Loss: squared, \(\ell(y, f(\mathbf x)) = (y - f(\mathbf x))^2\). Class: \(\mathcal F = \{ f_\beta(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^T \beta : \beta \in \mathbb R^{p+1} \}\). Algorithm: OLS, closed form (memorized yet?) \[\underset{\beta \in \mathbb R^{p+1}}{\text{minimize }} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \mathbf x_i^T \beta)^2\]

GLM. Probability model: family = binomial(), poisson(), etc. Loss: negative log-likelihood, so \(\hat R_n(\beta) = -\ell(\beta)/n\). Class: \(\{ g^{-1}(\mathbf x^T \beta) : \beta \in \mathbb R^{p+1} \}\), link \(g\) fixed. Algorithm: ERM (here also MLE), usually by an iterative algorithm \[
\underset{\beta \in \mathbb R^{p+1}}{\text{minimize }} -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \log L(\beta ; y_i | \mathbf x_i)
\]

title: Machine learning
text:
(Iterative) optimization algorithms
Downside of Newton-Raphson: requires second derivatives, including inverting the \(p \times p\) Hessian matrix when optimizing over \(p > 1\) parameters
If \(p\) is large, second-order optimization methods like Newton’s are very costly

First order methods only require computing the \(p \times 1\) gradient vector
Recall that the gradient is a vector in the direction of steepest increase in the parameter space

title: Machine learning
text:
Gradient (steepest) descent
i.e. skiing as fast as possible. Notation: the objective is the empirical risk \(\hat R_n(\beta)\), and \(t\) counts steps

Start at an initial point \(\beta_0\)
For step \(t = 1, \ldots\)

Compute \(\mathbf d_t = \nabla \hat R_n(\beta_{t-1}) \color{#b73779}{\text{ (gradient)}}\)
Update \(\beta_{t} = \beta_{t-1} - \gamma_t \mathbf d_t\)

Until some convergence criteria is satisfied


Where the step size \(\gamma_t > 0\) is made small enough to not “overshoot” and increase the loss, i.e. the loss only decreases

title: Machine learning
text:
Which step size?












The valley: \(f(\beta) = \tfrac12(\beta_1^2 + 10\beta_2^2)\), ten times steeper across than along. Gradient descent from the orange point, \(\gamma = 0.15\)
A few zigzags across, then a crawl along


The valley, same start, three step sizes: \(\gamma = 0.05\), \(\gamma = 0.18\), \(\gamma = 0.21\). For each, commit: converges, converges slowly, or diverges?

title: Machine learning
text:
Three step sizes


































Across the valley the update multiplies \(\beta_2\) by \(1 - 10\gamma\): \(0.5\), \(-0.8\), \(-1.1\)
The largest curvature sets the largest safe step; the smallest sets how long it takes

title: Machine learning
text:
The quadratic case, exactly
One direction with curvature \(a > 0\): \(f(\beta) = \tfrac12 a\beta^2\), \(\nabla f = a\beta\), so
\[
\beta_{t+1} = \beta_t - \gamma a\beta_t = (1 - \gamma a)\,\beta_t, \qquad \beta_t = (1 - \gamma a)^t \beta_0
\]
Converges iff \(|1 - \gamma a| < 1\), i.e. \(0 < \gamma < 2/a\). The step \(\gamma = 1/a\) reaches the minimum in one move

Several directions with curvatures \(a_1 \ge \dots \ge a_d > 0\), one step size for all of them: \(\gamma < 2/a_1\) to converge, and the slowest direction shrinks like \(\max_j |1 - \gamma a_j|^t\), which for \(\gamma \le 1/a_1\) is \((1 - \gamma a_d)^t\)

The largest curvature sets the safe step; the ratio \(a_1/a_d\), the shape of the valley, sets the speed (a direction with \(a_j = 0\), as in least squares with \(p > n\), never moves). For least squares, \(\hat R_n(\beta) = \frac1n\|\mathbf y - \mathbf X\beta\|^2\), the \(a_j\) are the eigenvalues of \(2\mathbf X^T\mathbf X/n\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Reading the gradient










Your loss has stopped falling. Which of the four places are you at, and how would you tell?

title: Machine learning
text:
Landscapes










The saddle: compute the gradient at \((0, 0)\); is it a minimum? One of the three starts is \((0, 1.2)\): where does its path end, and why does it never leave?

Where you start decides where you end. Least squares and logistic regression have one valley (convex); a neural network, later in the course, does not

title: Machine learning
text:
Too big, too small









Too big a step (\(\gamma = 12 > 2/L = 8\)): overshoot and bounce. Too small a gradient (the plateau, \(0.01\)): creep for hundreds of steps, then move all at once. In deep networks the chain rule can make gradients explode or vanish

title: Machine learning
text:
Has it converged?










Three runs, 200 steps, log scales. One has converged, one is on a plateau, one has a step size that shrank to nothing. Which is which?

title: Machine learning
section: Has it converged? The next 600 steps
text:
Has it converged? The next 600 steps










A, the valley: converged. B, the hilly road: its loss fell by 0.005 in 200 steps, its gradient is \(0.01\) and not shrinking; the drop comes at step 445. C, the valley with steps \(0.3 \cdot 0.6^t\): stopped short

title: Machine learning
text:
Directions with zero slope
In \(\mathbb R^d\) the slope is zero in \(d - 1\) directions; whether they lead down is a question of curvature










The gradient is zero. What else would tell you a minimum from a saddle?

title: Machine learning
text:
Curvature

Taylor, to second order, with \(H = \nabla^2 f(x)\) the Hessian: for a smooth \(f\) and a small move \(\delta\), \(f(x + \delta) \approx f(x) + \nabla f(x)^T\delta + \tfrac12\,\delta^T H\,\delta\).

What decides whether a step helps is how fast the gradient changes along it. Take the step \(\delta = -\gamma\nabla f(x)\): \[
f(x - \gamma\nabla f(x)) \approx f(x) \;\underbrace{-\; \gamma\,\|\nabla f(x)\|^2}_{\text{always down}} \;\underbrace{+\; \tfrac12\gamma^2\, \nabla f(x)^T H\, \nabla f(x)}_{\text{the curvature pushes back}}
\]
In the quadratic case the curvature was a fixed number \(a\). On the saddle it is \(+8\) at the two minima and \(-4\) at the saddle point; on the hilly road’s plateau it is about \(0\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Curvature at most \(L\)
If the curvature in every direction is at most \(L\) in size, the push-back is at most \(\tfrac12 L\gamma^2\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\), and then \[
f(x - \gamma\nabla f(x)) \lesssim f(x) - \gamma\underbrace{\big(1 - \tfrac12 L\gamma\big)}_{> 0 \text{ for } \gamma < 2/L}\|\nabla f(x)\|^2
\] The bound is best at \(\gamma = 1/L\): the quadratic case’s rule, in general

To make it a theorem, say “curvature at most \(L\)” about the gradient: Assumption. \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz for some \(L > 0\): \(\|\nabla f(x) - \nabla f(y)\| \le L\,\|x - y\|\) for all \(x, y\)
A quadratic with curvatures \(a_j\) has \(L = \max_j |a_j|\) (the valley: 10); least squares, \(L = 2\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X)/n\); the saddle has no single \(L\) (curvature \(12u^2 - 4\) in \(u\))

title: Machine learning
text:
Descent lemma

Descent lemma. If \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then for every \(x\) \[
f\!\left(x - \tfrac1L\nabla f(x)\right) \le f(x) - \frac{\|\nabla f(x)\|^2}{2L}
\] Every step of size \(1/L\) decreases \(f\) by at least the squared gradient over \(2L\) (strictly, unless \(\nabla f(x) = 0\)).

Says: each step helps, more where the gradient is large. No convexity needed
Does not say: where the steps end, or that they end

title: Machine learning
text:
Cost per step
Second-order methods invert the \(p \times p\) Hessian; first-order methods compute the \(p \times 1\) gradient. For a linear model or a GLM, where one row’s gradient costs about \(p\) operations:









Operations
Once or per step?




Least-squares formula \((\mathbf X^T\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^T\mathbf y\)
about \(np^2 + p^3\)
once


One gradient-descent step
about \(np\)
per step


One step on a random batch of \(b\) rows
about \(bp\)
per step




\(n = 1{,}200{,}000\) images, \(p = 60{,}000{,}000\) parameters. If one image’s gradient cost about \(p\) operations, roughly how many is one full gradient? And one step on a batch of 128?

title: Machine learning
text:
Stochastic/random descent

Instead of computing the gradient of the loss function on the entire dataset, compute it on a random sample


Pick one row \(I\) uniformly at random from \(\{1, \ldots, n\}\) and use its gradient \(\nabla\ell_I(\beta)\) in place of the average over all \(n\) rows. Commit: is it biased for the full gradient \(\nabla\hat R_n(\beta)\), yes or no? And does the descent lemma’s guarantee carry over to a step along it?

title: Machine learning
text:
The stochastic gradient is unbiased

How would you prove this?


With the data and \(\beta\) held fixed, only \(I\) is random, and by linearity of \(\nabla\), \(\mathbb E\) and \(\sum\), \[
\mathbb E_I\big[\nabla\ell_I(\beta)\big] = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac1n\,\nabla\ell_i(\beta) = \nabla\hat R_n(\beta)
\]
Unbiased, whatever the data are. A batch of \(b\) rows drawn with replacement averages \(b\) such gradients: still unbiased
Compute update using one randomly sampled observation, or a randomly sampled subset (“mini-batch SGD”). Correct on average, cheap, and not guaranteed to decrease the training loss on any one step: the descent lemma is about the full gradient

title: Machine learning
text:
The two paths












Simulated least squares, \(n = 200\), two inputs; \(\times\) is the answer
Blue: 30 full gradient steps, \(6{,}000\) row-gradients. Orange: 600 single-row steps, \(600\) row-gradients, step \(0.05/(1 + t/100)\)
A tenth of the work, and it never sits still. The step must shrink, but not so fast that it stops short like panel C (Robbins and Monro, 1951)

parameters in the network described in the paper, fitted in five to six days on two gaming graphics cards by stochastic gradient descent, on a loss with every feature of part 3

title: Machine learning
text:
Early stopping
Optimization time = complexity

For many optimization algorithms the model fits closer to the training data the longer the optimization algorithm runs



e.g. the more steps of (stochastic) gradient descent used in combination with a flexible function class
e.g. the more steps of forward stepwise (adding more predictor variables)



Idea: control model complexity by stopping the algorithm before convergence
This is early stopping – we’ll come back to it later

title: Machine learning
section: Stopping early: choose a stopping point
text:
Stopping early: choose a stopping point












The wide regression: simulated least squares, \(n = 80\), \(p = 60\), noise sd 3, from \(\beta_0 = \mathbf 0\) with step \(1/2L\)
The training error, the number the algorithm minimizes, falls at every step and is still falling at 300

You may stop the algorithm at any step. Which one, and why?

title: Machine learning
text:
Stopping early: the held-out error












The wide regression scored on 2,000 new rows from the same model: the held-out error falls, turns at step 7, and ends far above its minimum
Every diagnostic in part 3 was computed from the training loss, and every one said “keep going”

title: Machine learning
section: Where the error comes from, this time
text:
Where the error comes from, this time
Three functions. \(f^\star = \arg\min_f R(f)\): the best of all (squared loss: the conditional mean, by the optimal model theorem). \(f_{\mathcal F} = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal F} R(f)\): the best in the class, fixed once \(\mathcal F\) is. \(\hat f = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal F} \hat R_n(f)\): what the data give, random
Bias–variance decomposition, ERM form. Both underbraced terms are \(\ge 0\): \[
R(\hat f) = R(f^\star) + \underbrace{\big[R(\hat f) - R(f_{\mathcal F})\big]}_{\text{estimation}} + \underbrace{\big[R(f_{\mathcal F}) - R(f^\star)\big]}_{\text{approximation}}
\]
Proof: exercise 2

title: Machine learning
text:
No free lunch
No free lunch (stated). No method has lower error than every other on every distribution. Binary classification, 0–1 loss: for any learning method and any training size \(n\), on a domain with at least \(2n\) points there is a distribution for which a perfect predictor exists and the method’s expected error (over training samples) is at least \(1/4\)
Says: choosing a method is an assumption about the world; the ERM form shows where one such assumption enters, the class \(\mathcal F\) chosen before the data
Does not say: all methods are equally good

In the gapminder competition, a line and \(k\) nearest neighbors often scored within a standard error of each other. A fact about the methods, or about the data?

title: Machine learning
section: Conclusion: optimization in ML is a big topic
text:
Conclusion: optimization in ML is a big topic
The fitting algorithm
Each small step helps when curvature is bounded; where it ends, and whether it has ended, the guarantee does not say
Training loss
Every diagnostic today was computed from the training loss. A lower training loss is numerical progress; whether it is a better model is a different question
Stopping at the right amount of complexity
Maybe the most important part! Next lecture

title: Machine learning
text: Part 2: ridge and lasso

title: Machine learning
text:
Regularized (i.e. penalized) regression
Motivation: early stopping made the number of gradient-descent steps a knob that controlled how far the fit went. Can the knob be written into the objective instead?

For some penalty function \(\mathcal P_\lambda\), which depends on a tuning parameter \(\lambda\), the estimator
\[\hat \beta_\lambda = \arg \min_\beta \| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|^2_2 + \mathcal P_\lambda(\beta)\] is “regularized” or shrunk (shranken?) toward values that decrease the penalty. Often \(\mathcal P_\lambda = \lambda \| \cdot \|\) for some norm


Many ML methods are optimizing “loss + penalty”

title: Machine learning
text:
Ridge (i.e. L2 penalized) regression

Originally motivated by problems where \(\mathbf X^T \mathbf X\) is uninvertible (or badly conditioned, i.e. almost uninvertible)
If \(p > n\) then this always happens
Least squares estimator is undefined or numerically unstable

For some constant \(\lambda > 0\), \[\text{minimize } \| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|^2_2 + \lambda \| \beta \|^2\] Shrinks coefficients \(\hat \beta\) toward 0
Larger coefficients are penalized more (squared penalty)

title: Machine learning
text:
The ridge estimator


Set the gradient of \(\| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|^2 + \lambda \| \beta \|^2\) to zero (exercise 2): \[
(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X + \lambda I)\,\hat\beta_\lambda = \mathbf X^T\mathbf y
\] \[
\hat\beta_\lambda = (\mathbf X^T\mathbf X + \lambda I)^{-1}\mathbf X^T\mathbf y
\]
\(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X + \lambda I\) is invertible for every \(\lambda > 0\), whatever \(n\) and \(p\): one solution even when \(p > n\)
\(\lambda \to 0\): least squares (when it exists). \(\lambda \to \infty\): \(\hat\beta_\lambda \to \mathbf 0\)










\(\hat\beta_\lambda\) against \(-\log\lambda\): the 16 standardized inputs (eleven numeric, five genre dummies), six named

title: Machine learning
section: Lasso vs ridge: L1 vs L2 norm penalties
text:
Lasso vs ridge: L1 vs L2 norm penalties
A simple diff to remember lasso/ridge is via the penalty/constraint (1-norm instead of 2-norm). Lasso is
\[\text{minimize } \frac{1}{2n}\| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|_2^2 \text{ s. t. } \| \beta \|_1 \leq t\] where \(\| \beta \|_1 = \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j|\). Lagrangian form
\[\text{minimize } \frac{1}{2n} \| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|_2^2 + \lambda \| \beta \|_1\]
The lasso often gives estimates with many coefficients set to exactly zero

title: Machine learning
section: Lasso vs ridge: solution paths of \(\hat \beta\)
text:
Lasso vs ridge: solution paths of \(\hat \beta\)






















Spotify, the same 16 inputs, large \(\lambda\) on the left. The lasso’s coefficients are exactly zero over whole ranges of \(\lambda\) and enter one at a time; ridge’s are never zero

title: Machine learning
section: Two ways to estimate a curve
text:
Two ways to estimate a curve
Life expectancy on GDP per capita, 142 countries in 2007 (no log this time). Two ways to turn a line into a curve









Average nearby (\(k\)-NN; a kernel weights by distance instead of cutting at \(k\)). Fit a basis: fixed curves, combined by least squares. We now focus on the second

title: Machine learning
section: A spline is regression on basis functions
text:
A spline is regression on basis functions












A basis: fixed functions \(b_1(x), \ldots, b_J(x)\) of one input, combined by least squares: \[
f(x) = \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^J \beta_j\, b_j(x)
\] linear in \(\beta\): ns(gdpPercap, df = J) builds the \(J\) columns for lm()
A natural cubic spline: cubic pieces joined smoothly at knots, linear beyond the ends. The basis functions are the bends the knots allow; lm adds \(\beta_0\)

title: Machine learning
section: The basis size is the knob
text:
The basis size is the knob









Small \(J\): almost a line. Large \(J\): the curve follows the points, and at \(J = n\) it passes through every one (training error zero). Which \(J\)? The selection set, as for \(k\) and \(\lambda\). Later in the course: a penalty on wiggliness instead, with \(J\) as a ceiling

title: Machine learning
text:
Additive modeling assumption

Linearity assumption: each predictor has a coefficient

\[g(\mathbb E[\mathbf y | \mathbf X]) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \mathbf x_1 + \beta_2 \mathbf x_2 + \cdots + \beta_p \mathbf x_p\]

Additivity assumption: each predictor has a function

\[g(\mathbb E[\mathbf y | \mathbf X]) = \beta_0 + f_1( \mathbf x_1) + f_2( \mathbf x_2) + \cdots + f_p(\mathbf x_p)\]
Includes linear models as special case if \(f_j(\mathbf x_j) = \beta_j \mathbf x_j\)
Today each \(f_j\) is a spline with \(J\) basis functions, so the whole model is one least-squares fit on \(pJ\) columns: lm(y ~ ns(x1, J) + ns(x2, J) + ...). The GAM in the reading is this model, with a link

“Stratification of the feature space”
Input: subset of data

The 142 countries resampled eight times, one fit per resample (blue). The trees’ cutoffs jump with the sample; the splines barely move. Orange: the eight trees’ average

title: Machine learning
text:
A GLM of GLMs
A GLM: the inverse link applied to a linear predictor, \(g^{-1}(\mathbf x^T\beta)\). Now iterate it












Hidden unit \(k\): a logistic regression of the inputs, with its own weights, \(h_k(x) = g^{-1}(w_{k0} + w_k^T x)\), \(g\) the logit link
Output: a linear regression on the hidden units, \(f(x) = \beta_0 + \sum_{k=1}^M \beta_k\, h_k(x)\) (logistic, for a label)
A GLM whose inputs are \(M\) GLMs. Iterate again: a deep network

title: Machine learning
text:
Fitting and tuning a network
How it is fitted. All \(M(p + 1) + M + 1\) weights at once, by gradient-based optimization of a loss that is not convex: many valleys, with plateaus and saddles between them. Today’s fits: nnet(), a quasi-Newton method
The knob. \(M\), the number of hidden units, chosen on the selection tracks. Depth, and a penalty on the weights: later knobs. In R, nnet(size = M, linout = TRUE)

title: Machine learning
text:
Comparison across three functional structures
\(p = 10\) inputs on \([-1, 1]\), \(y = f^\star(x) + \varepsilon\), \(\sigma^2 = 1\). Three truths:


A, sparse linear: \(f^\star(x) = 2x_1 - 1.5x_2 + x_3\)
B, additive smooth: \(f^\star(x) = 1.5\,[f_1(x_1) + f_2(x_2) + f_3(x_3)]\): \(f_1 = -1 + 2x - x^2\), \(f_2 = \sin \pi x\), \(f_3 = e^{-5(x - 1/2)^2}\)
C, one step, two inputs at once: \(f^\star(x) = 4 \cdot \mathbf 1\{x_1 > 0,\ x_2 > 0\}\)


One task. 300 training, 100 selection, 2,000 test rows. Seven competitors: least squares; lasso (\(\lambda\)); \(k\)-NN (\(k\)); additive splines (\(J\)); a tree (depth); a forest; a network (\(M\)). Knobs chosen on the selection rows, refit on both, scored once

For each truth: which family wins, which loses, and why?

title: Machine learning
text:
Four dimensions, not one









Axis
The question about \(f^\star\)
Who bets which way




wide or tall
how \(p\) compares with \(n\)
least squares needs full column rank for one fit; the additive fit and a network overfit when \(n\) is small; ridge and the lasso fit at any \(p\)


sparse or dense
how many inputs matter
the lasso bets few; least squares and ridge spread the fit over all; a forest tolerates idle inputs, \(k\)-NN is hurt by them


smooth or discontinuous
how \(f^\star\) moves with each input
splines, \(k\)-NN and networks bet smooth; trees bet on steps


additive or interactive
whether inputs act separately
the additive fit bets separately; trees, forests, \(k\)-NN and networks allow interactions




Four separate questions, not one scale from simple to complex. A family is a bet on the answers. A selection set shows which bet did best on these data

Curse of dimensionality: \(k\)-NN last on truths A and B, seven idle inputs. No free lunch theorem: no family won every truth, and none can.

title: Machine learning
text:
Training error and risk
On most rows of the leaderboards the training MSE sat below the test or selection MSE; on a few it sat above. Luck, or a law?
Training data i.i.d. from the population; a class \(\mathcal F\) fixed before the data; \(f_{\mathcal F}\) the best in \(\mathcal F\) (smallest \(R\)); \(\hat f\) the empirical risk minimizer (smallest \(\hat R_n\) over \(\mathcal F\))

Three numbers: \(\mathbb E[\hat R_n(\hat f)]\), \(R(f_{\mathcal F})\), \(\mathbb E[R(\hat f)]\). Put them in order, and write down what you used.

title: Machine learning
text:
Optimism theorem
A function fixed before the data has an unbiased training error; \(\hat f\) was chosen to make its own small, and cannot beat \(f_{\mathcal F}\) on the population
Training data i.i.d.; \(\mathcal F\) fixed before the data; \(\hat f\) the empirical risk minimizer over \(\mathcal F\); \(f_{\mathcal F}\) the best in \(\mathcal F\) (risks finite, minimizers exist). Then \[
\mathbb E\big[\hat R_n(\hat f)\big] \;\le\; R(f_{\mathcal F}) \;\le\; \mathbb E\big[R(\hat f)\big]
\]

Training error underestimates the risk: on average it is below the best risk the class can reach, and the fitted model’s risk above it. A test set estimates \(R(\hat f)\); its average is the right end.

Proof: exercise 1

Conclusion
Each family is a bet on the shape of \(f^\star\)
A plane, a sparse plane, a sum of curves, a set of rectangles, an average of many, a composition. Four questions about the world decide which bet pays
The data split decides what you may believe
Fit on the training rows, tune on the selection rows, open the test set once
Training error underestimates risk
Optimistic on average for every minimizer over a fixed class

knn_predict <- function(Xnew, Xtrain, ytrain, k) {

title: Week 7 seminar
text:
Before the seminar

The lecture stated the bias–variance decomposition in ridge form and left its proof to you (exercise 1). It proved the \(k\)-nearest-neighbor rate from a stated lemma; exercise 2 is that proof again, with the slides closed. Do both on paper before the seminar; the seminar’s problems are variations on them. You may use, without proof: linearity of expectation; that the variance of a sum of independent variables is the sum of their variances; that for a symmetric matrix \(\mathbf A\) the gradient of \(\beta^T\mathbf A\beta\) is \(2\mathbf A\beta\) and its Hessian is \(2\mathbf A\); and the tower property, \(\mathbb E[W] = \mathbb E\big[\mathbb E[W \mid V]\big]\). Throughout, assume that every expectation that appears exists.






WarningHints



Each exercise has hints, collapsed below it. Do not open a hint unless you have been stuck for at least a few minutes, and open them in order. Solutions are shown in the seminar if you ask.


Exercise 1 (bias–variance decomposition, ridge form). \(\mathbf X\) is \(n \times p\) with orthonormal columns, \(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X = \mathbf I\) (so \(p \le n\); the lecture’s identity design is the case \(\mathbf X = \mathbf I\), \(n = p\)). The outcome is \(\mathbf y = \mathbf X\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon\) with \(\beta\) fixed and unknown and the \(\varepsilon_i\) independent, mean \(0\), variance \(\sigma^2 > 0\). Expectations are over \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\), with \(\mathbf X\) fixed. The least-squares estimator solves the normal equations \(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X\beta = \mathbf X^T\mathbf y\), so here \(\hat\beta = \mathbf X^T\mathbf y\). For \(\lambda > 0\) the ridge estimator \(\hat\beta_\lambda\) minimizes \(\|\mathbf y - \mathbf X\beta\|^2 + \lambda\|\beta\|^2\).

Show that \(\hat\beta\) is unbiased, \(\mathbb E[\hat\beta] = \beta\), and that each coordinate has variance \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_j) = \sigma^2\). Deduce \(\mathbb E\|\hat\beta - \beta\|^2 = p\sigma^2\).
Derive the stationarity condition of the ridge objective, \((\mathbf X^T\mathbf X + \lambda\mathbf I)\beta = \mathbf X^T\mathbf y\), and show that in this design \(\hat\beta_\lambda = \hat\beta/(1 + \lambda)\).
Compute the bias \(\mathbb E[\hat\beta_{\lambda,j}] - \beta_j\) and the variance \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_{\lambda,j})\) of each coordinate, and show \[
\mathrm{MSE}(\lambda) = \mathbb E\|\hat\beta_\lambda - \beta\|^2 = \sum_{j=1}^p \frac{\lambda^2\beta_j^2 + \sigma^2}{(1 + \lambda)^2}.
\]
Differentiate \(\mathrm{MSE}(\lambda)\) and show that its derivative at \(\lambda = 0\) is \(-2p\sigma^2\), whatever \(\beta\) is. Conclude that for every \(\beta\) there is a \(\lambda > 0\) with \(\mathrm{MSE}(\lambda) < \mathrm{MSE}(0) = p\sigma^2\).
For \(\beta \ne \mathbf 0\), find the \(\lambda\) that minimizes \(\mathrm{MSE}(\lambda)\), in terms of \(\sigma^2\) and \(\|\beta\|^2/p\), and the minimum value. What happens when \(\beta = \mathbf 0\)? Why can this \(\lambda\) not be used in practice?







NoteHint 1






\(\hat\beta = \mathbf X^T(\mathbf X\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \beta + \mathbf X^T\boldsymbol\varepsilon\). What are the mean vector and the covariance matrix of \(\mathbf X^T\boldsymbol\varepsilon\)? The covariance matrix of \(\mathbf A\boldsymbol\varepsilon\) is \(\mathbf A\,\mathrm{Cov}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)\,\mathbf A^T\).










NoteHint 2





(b), (c) With \(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X = \mathbf I\) the stationarity condition reads \((1 + \lambda)\beta = \mathbf X^T\mathbf y\). For a constant \(c\), the estimator \(c\hat\beta_j\) has bias \((c - 1)\beta_j\) and variance \(c^2\sigma^2\).









NoteHint 3





(d), (e) Write \(\mathrm{MSE}(\lambda) = (\lambda^2\|\beta\|^2 + p\sigma^2)/(1 + \lambda)^2\) and use the quotient rule; after cancelling a factor \((1 + \lambda)\) the numerator of the derivative is \(2\lambda\|\beta\|^2 - 2p\sigma^2\).



Exercise 2 (the \(k\)-nearest-neighbor rate, with the slides closed). Inputs \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) i.i.d. uniform on \([0, 1]^p\); outcomes \(y_i = f^\star(x_i) + \varepsilon_i\) with the \(\varepsilon_i\) independent of each other and of the inputs, mean \(0\), variance \(\sigma^2\); \(f^\star\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(|f^\star(x) - f^\star(x')| \le L\|x - x'\|\), with \(L > 0\) and \(\sigma^2 > 0\). For a point \(x_0\), \(r_k(x_0)\) is the distance from \(x_0\) to its \(k\)th nearest input, \(x_{(1)}, \ldots, x_{(k)}\) are the \(k\) nearest inputs, and \(\hat f_k(x_0) = \tfrac1k\sum_{l=1}^k y_{(l)}\) is the mean of their outcomes. You may use the lemma stated in the lecture: for \(x_0\) away from the boundary, \(\mathbb E[r_k(x_0)^2] \le C_p (k/n)^{2/p}\), with \(C_p\) depending on \(p\) only.

Conditional on the inputs, write \(\hat f_k(x_0) - f^\star(x_0)\) as the sum of a term that depends only on \(f^\star\) and the inputs and a term that depends on the noise. Show that the first term is at most \(L\,r_k(x_0)\) in absolute value.
Show that, conditional on the inputs, the noise term has mean \(0\) and variance \(\sigma^2/k\).
Deduce \(\mathbb E\big[(\hat f_k(x_0) - f^\star(x_0))^2 \mid \text{inputs}\big] \le L^2 r_k(x_0)^2 + \sigma^2/k\), then take the expectation over the inputs and apply the lemma.
Treat \(k\) as a continuous variable and minimize the bound \(C_p L^2 (k/n)^{2/p} + \sigma^2/k\) over \(k\). Show that the minimizer is \(k = c\,n^{2/(p+2)}\) for a constant \(c\) that depends on \(p\), \(L\), \(\sigma^2\) and \(C_p\) but not on \(n\), and that the minimized bound is proportional to \(n^{-2/(p+2)}\).
By what factor must \(n\) grow to halve the bound when \(p = 10\)? When \(p = 1\)?







NoteHint 1






\(\hat f_k(x_0) - f^\star(x_0) = \tfrac1k\sum_l \big(f^\star(x_{(l)}) - f^\star(x_0)\big) + \tfrac1k\sum_l \varepsilon_{(l)}\). Every one of the \(k\) nearest inputs is within \(r_k(x_0)\) of \(x_0\).










NoteHint 2





(b), (c) Given the inputs, which \(k\) noise terms are averaged is fixed, and they are independent with variance \(\sigma^2\). For (c), expand \((a + b)^2\) with \(a\) the first term and \(b\) the noise term; what is the conditional mean of the cross term?









NoteHint 3






Write the bound as \(A k^{2/p} + B/k\) with \(A = C_p L^2 n^{-2/p}\) and \(B = \sigma^2\). The derivative is zero when \((2A/p)\,k^{2/p - 1} = B/k^2\), that is, \(k^{(p+2)/p} = pB/(2A)\).

title: Week 7 seminar
text:
Problems

Problem 1 (soft thresholding). One coordinate of an orthonormal design: \(z\) is the least-squares coefficient, a number, and \(b\) the estimate. The lasso’s one-coordinate objective is \(\tfrac12(z - b)^2 + \lambda|b|\) with \(\lambda > 0\).

Show that the minimizer is \(\hat b = \mathrm{sign}(z)\,(|z| - \lambda)_+\): \(z\) moved toward zero by \(\lambda\), stopping at zero.
The lecture writes the lasso objective as \(\|\mathbf y - \mathbf X\beta\|^2 + \lambda\|\beta\|_1\), without the \(\tfrac12\). In the orthonormal design (\(\mathbf X\) is \(n \times p\) with \(\mathbf X^T\mathbf X = \mathbf I\)), show that this objective splits into one problem per coefficient, and find by how much that lasso moves each coefficient toward zero.

Problem 2 (the distance lemma in one dimension). \(n\) inputs i.i.d. uniform on \([0, 1]\), the point \(x_0 = \tfrac12\), and \(r_1\) the distance from \(x_0\) to the nearest input.

For \(0 \le r \le \tfrac12\), show that \(\mathbb P(r_1 > r) = (1 - 2r)^n\).
Compute \(\mathbb E[r_1]\). You may use \(\mathbb E[W] = \int_0^\infty \mathbb P(W > w)\,dw\) for \(W \ge 0\).
Compute \(\mathbb E[r_1^2]\) (use \(\mathbb E[W^2] = \int_0^\infty 2w\,\mathbb P(W > w)\,dw\)) and compare it with the lemma’s \((k/n)^{2/p}\) at \(k = 1\), \(p = 1\).
Let \(N(r)\) be the number of inputs within distance \(r\) of \(x_0\). What is its distribution? The distance \(r_k\) to the \(k\)th nearest input satisfies \(r_k > r\) exactly when \(N(r) < k\). Without computing, explain why \(r_k\) is about \(k/(2n)\) when \(k\) is much smaller than \(n\).
In \(p\) dimensions a ball of radius \(r\) has volume \(c_p r^p\). Repeat the argument of (d) to find the order of \(r_k\), and hence of \(r_k^2\), in \(p\) dimensions. Why does the lemma say “away from the boundary”?

Problem 3 (the smoothing penalty as weighted ridge). A one-input curve written in a spline basis, \(f(x) = \sum_{j=1}^J \beta_j b_j(x)\): the \(b_j\) are twice differentiable and their span contains the constant and the linear functions. \(\lambda \ge 0\). \(\mathbf B\) is the \(n \times J\) matrix with \(B_{ij} = b_j(x_i)\), and \(\boldsymbol\Omega\) the \(J \times J\) matrix with \(\Omega_{jk} = \int b_j''(x)\,b_k''(x)\,dx\). The smoothing objective is \(\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - f(x_i))^2 + \lambda\int f''(x)^2\,dx\).

Show that \(\int f''(x)^2\,dx = \beta^T\boldsymbol\Omega\beta\), so the objective is \(\|\mathbf y - \mathbf B\beta\|^2 + \lambda\beta^T\boldsymbol\Omega\beta\). Show that \(\boldsymbol\Omega\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
Show that the minimizer satisfies \((\mathbf B^T\mathbf B + \lambda\boldsymbol\Omega)\beta = \mathbf B^T\mathbf y\), and that \(\mathbf B^T\mathbf B + \lambda\boldsymbol\Omega\) is invertible when \(\mathbf B\) has full column rank.
Suppose \(\mathbf B\) has full column rank and the basis has been chosen so that \(\mathbf B^T\mathbf B = \mathbf I\) and \(\boldsymbol\Omega = \mathrm{diag}(w_1, \ldots, w_J)\) with every \(w_j \ge 0\) (such a basis exists; the lecture’s figure showed four of its functions, ordered by wiggliness). With \(\mathbf z = \mathbf B^T\mathbf y\), show that \(\hat\beta_j = z_j/(1 + \lambda w_j)\).
Which basis functions have \(w_j = 0\)? What happens to their coefficients as \(\lambda \to \infty\), and to the others? What does the fit tend to?

Problem 4 (how many folds?). \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\) are i.i.d. with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), and \(K\) divides \(n\). The method predicts a new \(Y\) (independent of the \(y_i\), with the same distribution) by the mean of the rows it is fitted on, with squared-error loss. \(K\)-fold cross-validation scores each \(y_i\) against the mean of the \(n - n/K\) rows outside its fold, and averages the \(n\) losses.

Show that the mean \(\bar Y_m\) of \(m\) such rows has expected loss \(\mathbb E[(Y - \bar Y_m)^2] = \sigma^2(1 + 1/m)\) on a new \(Y\). Deduce that the \(K\)-fold CV score has expectation \(\sigma^2\big(1 + \tfrac{K}{(K-1)n}\big)\), and that it overestimates the expected loss of the mean fitted on all \(n\) rows by \(\tfrac{\sigma^2}{(K-1)n}\). Compare \(K = 2\), \(K = 10\) and \(K = n\).
Leave-one-out is \(K = n\). With \(\bar y\) the mean of all \(n\) rows and \(\bar y_{(-i)}\) the mean without row \(i\), show that \(y_i - \bar y_{(-i)} = \tfrac{n}{n-1}(y_i - \bar y)\), so that the leave-one-out score needs only one fit: \(\mathrm{CV}_{(n)} = \tfrac{n}{n-1}\,s^2\) with \(s^2 = \tfrac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2\). Check its expectation against (a).
For tuning, the question is what \(K\) does to the choice. Take \(k\)-NN with \(p\) inputs, and suppose, as an idealization, that fitted on \(m\) rows its excess risk (its expected loss minus the noise variance \(\sigma^2\)) is exactly \(g_m(k) = a\,(k/m)^{2/p} + \sigma^2/k\), with \(a > 0\) and \(k\) treated as a continuous variable. First, show that \(g_m\) has a unique minimizer \(k^\star(m)\), proportional to \(m^{2/(p+2)}\). Second, suppose \(K\)-fold cross-validation measured \(g_m\) without error at \(m = n(K-1)/K\), so that it chooses \(k^\star(m)\), which is then used with all \(n\) rows. Show that this choice is \(\rho\,k^\star(n)\) with \(\rho = \big(\tfrac{K-1}{K}\big)^{2/(p+2)}\), and that \[
\frac{g_n(\rho\,k^\star(n))}{g_n(k^\star(n))} = \frac{p\,\rho^{2/p} + 2/\rho}{p + 2}.
\] Third, show that this ratio is \(1 + (1 - \rho)^2/p\) up to terms of order \((1 - \rho)^3\), and say why there is no term of first order. Evaluate the ratio for \(p = 1\) and \(p = 11\) with \(K = 2\) and \(K = 10\): what does it say about the choice of \(K\) for tuning, as against for reporting the error?

title: Week 7 seminar
text:
Coding


1. The cross-validation pipeline

The structures seminar’s task: predict a track’s popularity from ten audio features and its release year, squared loss (data note), genre left out. The same split as there: 5,000 training, 2,000 tuning and 3,000 test tracks, one seed. Today the tuning tracks are a check on cross-validation and the test tracks are not opened; the last step uses a split by year of the 7,000 development tracks instead of the random one.

feat <- c("danceability", "energy", "loudness", "speechiness", "acousticness",
          "instrumentalness", "liveness", "valence", "tempo", "duration_min", "release_year")
sp_file <- read_csv("https://ml4ds.com/files/spotify_tracks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  distinct(track_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>          # one row per track
  mutate(duration_min = duration_ms / 60000)
sp <- sp_file |> select(track_popularity, all_of(feat))   # the outcome and the eleven inputs
set.seed(310)   # change this number: a different split, and different numbers below
id <- sample(nrow(sp))
sp_train <- sp[id[1:5000], ]
sp_tune <- sp[id[5001:7000], ]
sp_test <- sp[id[7001:10000], ]
y_train <- sp_train$track_popularity
y_tune <- sp_tune$track_popularity
K <- 10          # folds, for the whole seminar

Step 1. One function for every pipeline. cv_mse(fit_predict, d, fold) takes a function fit_predict(tr, ho) that fits on the rows tr and returns predictions for the rows ho, the data d, and a vector fold giving each row’s fold. For each fold it fits on the other folds, predicts the held-out fold, and stores each held-out row’s squared loss; it returns the mean of all the losses, so every row is scored once. Assign the folds at random, the same folds for every method today.

fold <- sample(rep(1:K, length.out = nrow(sp_train)))   # each row's fold, 500 rows in each
cv_mse <- function(fit_predict, d, fold) {
  loss <- rep(NA, nrow(d))
  for (k in 1:max(fold)) {
    # tr <- ____                        # the rows whose fold is not k
    # ho <- ____                        # the rows whose fold is k
    # loss[fold == k] <- (ho$track_popularity - ____)^2
  }
  mean(loss)
}

Checkpoint (run it; if it stops, fix step 1 before going on): the mean of the training rows, as a pipeline, should score close to the variance of y_train.

mean_fp <- function(tr, ho) rep(mean(tr$track_popularity), nrow(ho))
stopifnot(abs(cv_mse(mean_fp, sp_train, fold) - var(y_train)) < 5)

Step 2. The CV curve for \(k\) nearest neighbors. knn_fp(k) returns a fit_predict function for one value of \(k\): it standardizes the inputs with the fold’s training rows (the means and standard deviations of tr, applied to both tr and ho), then calls knn_predict(). Run it over ks, find the \(k\) at the minimum, and draw the curve.

ks <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500)
knn_fp <- function(k) function(tr, ho) {
  mu <- colMeans(tr[, feat]); s <- apply(tr[, feat], 2, sd)
  # knn_predict(____, ____, tr$track_popularity, k)
}
# cv_knn <- sapply(ks, function(k) ____)
# k_cv <- ____
# plot: cv_knn against ks, log scale on k

Question 1. The structures seminar chose \(k\) on the 2,000 tuning tracks instead. The chunk below scores the same ks that way, from fits on all 5,000 training tracks. Compare the two curves: where is each minimum, and how far apart are the two curves at the bottom? Which curve do you trust more, and what did each cost in rows? The tuning scores come with a standard error (the lecture’s formula); why does cv_mse() not return one?

mu <- colMeans(sp_train[, feat]); s <- apply(sp_train[, feat], 2, sd)
X_train <- scale(sp_train[, feat], mu, s); X_tune <- scale(sp_tune[, feat], mu, s)
tune_knn <- sapply(ks, function(k) mse(y_tune, knn_predict(X_tune, X_train, y_train, k)))
tune_se <- sapply(ks, function(k) se_loss(y_tune, knn_predict(X_tune, X_train, y_train, k)))
rbind(k = ks, cv = round(cv_knn), tune = round(tune_knn), tune_se = round(tune_se))

Step 3. The lasso through the same pipeline. lasso_fp(lam) standardizes inside the fold, fits the path on the training rows and predicts at the one \(\lambda\) lam. The sequence lam_seq comes from a fit on all 5,000 training tracks, so every fold uses the same values (a small step outside the folds, which cv.glmnet() takes too). Run the pipeline over lam_seq and find \(\lambda\) at the minimum.

lam_seq <- glmnet(X_train, y_train, standardize = FALSE, nlambda = 20)$lambda
lasso_fp <- function(lam) function(tr, ho) {
  mu <- colMeans(tr[, feat]); s <- apply(tr[, feat], 2, sd)
  fit <- glmnet(scale(tr[, feat], mu, s), tr$track_popularity, lambda = lam_seq, standardize = FALSE)
  as.vector(predict(fit, scale(ho[, feat], mu, s), s = lam))
}
# cv_lasso <- ____
# lam_cv <- ____

Question 2. cv.glmnet() does the same with its own code. Run it on X_train (standardized once, on all 5,000 training rows, which is why the call says standardize = FALSE) with the same folds (foldid = fold) and compare lambda.min with your lam_cv. Its lambda.1se is larger: what rule chose it, and how many coefficients does the lasso set to zero at each of the two?

cvg <- cv.glmnet(X_train, y_train, foldid = fold, standardize = FALSE)
c(lambda.min = signif(cvg$lambda.min, 2), lambda.1se = signif(cvg$lambda.1se, 2), lam_cv = signif(lam_cv, 2))
c(zero_at_min = sum(coef(cvg, s = "lambda.min")[-1] == 0), zero_at_1se = sum(coef(cvg, s = "lambda.1se")[-1] == 0))

Question 3 (how many folds?). Ten folds is a convention. The chunk below reruns the CV curves of \(k\)-NN and of the lasso with \(K = 2, 5, 10\) and \(50\) folds, twice for each \(K\) with fresh random folds, the same folds for both methods. lasso_curve() does for the lasso’s whole path what cv_mse() does for one method, on X_train, standardized once as in question 2 (cv.glmnet() refuses fewer than three folds). The \(k\)-NN curves take a minute or more, so read the questions while it runs. (a) With \(K\) folds, each fit uses what share of the 5,000 training tracks? Which \(K\) should estimate the error of a fit on all 5,000 most pessimistically? Do the curves agree, and for which method is the effect larger? (b) For which \(K\) do the scores move most between the two draws of folds? (c) The best \(k\) for \(k\)-NN grows with the number of fitting rows (where the rate’s two terms balance, \(k\) is proportional to \(n^{2/(p+2)}\)); the best \(\lambda\) for the lasso, on glmnet’s scale, shrinks, since the chance correlations the penalty has to overrule shrink as rows are added. Which way should a small \(K\) push each choice, toward a more or a less complex fit, and by about how much for \(k\)-NN here, with \(p = 11\)? Do the chosen values show it? (d) Leave-one-out cross-validation is \(K = n\). What would it cost, and what would it gain?

Ks <- c(2, 5, 10, 50)
ks_K <- c(20, 50, 100, 200)
lam_path <- glmnet(X_train, y_train, standardize = FALSE)$lambda   # cv.glmnet()'s path in question 2
lam_K <- lam_path[lam_path <= 1]
lasso_curve <- function(fold, lam) {          # the lasso's CV MSE at every lambda, for any folds
  loss <- matrix(NA, nrow(X_train), length(lam))
  for (k in 1:max(fold)) {
    fit <- glmnet(X_train[fold != k, ], y_train[fold != k], lambda = lam, standardize = FALSE)
    loss[fold == k, ] <- (y_train[fold == k] - predict(fit, X_train[fold == k, ]))^2
  }
  colMeans(loss)
}
cv_by_K <- map_dfr(Ks, function(K_try) map_dfr(1:2, function(draw) {
  # fresh folds for each K and each draw, the same for both methods
  fold_K <- sample(rep(1:K_try, length.out = nrow(sp_train)))
  bind_rows(
    tibble(method = "k-NN", knob = ks_K,
           mse = sapply(ks_K, function(k) cv_mse(knn_fp(k), sp_train, fold_K))),
    tibble(method = "lasso", knob = lam_K, mse = lasso_curve(fold_K, lam_K))) |>
    mutate(K = K_try, draw = draw)
}))
by_K <- cv_by_K |> group_by(method, K, draw) |>
  summarize(chosen = signif(knob[which.min(mse)], 2), min_cv_mse = round(min(mse), 1),
            .groups = "drop")
by_K |> pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = c(chosen, min_cv_mse))
ggplot(cv_by_K, aes(knob, mse, colour = factor(K), group = interaction(K, draw))) +
  geom_line() + scale_x_log10() + facet_wrap(~ method, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "k for k-NN, lambda for the lasso", y = "CV MSE", colour = "K",
       title = "two draws of folds for each K")



2. Learning curves and the rate

The lecture’s rate says how the error of \(k\) nearest neighbors falls with \(n\): the bound on the squared estimation error at a point is proportional to \(n^{-2/(p+2)}\), with \(p\) the number of inputs, at the best \(k\). The simulation below checks it. Inputs uniform on \([0, 1]^p\) for \(p = 1, 2, 5, 10\); the truth \(f^\star(x) = \sum_{j=1}^p \sin(2\pi x_j)/\sqrt p\), which depends on every input and is Lipschitz; noise with variance \(1\). For each \(n\) it fits \(k\)-NN at every \(k\) in ks, measures the squared estimation error \(\tfrac1{400}\sum (\hat f_k(x_0) - f^\star(x_0))^2\) on 400 new points (against the truth, not the noisy outcome), averages over three draws of the training data, and keeps the best \(k\). The chunk takes about 40 seconds.

f_star <- function(X) rowSums(sin(2 * pi * X)) / sqrt(ncol(X))
ps <- c(1, 2, 5, 10)
ns <- c(100, 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200, 6400)
ks_lc <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500)
lc <- map_dfr(ps, function(p) map_dfr(ns, function(n) {
  err <- rowMeans(sapply(1:3, function(rep) {
    X <- matrix(runif(n * p), n, p); y <- f_star(X) + rnorm(n)
    X0 <- matrix(runif(400 * p), 400, p); f0 <- f_star(X0)
    sapply(ks_lc, function(k) if (k <= n / 2) mean((knn_predict(X0, X, y, k) - f0)^2) else NA)
  }))
  tibble(p = p, n = n, k_best = ks_lc[which.min(err)], mse = min(err, na.rm = TRUE))
}))
ggplot(lc, aes(n, mse, colour = factor(p))) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(colour = "p", y = "squared estimation error at the best k (log scale)", x = "n (log scale)")








Step 4. On log scales a rate is a slope: if the error is \(c\,n^{-a}\) then \(\log(\text{error}) = \log c - a\log n\). For each \(p\), fit a line of log(mse) on log(n) and read off the slope. Put the slopes next to the rate’s exponent, \(-2/(p + 2)\).

# slopes <- lc |> group_by(p) |> summarize(slope = ____)
# slopes |> mutate(rate = ____)

Question 4. Read the figure against the lecture. (a) From \(n = 100\) to \(n = 6400\) is 64 times the data. By what factor did the error fall for \(p = 1\), and for \(p = 10\)? What does the rate predict for each? (b) Look at lc$k_best: how does the best \(k\) move with \(n\) for \(p = 1\) and for \(p = 10\), and what does the rate’s derivation say it should do?


3. Three ways cross-validation goes wrong

Cross-validation has worked. It assumes that a held-out row is like a new draw: independent of the rows it was fitted on, and from the same population. Three ways that fails: copies of a track break the independence, drift over time breaks the same population, and a step that looks at the outcome outside the folds lets the held-out rows into the fit.
Step 5. The same track on both sides of a fold. The file has 11,554 rows for 10,000 tracks: 1,101 tracks are in more than one playlist, and every copy has the same audio features, year and popularity. The loader removed the copies with distinct(). Load the rows again without it, keep the 5,000 training tracks with all their copies, and build two fold assignments: fold_row, at random over rows, and fold_track, at random over tracks, so that every copy of a track is in the same fold. Then run the \(k\)-NN pipeline at \(k = 1\), \(5\) and \(50\) with each.

rows <- read_csv("https://ml4ds.com/files/spotify_tracks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(duration_min = duration_ms / 60000) |>
  filter(track_id %in% sp_file$track_id[id[1:5000]]) |>   # the training tracks, copies kept
  select(track_id, track_popularity, all_of(feat))
fold_row <- sample(rep(1:K, length.out = nrow(rows)))
tracks <- unique(rows$track_id)
fold_of_track <- sample(rep(1:K, length.out = length(tracks)))   # one fold per track
# fold_track <- ____                                              # each row gets its track's fold
# cv_row <- sapply(c(1, 5, 50), function(k) ____)
# cv_track <- sapply(c(1, 5, 50), function(k) ____)
# rbind(k = c(1, 5, 50), by_row = round(cv_row), by_track = round(cv_track))

Checkpoint:

stopifnot(length(fold_track) == nrow(rows), all(tapply(fold_track, rows$track_id, function(f) length(unique(f))) == 1))

Question 5. What happened to the scores at \(k = 1\), and why is the effect smaller at \(k = 50\)? Which of the two numbers is the one to believe, and what is the rule? About a quarter of these rows have a copy; in a dataset of patients with several visits each, or of songs in many playlists, what would you expect?
Step 6. A random split against a split in time. Popularity is Spotify’s score in January 2020, and it rewards recent plays: the mean popularity by release year, below, rises through the 2010s. A random split mixes the years, so cross-validation answers “how well does this predict a track like the ones we have?”. The question a user of the model might ask is “how well will it predict this year’s releases?”. Fit least squares on the eleven inputs to the development tracks (training and tuning, 7,000) released up to 2018 (old), and score it two ways: by cross-validation on old, and on the development tracks released in 2019 and 2020 (new). For each, report the MSE and the mean error, \(\tfrac1m\sum_j (y_j - \hat f(x_j))\); cv_mean_error() does for the mean error what cv_mse() does for the MSE.

sp_dev <- sp[id[1:7000], ]                              # the training and tuning tracks
sp_dev |> filter(release_year >= 2012) |> group_by(release_year) |>
  summarize(tracks = n(), mean_popularity = round(mean(track_popularity), 1)) |> t()

                  [,1]   [,2]   [,3]   [,4] [,5]   [,6]   [,7]   [,8]   [,9]
release_year    2012.0 2013.0 2014.0 2015.0 2016 2017.0 2018.0 2019.0 2020.0
tracks           152.0  220.0  342.0  388.0  433  552.0  714.0 1823.0  155.0
mean_popularity   34.3   28.2   27.4   33.9   36   39.1   42.9   47.3   41.7

old <- sp_dev |> filter(release_year <= 2018)
new <- sp_dev |> filter(release_year >= 2019)
fold_old <- sample(rep(1:K, length.out = nrow(old)))
plane_fp <- function(tr, ho) predict(lm(track_popularity ~ ., tr), ho)
cv_mean_error <- function(fit_predict, d, fold) {        # cv_mse() with the loss replaced by the error
  err <- rep(NA, nrow(d))
  for (k in 1:max(fold)) {
    tr <- d[fold != k, ]; ho <- d[fold == k, ]
    err[fold == k] <- ho$track_popularity - fit_predict(tr, ho)
  }
  mean(err)
}


# cv_plane <- ____                                     # the MSE by cross-validation on old
# cv_me <- ____                                        # the mean error by cross-validation on old
# pred_new <- ____                                     # the plane fitted on old, predicting new
# c(cv_mse = cv_plane, cv_mean_error = cv_me, new_mse = ____, new_mean_error = ____)
# the two baselines on new: the mean of old, and the mean of new itself
# c(old_mean = ____, new_mean = ____)

Question 6. The plane’s predictions for the new tracks are too low on average, and nothing in the cross-validation scores hinted at it. Why can a random split not see this? Its MSE on the new tracks is lower than its CV score; is that good news? Which of the two scores answers the user’s question?
Step 7. The wrong way to cross-validate. Every step of a pipeline that looks at the outcome belongs inside the fold. Here is the classic way to get that wrong (ESL, section 7.10.2). Pure noise: \(n = 100\) rows, \(p = 1{,}000\) inputs and an outcome, all independent standard normal, so the best possible risk is \(1\) and no method can do better than the mean. The wrong way: screen the 20 inputs most correlated with the outcome on all 100 rows, then cross-validate least squares on those 20. The right way: screen inside each fold, on the fitting rows only. Write both as fit_predict functions for cv_mse() and compare the two CV scores with the mean’s.

n_w <- 100; p_w <- 1000
noise <- as_tibble(matrix(rnorm(n_w * p_w), n_w, p_w), .name_repair = ~ paste0("x", seq_along(.x))) |>
  mutate(track_popularity = rnorm(n_w))              # named so that cv_mse() finds the outcome
fold_w <- sample(rep(1:K, length.out = n_w))
top20 <- function(d) {                               # the 20 inputs most correlated with the outcome in d
  r <- cor(select(d, -track_popularity), d$track_popularity)
  rownames(r)[order(-abs(r))[1:20]]
}
# wrong: screened once, on all rows, before cross-validation
# keep <- top20(noise)
# wrong_fp <- function(tr, ho) predict(lm(____), ho)
# right: screened inside the fold
# right_fp <- function(tr, ho) { keep <- top20(tr); predict(lm(____), ho) }
# c(wrong = cv_mse(wrong_fp, noise, fold_w), right = cv_mse(right_fp, noise, fold_w), mean = cv_mse(mean_fp, noise, fold_w))

Question 7. On pure noise nothing can beat the mean. Why does the wrong way score far below it? Which steps of a pipeline have to happen inside the fold?


Optional, can be done at home: the weighted-ridge form on a real fit
Problem 3 says the penalized spline’s coefficients solve \((\mathbf B^T\mathbf B + \lambda\boldsymbol\Omega)\beta = \mathbf B^T\mathbf y\). Check it on mgcv’s fit of popularity on the release year, as in the lecture: model.matrix() gives \(\mathbf B\) (the intercept and nineteen smooth columns), g$smooth[[1]]$S[[1]] gives the penalty matrix of the smooth columns, and g$sp the \(\lambda\) that GCV chose. Build \(\boldsymbol\Omega\) with a row and column of zeros for the intercept, solve, and compare with coef(g).

g <- gam(track_popularity ~ s(release_year, k = 20, bs = "cr"), data = sp_train)
B <- model.matrix(g)
S <- g$smooth[[1]]$S[[1]]
Omega <- matrix(0, ncol(B), ncol(B)); Omega[-1, -1] <- S
# beta <- solve(____, ____)
# max(abs(beta - coef(g)))

title: Week 8 seminar
text:
Before the seminar

The lecture proved the variance of an average of correlated variables; exercise 1 is that proof again, with the slides closed. It derived boosting as approximate gradient descent; exercise 2 takes one boosting step by hand. Do both on paper before the seminar. You may use, without proof: \(\mathrm{Var}\big(\sum_b V_b\big) = \sum_b\sum_{b'}\mathrm{Cov}(V_b, V_{b'})\), and \(\mathrm{Cov}(V, V) = \mathrm{Var}(V)\).






WarningHints



Each exercise has hints, collapsed below it. Do not open a hint unless you have been stuck for at least a few minutes, and open them in order. Solutions are shown in the seminar if you ask.


Exercise 1 (correlated-average variance, with the slides closed). \(V_1, \ldots, V_B\) are random variables, each with variance \(\tau^2 > 0\), and every pair has correlation \(\rho\).

Show that \(\mathrm{Var}\big(\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^B V_b\big) = \rho\tau^2 + (1 - \rho)\tau^2/B\).
What is left as \(B \to \infty\)? What does the formula give when \(\rho = 1\), and when \(\rho = 0\)?
In a bagged ensemble or a random forest, \(V_b\) is the \(b\)th tree’s prediction at one input \(x\), and the randomness is the draw of the training data and of the resampling. Which term can more trees shrink, and which term does a random forest try to shrink instead?







NoteHint 1






Write the variance of the sum as a double sum of covariances. How many terms have \(b = b'\), and how many have \(b \ne b'\)? What is each one?










NoteHint 2






The covariance of two variables with correlation \(\rho\) and variances \(\tau^2\) is \(\rho\tau^2\). Divide the variance of the sum by \(B^2\), then write \(\frac{B(B-1)}{B^2} = 1 - \frac1B\) and regroup.




Exercise 2 (one boosting step by hand). The five Star Wars films in the lecture’s data, with their year and average IMDb rating (in the data, which end in 2005):

The training loss of fitted values \(\mathbf f = (f_1, \ldots, f_5)\) is \(L(\mathbf f) = \sum_i \frac12(y_i - f_i)^2\).

Start from \(f_i = \bar y\) for every film. Compute \(\bar y\) and the negative gradient of \(L\) at this \(\mathbf f\).
Fit a tree with one split on year to the negative gradient: for each of the four cutoffs halfway between consecutive years, compute the residual sum of squares of the two leaves, each predicting its mean. Which cutoff wins, and what does each leaf predict?
Take a step of size \(\gamma = 0.5\) along that tree. Give the new fitted values, and the training loss before and after the step.







NoteHint 1






The derivative of \(\frac12(y_i - f_i)^2\) with respect to \(f_i\).










NoteHint 2





(b), (c) A leaf predicts the mean of the residuals in it. The step is \(f_i \leftarrow f_i + \gamma\,t(x_i)\), with \(t\) the tree.

text:
Problems

Both problems use two inequalities. Markov’s inequality: if \(W \ge 0\) and \(a > 0\), then \(P(W \ge a) \le \mathbb E[W]/a\). Hoeffding’s inequality (Hoeffding 1963): if \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_m\) are independent with \(0 \le Z_i \le 1\) and \(\bar Z\) is their mean, then for every \(t > 0\), \[
P\big(|\bar Z - \mathbb E\bar Z| \ge t\big) \le 2e^{-2mt^2}.
\]
Problem 1 (how far a score can be from the risk). A classifier predicts a track’s playlist genre, one of six, from its audio features (data note). It was fitted on training tracks and is now fixed; its risk \(R\) is its error rate on new tracks. On \(m = 2000\) tuning tracks, drawn independently of each other and of the training tracks, it errs on 1,062, so its score is \(\hat R = 0.531\), the mean of \(m\) losses \(\ell_i \in \{0, 1\}\) with mean \(R\). Write \(D = \hat R - R\). We want an interval \(\hat R \pm t\) that contains \(R\) with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for \(\delta = 0.001\): a \(t\) with \(P(|D| \ge t) \le \delta\).

Show that \(\mathrm{Var}(\ell_i) \le \frac14\), so that \(\mathrm{Var}(D) \le \frac{1}{4m}\).
Apply Markov’s inequality to \(W = |D|\), using \(\mathbb E|D| \le \sqrt{\mathbb E[D^2]}\), and find \(t\).
Apply it to \(W = D^2\) instead (this is Chebyshev’s inequality), and find \(t\).
Find \(t\) from Hoeffding’s inequality.
Compute the three intervals. Guessing a genre at random errs with probability \(\frac56\): which interval rules that out for this classifier? How does each \(t\) grow as \(\delta\) shrinks?
Optional. Hoeffding’s lemma says that if \(0 \le Z \le 1\) with mean \(\mu\), then \(\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda(Z - \mu)}\big] \le e^{\lambda^2/8}\) for every \(\lambda\). Apply Markov’s inequality to \(W = e^{\lambda D}\) with \(\lambda > 0\), and use independence and the lemma to show that \(P(D \ge t) \le e^{-\lambda t + \lambda^2/(8m)}\). Then choose \(\lambda\) to get \(P(D \ge t) \le e^{-2mt^2}\).

Problem 2 (the size of a search). A model’s risk is its expected loss on a new unit, \(R = \mathbb E[\ell]\), for a loss with \(0 \le \ell \le 1\) (for example, the 0–1 loss of a classifier). Before the tuning data are seen, \(K\) candidate models are fixed, fitted on the training data, with risks \(R_1, \ldots, R_K\); treat the fitted models as fixed, so that everything below is conditional on the training data. On \(m\) tuning units, drawn independently of each other and of the training data, candidate \(k\) scores \(\hat R_k\), the mean of its \(m\) losses.

Find \(t_K\) such that, with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), \(|\hat R_k - R_k| < t_K\) for every \(k\) at once. Did you need the \(K\) scores to be independent of each other?
Let \(\hat k\) be the candidate with the lowest tuning score and \(k^\star\) the candidate with the lowest risk. On the event of (a), show that \(R_{\hat k} < \hat R_{\hat k} + t_K\) and \(R_{\hat k} < R_{k^\star} + 2t_K\).
Take \(m = 2000\) and \(\delta = 0.05\). Compute \(t_K\) for \(K = 1\), \(10\), \(100\) and \(1{,}000{,}000\). How many candidates double \(t_1\)? How many tuning units halve \(t_K\)? What would Chebyshev’s inequality give in place of Hoeffding’s, for \(K = 100\)? What does this say about searching a larger grid?
The argument needs the \(K\) candidates to be fixed before any tuning score is seen. Give an example of a search that breaks this, and one that chooses adaptively but does not.

title: Week 8 seminar
text:
Coding

The lecture’s task: predict a film’s average IMDb rating from its year, length and seven genre indicators, squared loss (data note). The same split as the lecture: 5,000 training, 2,000 tuning and 3,000 test films, one seed. The tuning films choose the knobs; the test films are opened once, at the end.

mv <- movies |>
  filter(length <= 200, length > 10, year > 1918, votes >= 20) |>
  select(title, rating, year, length, Action, Animation, Comedy, Drama, Documentary, Romance, Short)
set.seed(310)   # change this number: a different split, and different numbers below
mv_id <- sample(nrow(mv), 10000)
mv_train <- mv[mv_id[1:5000], ]
mv_tune <- mv[mv_id[5001:7000], ]
mv_test <- mv[mv_id[7001:10000], ]
mse(mv_tune$rating, mean(mv_train$rating))   # the training mean, scored on the tuning films

[1] 2.003116



1. A random forest, two knobs

rf_fit(mtry, nodesize) fits a forest of 300 trees on the training films. Its two knobs: mtry, the number of inputs tried at each split (randomForest’s default for 9 inputs is 3), and nodesize, the size below which a node is not split (default 5). rf_score() returns a forest’s MSE on the tuning films.

rf_fit <- function(mtry, nodesize) {
  randomForest(rating ~ year + length + Action + Animation + Comedy + Drama + Documentary + Romance + Short,
               data = mv_train, ntree = 300, mtry = mtry, nodesize = nodesize)
}
rf_score <- function(mtry, nodesize) mse(mv_tune$rating, predict(rf_fit(mtry, nodesize), mv_tune))

Question 1. Fit the forest with the default knobs. Compute its MSE on the training films, out of bag (predict(fit) with no new data predicts each training film from the trees that did not have it in their bootstrap sample), and on the tuning films. Which two agree, and why is the third lower? Why do we not tune the number of trees?

fit_default <- rf_fit(mtry = 3, nodesize = 5)
# c(training = mse(mv_train$rating, ____),
#   out_of_bag = mse(mv_train$rating, ____),
#   tuning = mse(mv_tune$rating, ____))

Question 2. Tune one knob at a time, leaving the other at its default: mtry in 1, 2, 3, 5 and 9 with nodesize = 5; then nodesize in 5, 50 and 200 with mtry = 3. Which value of each wins? (Eight forests, the default twice, about 20 seconds.)

  mutate(tune_mse = map2_dbl(mtry, nodesize, rf_score))

2. Boosted trees, three knobs

xgboost has three knobs that matter most here: the depth of each tree, the learning rate \(\gamma\), and the number of iterations. Its defaults are depth 6, rate 0.3 and 100 iterations. One fit of 800 iterations gives the predictions after any smaller number, so the chunk below makes 12 fits (4 depths, 3 rates) and scores each after 5, 10, 25, …, 800 iterations: 96 models in a table, models, with each one’s MSE on the tuning films. loss holds every model’s squared errors on the 2,000 tuning films, one column per model, in the order of the rows of models; col is that column. (About 5 seconds.)

X_train <- as.matrix(select(mv_train, -title, -rating))
X_tune <- as.matrix(select(mv_tune, -title, -rating))
X_test <- as.matrix(select(mv_test, -title, -rating))
boost_fit <- function(depth, rate) {
  xgboost(x = X_train, y = mv_train$rating, nrounds = 800, max_depth = depth, learning_rate = rate, nthread = 1)
}
iters <- c(5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800)
models <- expand_grid(depth = c(1, 2, 4, 6), rate = c(0.03, 0.1, 0.3), iters = iters) |>
  mutate(col = row_number())
loss <- matrix(NA, nrow(mv_tune), nrow(models))
for (d in c(1, 2, 4, 6)) for (r in c(0.03, 0.1, 0.3)) {
  fit <- boost_fit(d, r)
  for (b in iters) {
    j <- models |> filter(depth == d, rate == r, iters == b) |> pull(col)
    loss[, j] <- (mv_tune$rating - predict(fit, X_tune, iteration_range = c(1, b)))^2
  }
}
models$tune_mse <- colMeans(loss)

3. The size of the search

Three searches over the same 96 boosting models: one model fixed in advance, the defaults (fixed); the 13 models that question 5’s one-knob-at-a-time searches looked at (one_knob); and all 96. On one split of the tuning films the effect is too small to see, so we repeat the searches on many random halves, all three on the same halves.
Question 8. Complete half_gap(cols, A): among the models in cols, find the one with the lowest MSE on the half A of the tuning films; return that MSE and the same model’s MSE on the other half. The chunk then draws 2,000 random halves, runs the three searches on each and averages. Which search’s best model looks best on the films that chose it? Which is best on the other films?

one_knob <- models |> filter((depth == 6 & rate == 0.3) | (rate == 0.3 & iters == 100) | (depth == 6 & iters == 100)) |> pull(col)

}
