title: Week 8 seminar
text:
References

Hoeffding, W. (1963). Probability inequalities for sums of bounded random variables. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 58(301), 13–30. doi:10.1080/01621459.1963.10500830
The films: data note. The Spotify tracks in problem 1: data note.

title: Prediction intervals and calibration
text:
A prediction is one number. A decision usually needs to know how far off that number may be. This note covers two ways of saying so, and how to check them on data the model has not seen: an interval for a numerical outcome, and a probability for a binary one. Throughout, the numerical example is the lecture’s simulation, so that the right answers are known: \[
Y = f^\star(x) + (0.5 + 0.35\,x)\,\varepsilon, \qquad f^\star(x) = 3 + x + 2\sin x + 3e^{-(x - 3)^2/0.08}, \qquad \varepsilon \sim N(0, 1).
\] The noise grows with \(x\); the curve has a narrow bump at \(x = 3\); and \(x\) lies between 0 and 10, with few points between 4 and 6 (a quarter as many per unit of \(x\) as elsewhere). There are 1,000 points to fit on and 7,000 fresh points to check on.
Show the setup code
# quantreg and randomForest are on the course's package list; plotly draws the interactive figures and is needed only here.
library(tidyverse); library(quantreg); library(xgboost); library(randomForest); library(NHANES); library(plotly)

# Course palette (theme/st310.scss): viridis for the primary scale, magma for the second.
v_dark <- "#440154"; v_blue <- "#31688e"; v_teal <- "#21918c"; m_pink <- "#b73779"; m_orange <- "#fc8961"

# NHANES adults, split as in the lecture (data note: data/nhanes.md); then the simulation.
nh <- NHANESraw |>
  filter(Age >= 20) |>
  select(Diabetes, Gender, Age, Race1, Poverty, Weight, Height, BMI, Pulse, BPSysAve, TotChol, DirectChol, PhysActive) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(diabetes = as.numeric(Diabetes == "Yes"), male = as.numeric(Gender == "male"),
         active = as.numeric(PhysActive == "Yes"))
set.seed(310)
nh_id <- sample(nrow(nh))
nh_train <- nh[nh_id[1:4000], ]
nh_tune  <- nh[nh_id[4001:7000], ]

f_sim <- function(x) 3 + x + 2 * sin(x) + 3 * exp(-(x - 3)^2 / (2 * 0.2^2))
s_sim <- function(x) 0.5 + 0.35 * x
# x: uniform, except that a stretch of the line is spread over [4, 6], which leaves few points there.
x_thin <- function(n) { u <- runif(n, 0, 8.5); case_when(u < 4 ~ u, u < 4.5 ~ 4 + 4 * (u - 4), TRUE ~ u + 1.5) }
sim <- function(n) tibble(x = x_thin(n)) |> mutate(y = f_sim(x) + s_sim(x) * rnorm(n))
het_train <- sim(1000)
het_fresh <- sim(7000)
x_grid <- tibble(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 201))

title: Prediction intervals and calibration
text:
Two kinds of interval
At a new input \(x_0\) the outcome is \(Y_0 = f^\star(x_0) + \varepsilon_0\). A confidence interval is for \(f^\star(x_0)\), the average outcome at \(x_0\): it describes how far the fitted model may be from the regression function, and it narrows as the training sample grows. A prediction interval is for \(Y_0\) itself, so it must also cover \(\varepsilon_0\). The bias–variance decomposition at a point says why it cannot narrow to nothing: \[
\mathbb E\big[(Y_0 - \hat f(x_0))^2\big] = \sigma^2 + \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance},
\] and more data shrink the variance, never \(\sigma^2\). For a linear model with normal noise of constant variance, R gives both: predict(fit, newdata, interval = "confidence") and interval = "prediction".
The simplest interval of either kind is the prediction plus or minus one number, \(\hat C(x_0) = [\hat f(x_0) - C,\ \hat f(x_0) + C]\). For \(f^\star(x_0)\), \(C\) comes from how much \(\hat f(x_0)\) varies from one training sample to another: a multiple of its standard error, from a formula or the bootstrap. That interval is centered on \(f^\star(x_0)\) only if \(\hat f(x_0)\) has no bias, and a flexible model tuned to predict well usually has some. For \(Y_0\), \(C\) comes from how far outcomes fall from predictions: a quantile of the absolute residuals \(|y_i - \hat f(x_i)|\), for a 90% interval their 90th percentile. This note is about the second kind, without assuming normal noise of constant variance. Which rows the residuals should come from is taken up below; first, quantiles that change with \(x\), for when one \(C\) for every \(x\) is the wrong shape.

title: Prediction intervals and calibration
text:
Quantiles and the pinball loss
Squared error makes the conditional mean the best prediction, and absolute error the conditional median. The pinball loss makes it a conditional quantile. For an outcome \(y\) and a prediction \(\hat y\), \[
\rho_\tau(y - \hat y) = (y - \hat y)\,\big(\tau - \mathbf 1\{y < \hat y\}\big),
\] which charges \(\tau\) for each unit of underprediction and \(1 - \tau\) for each unit of overprediction; with \(\tau = \frac12\) it is half the absolute error. As a function of the error \(y - \hat y\) it is two lines that meet at zero: slope \(\tau\) to the right, where the prediction is too low, and slope \(-(1 - \tau)\) to the left, where it is too high. With \(\tau = 0.9\) a shortfall costs nine times an overshoot of the same size, so the best prediction is high.
Move the slider to change \(\tau\).


Show the code
pin <- function(e, tau) e * (tau - (e < 0))   # the pinball loss of an error e = y - y-hat
loss_grid <- expand_grid(tau = seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05), e = seq(-3, 3, by = 0.05)) |> mutate(loss = pin(e, tau))
if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
plot_ly(loss_grid, x = ~e, y = ~loss, frame = ~tau, type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
        line = list(color = v_dark, width = 3), showlegend = FALSE,
        hovertemplate = "error %{x:.2f}<br>loss %{y:.2f}<extra></extra>") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "error, y − ŷ"), yaxis = list(title = "pinball loss", range = c(0, 3))) |>
  animation_opts(frame = 300, redraw = FALSE) |>
  animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "τ = "))
} else {
  # The static version, for print: three values of tau.
  ggplot(filter(loss_grid, round(tau, 2) %in% c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)), aes(e, loss, colour = factor(tau))) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`0.1` = m_pink, `0.5` = v_dark, `0.9` = v_teal), name = expression(tau)) +
    labs(x = expression("error, " * y - hat(y)), y = "pinball loss") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
}






If \(Y\) given \(X = x\) has a continuous distribution with a finite mean, the conditional \(\tau\)-quantile \(q_\tau(x)\) minimizes the expected loss \(\mathbb E[\rho_\tau(Y - \hat y) \mid X = x]\) over \(\hat y\), uniquely unless the distribution function is flat at \(\tau\) (the quantile optimality theorem, stated in the lecture).
Fitting a model with the pinball loss is quantile regression: minimize \(\frac1n\sum_i \rho_\tau(y_i - f(x_i))\) over a class of functions \(f\), a line or a sum of trees, just as least squares minimizes the average squared error.

title: Prediction intervals and calibration
text:
Local intervals from two quantiles
A local interval has ends that change with \(x\). A 90% interval from two quantile fits is \(\hat C(x) = [\hat q_{0.05}(x), \hat q_{0.95}(x)]\). The true quantiles would cover \(Y\) with probability \(0.9\) at every \(x\); estimated quantiles aim at that, and miss by however much the fits are wrong. The figure compares four ways to make a 90% interval on the simulated data; the dashed lines are the true 5% and 95% quantiles.
Click a name in the legend to show or hide it.

Linear model, constant noise: least squares, with R’s prediction interval, which assumes normal noise of constant variance. It widens slightly toward the ends of the range, with the uncertainty in the fitted line.
Mean and variance: least squares for the mean, then a second regression, of the absolute residuals on \(x\), for the spread; the interval is the mean \(\pm\, 1.645 \times\) the spread (the absolute value of a normal error has mean \(\sqrt{2/\pi}\) times its standard deviation, so the second fit is scaled by \(\sqrt{\pi/2}\)).
Linear quantiles: two quantile regressions on a line, with quantreg::rq().
Boosted quantiles: two boosted-tree fits with the pinball loss, xgboost’s objective = "reg:quantileerror".



Show the code
z90 <- qnorm(0.95)
fit_lm <- lm(y ~ x, data = het_train)
fit_abs <- lm(abs(resid(fit_lm)) ~ x, data = het_train)
fit_qr <- rq(y ~ x, tau = c(0.05, 0.95), data = het_train)
boost_q <- function(tau) xgboost(x = as.matrix(het_train["x"]), y = het_train$y,
  objective = "reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha = tau,
  max_depth = 2, learning_rate = 0.05, nrounds = 300, min_child_weight = 30, nthread = 1)
fit_b05 <- boost_q(0.05)
fit_b95 <- boost_q(0.95)

intervals <- function(d) {
  pi_lm <- predict(fit_lm, d, interval = "prediction", level = 0.9)
  m <- predict(fit_lm, d); s <- predict(fit_abs, d) * sqrt(pi / 2)
  qr <- predict(fit_qr, d)
  X <- as.matrix(d["x"])
  list(`linear model, constant noise` = cbind(pi_lm[, "lwr"], pi_lm[, "upr"]),
       `mean and variance` = cbind(m - z90 * s, m + z90 * s),
       `linear quantiles` = qr,
       `boosted quantiles` = cbind(predict(fit_b05, X), predict(fit_b95, X)))
}
bands <- imap_dfr(intervals(x_grid), function(b, nm) tibble(x = x_grid$x, lo = b[, 1], hi = b[, 2], method = nm))

if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
p <- plot_ly() |>
  add_markers(data = het_train, x = ~x, y = ~y, marker = list(color = "rgba(0,0,0,0.25)", size = 4),
              name = "training points", hoverinfo = "skip")
band_cols <- c(`linear model, constant noise` = m_orange, `mean and variance` = v_blue, `linear quantiles` = m_pink, `boosted quantiles` = v_teal)
for (nm in names(band_cols)) {
  b <- filter(bands, method == nm)
  p <- p |> add_ribbons(data = b, x = ~x, ymin = ~lo, ymax = ~hi, name = nm,
                        fillcolor = paste0(band_cols[[nm]], "55"), line = list(color = band_cols[[nm]]),
                        visible = if (nm %in% c("linear model, constant noise", "boosted quantiles")) TRUE else "legendonly",
                        hovertemplate = paste0(nm, ": %{y:.1f}<extra></extra>"))
}
p |> add_lines(data = x_grid, x = ~x, y = ~f_sim(x) - z90 * s_sim(x), line = list(color = "black", dash = "dash"),
               name = "true quantiles", legendgroup = "true", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
  add_lines(data = x_grid, x = ~x, y = ~f_sim(x) + z90 * s_sim(x), line = list(color = "black", dash = "dash"),
            showlegend = FALSE, legendgroup = "true", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "x"), yaxis = list(title = "y"), legend = list(x = 0.02, y = 0.98))
} else {
  # The static version, for print: one panel per method.
  ggplot(mutate(bands, method = fct_inorder(method)), aes(x)) +
    geom_point(data = het_train, aes(y = y), alpha = 0.15, size = 0.5) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = v_teal, alpha = 0.35) +
    geom_line(data = x_grid, aes(y = f_sim(x) - z90 * s_sim(x)), linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(data = x_grid, aes(y = f_sim(x) + z90 * s_sim(x)), linetype = "dashed") +
    facet_wrap(~ method, nrow = 2) + labs(x = "x", y = "y") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
}






The first three are rigid: each uses every row at every \(x\), which makes it stable, and wrong wherever its shape is wrong, as at the bump. The boosted fits can follow the bump and the growing noise, at a cost. The ends of the interval near \(x\) are learned from the rows near \(x\), and between 4 and 6 there are only 63 of the 1,000. And the 5% and 95% quantiles are harder to learn than the mean: about one row in twenty lies beyond each.

title: Prediction intervals and calibration
text:
Checking an interval
Check a claimed 90% on data that played no part in the fit: the share of fresh outcomes inside their intervals (the coverage), the mean width, and both again within ranges of \(x\). Covering is not enough on its own, since widening an interval never lowers its coverage.


Show the code for the table
# Coverage of the fresh points, overall and within five ranges of x, and the mean width; one row per interval.
pct0 <- function(v) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * v)
coverage_table <- function(ints) {
  imap_dfr(ints, function(b, nm) tibble(
    method = nm, range = cut(het_fresh$x, c(0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10), right = FALSE, include.lowest = TRUE),
    inside = het_fresh$y >= b[, 1] & het_fresh$y <= b[, 2], width = b[, 2] - b[, 1])) |>
    group_by(method = fct_inorder(method)) |>
    summarise(all = mean(inside),
              `x in [0, 2)` = mean(inside[range == "[0,2)"]), `[2, 4)` = mean(inside[range == "[2,4)"]),
              `[4, 6)` = mean(inside[range == "[4,6)"]), `[6, 8)` = mean(inside[range == "[6,8)"]),
              `[8, 10]` = mean(inside[range == "[8,10]"]), `mean width` = mean(width)) |>
    mutate(across(all:`[8, 10]`, \(v) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * v)), `mean width` = sprintf("%.1f", `mean width`)) |>
    knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrrrr")
}

title: Prediction intervals and calibration
section: Residuals from training rows, and from held-out rows
text:
Residuals from training rows, and from held-out rows
Back to the simplest interval, \(\hat f(x) \pm C\) with one \(C\). Take \(C\) to be the 90th percentile of the absolute residuals on the rows the model was fitted to. Two things go wrong, one for each kind of model.


Show the code for the table
het_tune <- sim(1000); het_hold <- sim(1000)   # 1,000 rows to tune on, 1,000 held out
fit_rf <- randomForest(y ~ x, data = het_train, ntree = 300)   # the defaults: nodes of down to 5 rows
C_train <- function(fit) quantile(abs(het_train$y - predict(fit, het_train)), 0.9)
C_from <- function(fit, d) sort(abs(d$y - predict(fit, d)))[ceiling(0.9 * (nrow(d) + 1))]
# A forest whose node size is chosen on the tuning rows.
sizes <- c(5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320)
rf_sizes <- map(sizes, function(s) randomForest(y ~ x, data = het_train, ntree = 300, nodesize = s))
fit_rf_tuned <- rf_sizes[[which.min(map_dbl(rf_sizes, function(f) mean((het_tune$y - predict(f, het_tune))^2)))]]
plus_minus <- function(fit, C) cbind(predict(fit, het_fresh) - C, predict(fit, het_fresh) + C)
cover <- function(b) mean(het_fresh$y >= b[, 1] & het_fresh$y <= b[, 2])
res_ints <- list(`line, C from its training rows` = plus_minus(fit_lm, C_train(fit_lm)),
                 `forest (defaults), C from its training rows` = plus_minus(fit_rf, C_train(fit_rf)),
                 `tuned forest, C from 1,000 held-out rows` = plus_minus(fit_rf_tuned, C_from(fit_rf_tuned, het_hold)),
                 `tuned forest, C from the 1,000 tuning rows` = plus_minus(fit_rf_tuned, C_from(fit_rf_tuned, het_tune)))

Bias. The line misses the bends of the curve. Its residuals include that bias and the noise at every \(x\), so the level is about right overall (89%) and wrong by range.
Variance. The forest follows the noise in its own rows, so its residuals there are too small: with randomForest’s defaults the interval covers 67% of fresh points. Training error underestimates the risk, and the residuals behind it underestimate \(C\).

The repair for the second problem is to take the residuals from rows the model has not seen. Split conformal prediction (Lei et al. 2018, section 2.2): fit \(\hat f\) on the training rows; compute the absolute residuals \(R_i = |y_i - \hat f(x_i)|\) on \(m\) held-out rows; let \(C\) be the \(k\)-th smallest of them, with \(k = \lceil 0.9(m + 1) \rceil\) (if \(k > m\), take \(C = \infty\)); report \(\hat f(x) \pm C\). With \(m = 1{,}000\), \(k = 901\). For the forest, with its node size chosen on tuning rows (160 here), this gives 88% overall, for this one set of held-out rows.
Why it works. A new row \((X, Y)\) is inside the interval exactly when its own absolute residual \(R = |Y - \hat f(X)|\) is at most \(C\). Suppose all the rows, including the new one, are independent draws from one distribution.1 The fit used neither the held-out rows nor the new row, so given the training rows, the \(m + 1\) absolute residuals of these rows are independent draws from one distribution too. With no ties, the new one’s rank among them is then equally likely to be any of \(1, \dots, m + 1\), and it is at most the \(k\)-th smallest of the other \(m\) exactly when its rank is at most \(k\). So \[
P\big(Y \in \hat C(X)\big) = \frac{k}{m + 1}, \qquad 0.9 \;\le\; \frac{k}{m + 1} \;<\; 0.9 + \frac{1}{m + 1},
\] and with ties the probability is at least \(k/(m + 1)\). Nothing is assumed about the model: a poor fit gives a wide interval, not a wrong overall level.
Scope of the guarantee. First, the argument needs a fit that did not use the held-out rows in any way, and that includes tuning. If the rows that set \(C\) also chose the model’s settings, the setting chosen is one whose residuals there happen to be small, and the guarantee is lost. In the table the tuning rows happen to give a slightly wider interval than the held-out rows, which is sampling variation (below) and not the effect of tuning. In a simulation like the lecture’s, choosing a forest’s node size among six settings on 500 rows, the loss was too small to see in 150 repeats; with fewer rows or more candidates it grows. Use separate rows to fit, tune and compute \(C\), or tune by cross-validation within the training rows. Second, the probability is over the held-out rows and the new row together. For one fixed set of held-out rows, the coverage of future rows is the chance that a new residual is at most that set’s \(C\). If the residuals have a continuous distribution, this chance is the \(k\)-th smallest of \(m\) independent uniform draws, which has the \(\mathrm{Beta}(k, m + 1 - k)\) distribution: mean \(k/(m + 1)\), standard deviation about \(\sqrt{0.9 \times 0.1/m}\), 0.9 percentage points when \(m = 1{,}000\) and 1.3 when \(m = 500\). Third, the guarantee is an average over \(X\). The table shows what that leaves open: the tuned forest with a held-out \(C\) is right overall and wrong by range, too wide where the noise is small and too narrow where it is large.

title: Prediction intervals and calibration
text:
Coverage at every \(x\)
Marginal coverage averages over \(X\): \(P(Y \in \hat C(X)) \ge 0.9\). Conditional coverage asks for \(P(Y \in \hat C(X) \mid X = x) \ge 0.9\) at every \(x\), which is what a person with inputs \(x\) wants from an interval made for them. In the simulation the noise is normal with a known mean and standard deviation at each \(x\), so the coverage at \(x\) of any fitted interval can be computed exactly. The figure averages it over repeated training samples of \(n\) rows, for two intervals: boosted trees for the mean with one \(C\) from \(n\) held-out rows, and two boosted quantile fits.


Show the code
# P(Y in [lo, hi] | X = x) = pnorm((hi - f(x)) / s(x)) - pnorm((lo - f(x)) / s(x)), averaged over fits on fresh
# training rows: 5 fits for the first interval, which varies little between samples, and 12 for the second.
bst <- function(d, objective, ...) xgboost(x = as.matrix(d["x"]), y = d$y, objective = objective, ...,
  max_depth = 2, learning_rate = 0.05, nrounds = 300, min_child_weight = 30, nthread = 1)
gx <- tibble(x = seq(0.005, 9.995, by = 0.01)); gx_m <- as.matrix(gx)
cov_at <- function(lo, hi) pnorm((hi - f_sim(gx$x)) / s_sim(gx$x)) - pnorm((lo - f_sim(gx$x)) / s_sim(gx$x))
grow <- map_dfr(c(1000, 8000, 32000), function(n) map_dfr(1:12, function(r) {
  d <- sim(n)
  out <- tibble(method = "two quantile fits", n = n, x = gx$x,
                cov = cov_at(predict(bst(d, "reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha = 0.05), gx_m),
                             predict(bst(d, "reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha = 0.95), gx_m)))
  if (r <= 5) {
    h <- sim(n); m <- bst(d, "reg:squarederror"); p <- predict(m, gx_m)
    C <- sort(abs(h$y - predict(m, as.matrix(h["x"]))))[ceiling(0.9 * (n + 1))]
    out <- bind_rows(out, tibble(method = "one C for every x", n = n, x = gx$x, cov = cov_at(p - C, p + C)))
  }
  out
})) |> group_by(method, n, x) |> summarise(cov = mean(cov), .groups = "drop")
ggplot(grow, aes(x, cov, colour = factor(n))) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 4, xmax = 6, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.9, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ method) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.65, 1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`1000` = m_pink, `8000` = v_teal, `32000` = v_dark), labels = c("1,000", "8,000", "32,000"), name = "n") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, 2)) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "x (shaded: few rows)", y = "coverage at x") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









One \(C\) for every \(x\). Its coverage is too high where the noise is small and too low where it is large, and more data do not change that: as \(n\) grows the interval tends to the true curve plus or minus one number, the 90th percentile of the absolute noise over all \(x\).
Ends fitted near each \(x\). At \(n = 1{,}000\) the coverage of the two quantile fits dips in three places: near 0, where the curve is steep and the noise is smallest; just past the bump at 3; and between 4 and 6, where the rows are few. The dips fill in as \(n\) grows. An interval at \(x\) is learned from the rows near \(x\), say \(n_x\) of them, and its coverage there misses 90% for two reasons.

Variance. Two quantiles estimated from \(n_x\) rows give a coverage that varies by about \(\sqrt{0.9 \times 0.1/n_x}\) from sample to sample, as a share of 0.9 estimated from \(n_x\) rows does: 4 percentage points with 50 rows, 1.3 with 500.
Bias. Rows farther from \(x\) have different quantiles, so using them moves the ends. What counts is how fast the quantiles change with \(x\) compared with the noise: for a normal outcome, ends that are both half a noise standard deviation too high cover 86% instead of 90%.

A smaller neighborhood has less bias and fewer rows: the trade-off of every local method, here for quantiles. The number of inputs sets how many rows a neighborhood holds. With 2,000 rows spread evenly over 5 bins for each input, a bin has 400 rows with one input, 80 with two, 16 with three and under one with five; with 16 rows the variance term is 7.5 percentage points. The same limits apply to checking coverage near \(x\), which needs fresh rows near \(x\).
So coverage at every \(x\) is reachable as \(n\) grows, if the fits approach the true quantiles (consistency), and how fast depends on the rows near \(x\), on how quickly the quantiles change relative to the noise, and on the number of inputs. Each of these is an assumption about the distribution. With none, the answer is no: Barber, Candès, Ramdas and Tibshirani (2021) show that if a procedure guarantees conditional coverage in finite samples for every distribution, then wherever the inputs are continuous its intervals are infinitely long on average (their Proposition 2.2).2 Guarantees for groups, such as each range of \(x\), and results that rest on assumptions about the distribution, or hold as \(n\) grows, remain possible. No method does best on every distribution, and none can promise coverage at every \(x\) without saying something about the distribution.

title: Prediction intervals and calibration
text:
Conformalized quantile regression
Two quantile fits have the right shape when they are right, and no guarantee; split conformal prediction has a guarantee, and one width. Conformalized quantile regression (CQR; Romano, Patterson and Candès 2019, section 4) applies the held-out correction to the quantile fits: it measures how far they miss on rows they did not see, and moves both ends of the interval by that amount. For a \(1 - \alpha\) interval, here \(\alpha = 0.1\):

Split the training rows in two. On the first part, fit a lower and an upper quantile, \(\hat q_{\mathrm{lo}}\) and \(\hat q_{\mathrm{hi}}\) (here the 5% and 95% quantiles), by any method. Keep the other \(m\) rows, the calibration set, for the next step.
On each calibration row, compute the score \[
E_i = \max\big\{\hat q_{\mathrm{lo}}(x_i) - y_i,\ y_i - \hat q_{\mathrm{hi}}(x_i)\big\}
\] (their equation 6). If \(y_i\) is above the interval, \(E_i\) is how far above the upper end; if below, how far below the lower end; if inside, \(E_i \le 0\), minus the distance to the nearer end.
Let \(Q\) be the \(k\)-th smallest of the \(m\) scores, with \(k = \lceil (1 - \alpha)(m + 1) \rceil\); in their equation 8, the \((1 - \alpha)(1 + 1/m)\)-th empirical quantile. (If \(k > m\), take \(Q = \infty\).)
Report \[
\hat C(x) = \big[\hat q_{\mathrm{lo}}(x) - Q,\ \hat q_{\mathrm{hi}}(x) + Q\big]
\] (their equation 7). If the fits were too narrow, \(Q > 0\) and the interval widens; if too wide, \(Q < 0\) and it narrows.

The argument for split conformal prediction goes through with the score \(E\) in place of the absolute residual: a new row is inside \(\hat C(X)\) exactly when its own score is at most \(Q\), and its rank among the \(m + 1\) scores is uniform. This is their Theorem 1: coverage at least \(1 - \alpha\), and at most \(1 - \alpha + 1/(m + 1)\) when the scores are almost surely distinct, as they are when continuous. Split conformal prediction is the special case in which both quantile fits are the same fit of the mean, \(\hat q_{\mathrm{lo}} = \hat q_{\mathrm{hi}} = \hat f\): the score is then \(\lvert y_i - \hat f(x_i) \rvert\) and the interval is \(\hat f(x) \pm Q\). The scope is the same too: fits that did not use the calibration rows, an average over calibration sets, and a marginal guarantee. The same \(Q\) is added at every \(x\), so CQR corrects the overall level and not the shape: where the fits are too narrow in one range and too wide in another, the conformalized interval is too.
If the quantile fits are consistent, \(Q\) tends to zero, the CQR interval approaches \([q_{\alpha/2}(x), q_{1 - \alpha/2}(x)]\), and its coverage given \(X = x\) tends to \(1 - \alpha\), except on a set of \(x\) whose probability tends to zero (Sesia and Candès 2020, Theorem 1 and its corollary, for independent rows and scores with a density bounded away from zero near zero). The conditional coverage is the quantile fits’; the correction supplies the finite-sample average.
On the simulated data: boosted 5% and 95% fits, with the settings above, on the first 500 training points, and scores on the other 500, so \(m = 500\) and \(k = 451\). The figure shows the scores; the dashed line is \(Q\), and the points above it are the outcomes the interval still misses.


Show the code
fit_part <- 1:500; cal_part <- 501:1000
k90 <- ceiling(0.9 * (500 + 1))
boost_half <- function(tau) xgboost(x = as.matrix(het_train[fit_part, "x"]), y = het_train$y[fit_part],
  objective = "reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha = tau,
  max_depth = 2, learning_rate = 0.05, nrounds = 300, min_child_weight = 30, nthread = 1)
b05_half <- boost_half(0.05); b95_half <- boost_half(0.95)
plug_in <- function(d) cbind(predict(b05_half, as.matrix(d["x"])), predict(b95_half, as.matrix(d["x"])))
cal <- het_train[cal_part, ]
b_cal <- plug_in(cal)
cal$score <- pmax(b_cal[, 1] - cal$y, cal$y - b_cal[, 2])   # their equation 6
Q_cqr <- sort(cal$score)[k90]                               # their equation 8
b_own <- plug_in(het_train[fit_part, ])
cover_own <- mean(het_train$y[fit_part] >= b_own[, 1] & het_train$y[fit_part] <= b_own[, 2])
ggplot(cal, aes(x, score)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = score > Q_cqr), size = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = Q_cqr, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey50", `TRUE` = m_pink), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "score on the calibration rows") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









Here \(Q = 0.21\). The two fits cover 91% of their own 500 training points but only 87% of the calibration rows, so CQR widens each end by \(Q\). On the fresh points, against split conformal prediction around a least squares line fitted and calibrated on the same halves:


Show the code
lm_half <- lm(y ~ x, data = het_train[fit_part, ])
C_split <- sort(abs(het_train$y[cal_part] - predict(lm_half, het_train[cal_part, ])))[k90]
b_fresh <- plug_in(het_fresh)
cov_cqr <- mean(het_fresh$y >= b_fresh[, 1] - Q_cqr & het_fresh$y <= b_fresh[, 2] + Q_cqr)
cov_split <- mean(abs(het_fresh$y - predict(lm_half, het_fresh)) <= C_split)
coverage_table(list(
  `boosted quantiles, 500 points` = b_fresh,
  `conformalized, 500 + 500` = cbind(b_fresh[, 1] - Q_cqr, b_fresh[, 2] + Q_cqr),   # their equation 7
  `split conformal, least squares, 500 + 500` = cbind(predict(lm_half, het_fresh) - C_split, predict(lm_half, het_fresh) + C_split)))

title: Prediction intervals and calibration
text:
Ways to make an interval









Method
How
Assumes
Can claim




Linear model, normal noise
\(\hat f(x)\) plus or minus a multiple of the estimated noise sd
linear mean, constant variance, normal noise
90% at every \(x\), if the model is right


Mean and variance
a model for the mean, another for the spread
both models right, normal noise
about 90% at every \(x\), if right


Quantile regression
two fits with the pinball loss
the quantile model right
90% at every \(x\) as \(n\) grows, if right


Split conformal prediction
fit \(\hat f\) on part of the data; on the rest, find the residual size \(C\) that 90% of residuals stay within (with a small correction); report \(\hat f(x) \pm C\)
exchangeable rows
at least 90% marginally, in finite samples, with any model; the same width at every \(x\)


Conformalized quantile regression
fit two quantiles on part of the data; on the rest, find how far to widen (or narrow) them so that 90% of outcomes fall inside
exchangeable rows
at least 90% marginally, in finite samples; widths that follow the quantile fits; 90% at every \(x\) as \(n\) grows, if the fits are consistent



The first three rows rest on a model being right; the two conformal methods (Lei et al. 2018, section 2.2; Romano, Patterson and Candès 2019, Theorem 1) need only exchangeable rows, which independent draws from one distribution are,3 and in return their guarantee is marginal.

title: Prediction intervals and calibration
text:
Calibration
The same idea for a binary outcome: a stated probability should match a frequency. Of 500 adults given probability \(0.2\) of having diabetes by a model, about 100 should have it. Probabilities are acted on as probabilities: a risk told to a patient, a premium set from an expected cost, a threshold set from the costs of errors. If adults given \(0.2\) in fact have the condition 40% of the time, a threshold of \(0.25\) leaves them unreferred although referring them costs less on average. A score \(\hat p\) is calibrated if \(P\big(Y = 1 \mid \hat p(X)\big) = \hat p(X)\): it conditions on the score’s value, not on \(x\). A reliability diagram checks this on fresh data: sort the units by their score into bins of equal size, and plot each bin’s share of 1s against its average score.
Here the outcome is diabetes, as reported by adults in the NHANES survey (data note; 14% of the training adults). Two scores use nine measurements (age, sex, BMI, pulse, systolic blood pressure, total and HDL cholesterol, the income-to-poverty ratio and physical activity); they are fitted on 4,000 adults and checked on 3,000 others: logistic regression, and boosted trees with xgboost’s defaults (depth 6, learning rate 0.3, 100 iterations). The boosted score is too confident on fresh adults. Checked on the adults who fitted it (grey), it looks too cautious at the top instead, which is why the check needs fresh data.


Show the code
cal_inputs <- c("Age", "male", "BMI", "Pulse", "BPSysAve", "TotChol", "DirectChol", "Poverty", "active")
fit_lr <- glm(diabetes ~ Age + male + BMI + Pulse + BPSysAve + TotChol + DirectChol + Poverty + active,
              family = binomial, data = nh_train)
fit_xg <- xgboost(x = as.matrix(nh_train[cal_inputs]), y = factor(nh_train$diabetes), nthread = 1)
p_lr <- predict(fit_lr, nh_tune, type = "response")
p_xg <- predict(fit_xg, as.matrix(nh_tune[cal_inputs]))
y_tune <- nh_tune$diabetes
# The gap between a group's average score and its share with diabetes, in binomial standard errors.
gap_se <- function(g) { i <- nh_tune$Race1 == g; abs(mean(p_lr[i]) - mean(y_tune[i])) / sqrt(mean(y_tune[i]) * (1 - mean(y_tune[i])) / sum(i)) }
reliability <- function(p, y, bins = 10) tibble(p, y) |> mutate(bin = ntile(p, bins)) |>
  group_by(bin) |> summarise(n = n(), mean_p = mean(p), freq = mean(y), .groups = "drop")
rel <- bind_rows(reliability(p_lr, y_tune) |> mutate(score = "logistic regression, tuning adults"),
                 reliability(p_xg, y_tune) |> mutate(score = "boosted trees, tuning adults"),
                 reliability(predict(fit_xg, as.matrix(nh_train[cal_inputs])), nh_train$diabetes) |> mutate(score = "boosted trees, training adults"))
if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
plot_ly(rel, x = ~mean_p, y = ~freq, color = ~score, colors = c("grey60", v_dark, v_teal), type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers",
        text = ~n, hovertemplate = "average score %{x:.2f}<br>share with diabetes %{y:.2f}<br>%{text} adults<extra></extra>") |>
  add_lines(x = c(0, 1), y = c(0, 1), color = I("grey60"), line = list(dash = "dash"), inherit = FALSE,
            name = "calibrated", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "average score in the bin", range = c(0, 1)),
         yaxis = list(title = "share with diabetes", range = c(0, 1)),
         legend = list(x = 0.55, y = 0.12), height = 520, width = 640)
} else {
  # The static version, for print.
  ggplot(rel, aes(mean_p, freq, colour = score)) + geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
    geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`boosted trees, training adults` = "grey60", `boosted trees, tuning adults` = v_dark,
                                   `logistic regression, tuning adults` = v_teal), name = NULL) +
    coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(x = "average score in the bin", y = "share with diabetes") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "right")
}







Calibration and sharpness. The base rate, \(\hat p(x) = 0.14\) for every adult, is calibrated, and it does not separate those with diabetes from the rest at all. A useful score is calibrated and also sharp, with values near 0 and 1 where it can; Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery (2007) make this principle precise for forecasts of a continuous outcome: as sharp as possible, subject to calibration.
Calibration and the threshold. If \(\hat p\) is calibrated, the optimal threshold theorem applies with \(\hat p(X)\) as the input: when a false positive costs \(c_{FP}\) and a false negative \(c_{FN}\), predicting 1 when \(\hat p(x) > c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})\) is optimal among rules based on that score. It need not be optimal among rules that use all of \(x\). Without calibration, that threshold need not be the optimal cut on \(\hat p\): a miscalibrated score can still give the right decisions (with \(p\) the true class probability, \(\hat p = 0.25 + 0.5p\) does at the threshold \(0.5\)), but in general it does not.
Recalibration. A score can be repaired on rows not used to fit it. One method: a logistic regression of the label on \(\mathrm{logit}\,\hat p = \log\frac{\hat p}{1 - \hat p}\), giving \(\tilde p = 1/(1 + e^{-(a + b\,\mathrm{logit}\,\hat p)})\). For \(b > 0\) the map from \(\hat p\) to \(\tilde p\) is increasing, so the new score ranks the adults as the old one did (its AUC is unchanged), with new probabilities. Fitted on the first 1,500 tuning adults and checked on the other 1,500:



Show the code
logit_p <- function(p) qlogis(pmin(pmax(p, 1e-4), 1 - 1e-4))
half_a <- 1:1500; half_b <- 1501:3000
recal <- glm(y ~ s, family = binomial, data = tibble(y = y_tune[half_a], s = logit_p(p_xg[half_a])))
p_recal <- predict(recal, tibble(s = logit_p(p_xg[half_b])), type = "response")
logloss <- function(p, y) -mean(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p))
tibble(` ` = c("boosted trees", "recalibrated"),
       `log loss on the other 1,500 adults` = c(logloss(p_xg[half_b], y_tune[half_b]), logloss(p_recal, y_tune[half_b]))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)






log loss on the other 1,500 adults




boosted trees
0.375


recalibrated
0.329





The fitted slope is \(b = 0.39\): two adults whose boosted log-odds differ by 1 differ by 0.39 after recalibration, in the same order. Van Calster et al. (2019) describe the same checks and repairs for risk models in medicine, where a miscalibrated risk can change a treatment decision.
Calibration within groups. A score can be right on average and still too high for one group and too low for another, with the errors cancelling. Used with one threshold for everyone, such a score refers the first group for tests more often, and the second less often, than their risk warrants: it discriminates, even when group membership is not one of its inputs. Calibration within groups is one fairness criterion among several, and they conflict. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2017) show that when the groups’ base rates differ, a score that is calibrated within groups cannot also be balanced, meaning that its average is the same in each group among those with the outcome, and the same in each group among those without, unless it predicts perfectly. For a rule that thresholds a score, Chouldechova (2017) shows that with different base rates, equal positive predictive values across groups rule out equal false positive and false negative rates (for a rule whose positive predictive value is strictly between 0 and 1).
Multicalibration (Hébert-Johnson, Kim, Reingold and Rothblum 2018, definition 2.6) asks for calibration within every group in a collection named in advance: within each group, among the units with score near \(v\), the share of 1s should be within a tolerance of \(v\), for every \(v\). Their algorithm (section 3.2) repeatedly finds a group and a range of scores where the average score and the share of 1s differ by more than the tolerance, and shifts the scores there by the difference. The groups must be large enough to check, and a group not in the collection gets no guarantee.
On these data the logistic score above, which leaves race and ethnicity out, is right on average on the tuning adults (an average score of 14.1% against 13.7% with diabetes), but for White adults it averages 14.8% against 10.6% with diabetes, a gap of about 5 standard errors; for the survey’s other groups the gaps are within about two standard errors. Matching averages, overall or in a group, would not show calibration: errors at different scores can cancel, which is why multicalibration asks for calibration at every range of scores within each group. In the lecture, shifts learned on the tuning adults and checked on the test adults close the gap for White adults, the one gap the data can establish, and widen the gap for Mexican American adults: a gap of 2 or 3 percentage points in a group of a few hundred is within noise, and a shift fitted to it does not carry over. Applying the shifts also needs each person’s group when the score is used.

text:
Further reading

Barber, R. F., Candès, E. J., Ramdas, A. and Tibshirani, R. J. (2021). The limits of distribution-free conditional predictive inference. Information and Inference: A Journal of the IMA 10(2), 455–482. doi:10.1093/imaiai/iaaa017. Section 1 defines marginal and conditional coverage; Proposition 2.2 is the impossibility.
Chouldechova, A. (2017). Fair prediction with disparate impact: a study of bias in recidivism prediction instruments. Big Data 5(2), 153–163. doi:10.1089/big.2016.0047. Equal positive predictive values and equal error rates cannot hold together when base rates differ.
Gneiting, T., Balabdaoui, F. and Raftery, A. E. (2007). Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B 69(2), 243–268. doi:10.1111/j.1467-9868.2007.00587.x. The principle of a sharp forecast subject to calibration, for forecasts that are whole distributions.
Hébert-Johnson, Ú., Kim, M. P., Reingold, O. and Rothblum, G. N. (2018). Multicalibration: calibration for the (computationally-identifiable) masses. Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 80, 1939–1948. proceedings.mlr.press/v80/hebert-johnson18a.html. Definition 2.6 and the algorithm of section 3.2 (numbered as in the arXiv version, 1711.08513).
James, G., Witten, D., Hastie, T. and Tibshirani, R. (2021). An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R, 2nd edition. Springer. Section 3.2.2, its last question, on predictions: confidence against prediction intervals for a linear model. statlearning.com

Inherent trade-offs in the fair determination of risk scores. 8th Innovations in Theoretical Computer Science Conference (ITCS 2017), LIPIcs 67, 43:1–43:23. doi:10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2017.43. Romano, Y., Patterson, E. and Candès, E. J. (2019). Conformalized quantile regression. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32, 3543–3553. NeurIPS proceedings. Section 4, equations 6 to 8 and Theorem 1: the method above.

Van Calster, B., McLernon, D. J., van Smeden, M., Wynants, L. and Steyerberg, E. W. (2019). Calibration: the Achilles heel of predictive analytics. BMC Medicine 17, article 230. doi:10.1186/s12916-019-1466-7. Levels of calibration, how to check them, and an example of two heart-disease risk models in which the one with the slightly higher AUC overestimated risk and, at a 20% threshold, flagged about twice as many men.

title: Machine learning
text: Part 1: regression uncertainty and intervals

title: Machine learning
text:
A prediction for one person
So far, competitors submit models that predict, and the winning model is chosen by best score on the evaluation dataset: an average over many people
Now the winning model is deployed. A new person arrives with inputs \(x_0\) and is told \(\hat f(x_0)\). How far off might that be?

You are that person. What should a “90% interval” for your outcome promise you?


That the interval, call it \(\hat C(x_0)\), covers outcomes of people with your inputs 90% of the time: \(P\big(Y \in \hat C(X) \mid X = x_0\big) \ge 0.9\), conditional coverage

title: Machine learning
text:
Two kinds of interval
At a new \(x_0\), \(Y_0 = f^\star(x_0) + \varepsilon_0\)

Confidence interval for \(f^\star(x_0)\) (dark): uncertainty about the fit; it narrows as \(n\) grows
Prediction interval for \(Y_0\) (light): must also cover \(\varepsilon_0\); it does not narrow below the noise











Bias–variance at \(x_0\): \(\sigma^2 + \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance}\); no amount of data shrinks \(\sigma^2\)

title: Machine learning
text:
An interval \(\hat f(x_0) \pm C\)
The simplest interval: \(\hat C(x_0) = \big[\hat f(x_0) - C,\ \hat f(x_0) + C\big]\), for a number \(C\)

How could we compute \(C\) for each kind of interval, for \(f^\star(x_0)\) and for \(Y_0\)?



\(f^\star(x_0)\): how much \(\hat f(x_0)\) varies between samples (a standard error, the bootstrap)
\(Y_0\): how far outcomes fall from predictions, a quantile of the absolute residuals \(|y_i - \hat f(x_i)|\)




Squared loss: the mean. Absolute loss: the median. Which loss: the 90th percentile?

title: Machine learning
text:
Finding the quantile
Charge \(\tau\) for each unit of underprediction (\(y > \hat y\)) and \(1 - \tau\) for each unit of overprediction (\(y < \hat y\)). Move the prediction up from \(\hat y\) to \(\hat y + \delta\):



an outcome above \(\hat y\): its loss falls by \(\tau\delta\)
an outcome below \(\hat y\): its loss rises by \((1 - \tau)\delta\)












With \(F\) the distribution function of \(Y\) given \(X = x\), the expected change is about \[
\delta\,\big[(1 - \tau)F(\hat y) - \tau\,(1 - F(\hat y))\big] = \delta\,\big[F(\hat y) - \tau\big]
\]
Keep moving up while \(F(\hat y) < \tau\); stop where \(F(\hat y) = \tau\): the \(\tau\)-quantile. For the 90th percentile, \(\tau = 0.9\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Quantile optimality


Pinball loss: \[
\rho_\tau(y - \hat y) = (y - \hat y)\,\big(\tau - \mathbf 1\{y < \hat y\}\big)
\] \(\tau\,(y - \hat y)\) for an underprediction, \((1 - \tau)(\hat y - y)\) for an overprediction. With \(\tau = \frac12\), half the absolute error












Quantile optimality theorem. If \(Y \mid X = x\) has a continuous distribution with a finite mean and \(0 < \tau < 1\), then the conditional \(\tau\)-quantile \(q_\tau(x)\) minimizes \(\mathbb E[\rho_\tau(Y - \hat y) \mid X = x]\) over \(\hat y\) (uniquely, unless the distribution function is flat at \(\tau\))

Squared loss gave the mean; half the absolute error, \(\tau = \frac12\), gives the median

title: Machine learning
text:
Quantile regression
Minimize the average pinball loss over a class: \(\hat q_\tau = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal F} \frac1n \sum_i \rho_\tau\big(y_i - f(x_i)\big)\). Here \(\mathcal F\) is linear; 1,000 simulated points: noise that grows with \(x\), a bump at 3, few points with \(x\) between 4 and 6

fit_qr <- rq(y ~ x, tau = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), data = het_train)

title: Machine learning
section: The same loss, a flexible model
text:
The same loss, a flexible model
Boosted trees with the pinball loss: each tree is built from the negative gradient \(\tau - \mathbf 1\{y_i < \hat f(x_i)\}\), which pushes the fit up where points lie above it

xgboost(x, y, objective = "reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha = 0.95, max_depth = 2)











Boosting: each small tree approximates the negative gradient of the training loss

title: Machine learning
text:
Challenges with local intervals
A local interval’s edges change with \(x\): \(\hat C(x) = [\hat q_{0.05}(x), \hat q_{0.95}(x)]\), two quantile fits










Edges near \(x\) come from rows near \(x\): few in 4 to 6; at 3 the quantiles change fast
Extreme quantiles are harder to learn than the mean: 1 row in 20 lies beyond each edge
Rigid models (left, middle) use every row at every \(x\): stable, wrong where they misfit

title: Machine learning
text:
Checking an interval

We claim 90 percent intervals. With fresh data in hand, how do you check the claim, and what could the check miss?

title: Machine learning
section: Checking an interval on fresh data
text:
Checking an interval on fresh data









Top: coverage in each range of \(x\), pink if more than 3 points from 90%. Overall: 89%, 90%, 87%. Widening never lowers coverage: check width too

title: Machine learning
text:
Bias, variance and intervals
\(\hat f(x) \pm C\), with \(C\) the 90th percentile of the absolute residuals on the training rows













Bias: the line misses the bends
Variance: the forest follows the noise in its own rows; residuals there are too small
One \(C\) for every \(x\), though the noise grows



How could we choose \(C\) so that the forest’s interval covers 90% of new outcomes?

title: Machine learning
text:
Residuals from held-out rows
The forest again, its node size now tuned on 1,000 tuning rows












Split conformal (Lei et al. 2018): \(C\) from 1,000 rows not used to fit, their 901st smallest absolute residual, \(\lceil 0.9 \times 1001 \rceil\)
Overall 90% and 91%, but not in every range

The tuning rows chose the node size, so residuals on them may be slightly optimistic

Optimism theorem: training error underestimates the risk

title: Machine learning
section: Coverage on average, and at every \(x\)
text:
Coverage on average, and at every \(x\)

Conformal coverage theorem (split conformal: Lei et al. 2018). If the rows are independent draws from one distribution, then for any model \(P\big(Y \in \hat C(X)\big) \ge 0.9\), on average over \(X\): marginal coverage



Conditional coverage: \(P\big(Y \in \hat C(X) \mid X = x\big) \ge 0.9\) at every \(x\), what the one person wanted
One \(C\) for every \(x\), and noise that grows with \(x\): too wide where the noise is small, too narrow where it is large, whatever \(n\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Coverage at every \(x\), as \(n\) grows












Edges fitted near each \(x\): two quantile fits on \(n\) rows. The noise is known, so coverage at each \(x\) can be computed exactly; here averaged over 30 fits

At \(n\) = 1,000 it dips where the quantiles change fast relative to the noise (near 0, at the bump) and where the rows are few (4 to 6)
The dips fill in as \(n\) grows, if the fits approach the true quantiles (consistency)

title: Machine learning
section: Coverage at every \(x\) in many dimensions
text:
Coverage at every \(x\) in many dimensions
An interval at \(x\) is learned from the \(n_x\) rows near \(x\). Its coverage there misses 90% by

Variance: about \(\sqrt{0.9 \times 0.1 / n_x}\): 4 points with 50 rows, 1.3 with 500
Bias: rows farther from \(x\) have different quantiles. Edges off by half a noise standard deviation: 86%, not 90%

More inputs, fewer rows near \(x\). 2,000 rows, 5 bins for each input:



Inputs
1
2
3
5




Rows per bin, \(n_x\)
400
80
16
0.6


\(\sqrt{0.9 \times 0.1 / n_x}\), points
1.5
3.4
7.5
–




Curse of dimensionality: in ten dimensions, a cube holding 10% of the population spans 79% of each axis

title: Machine learning
text:
Conditional coverage without assumptions
Fits that approach the true quantiles, enough rows near \(x\), quantiles that change slowly: each is an assumption about the distribution. With none:

Impossibility of distribution-free conditional coverage. If a procedure covers with probability at least \(1 - \alpha\) given \(X = x\), in finite samples, for every distribution and almost every \(x\), then wherever the inputs are continuous its intervals have infinite expected length (Barber et al. 2021). Guarantees for groups (each range of \(x\), say), and results under assumptions or as \(n\) grows, remain possible


No free lunch theorem: no method does best on every distribution; a guarantee at every \(x\) needs an assumption about the distribution

title: Machine learning
text:
Ways to make an interval








Method
Assumes
Can claim




Linear model, normal noise
linear mean, constant variance
90% at every \(x\), if right


Mean and variance models
both right, normal noise
about 90% at every \(x\), if right


Quantile regression
the quantile model right
90% at every \(x\) as \(n\) grows, if right


Split conformal (Lei et al. 2018)
exchangeable rows
at least 90% marginally; one width


CQR (Romano et al. 2019)
exchangeable rows
at least 90% marginally; widths from the fits; at every \(x\) as \(n\) grows, if the fits are consistent



More in the note on the course page, “Prediction intervals and calibration”; CQR is also on the slide after the conclusion

title: Machine learning
text: Part 2: classification uncertainty and calibration

title: Machine learning
text:
Data: NHANES
The US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 2009 to 2012 (R package NHANES): interviews and physical examinations. We use 9,212 adults aged 20 and over







Outcomes
diabetes, as told by a doctor (14% yes); later, systolic blood pressure (mm Hg)


Measurements
age, gender, weight, height, BMI, pulse, total and HDL cholesterol, family income relative to the poverty line, physically active or not


Groups
race and ethnicity, in the survey’s five groups


Split
at random: 4,000 training adults; 3,000 tuning adults; 2,212 test adults, used once




Not a sample of the US population: the survey samples some groups at higher rates, and we do not use its weights

title: Machine learning
text:
Calibration

A model gives \(\hat p = 0.2\) to 500 adults: their probability of having diabetes. What should be true of them?


About 100 of them should have diabetes. A score \(\hat p\) is calibrated if \[
P\big(Y = 1 \mid \hat p(X)\big) = \hat p(X)
\]
The same idea as coverage: a stated probability should match a frequency. It conditions on the score, not on \(x\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Calibration and decisions
A probability is acted on: a risk told to a patient, a premium set from an expected cost, a threshold set from the costs of errors

The optimal threshold theorem cuts the true \(p(x)\) at \(c^\star\); we have only \(\hat p\). If \(\hat p\) is calibrated, cutting it at \(c^\star\) is optimal among rules based on that score
If not, \(c^\star\) can pick the wrong people. At \(c^\star = 0.25\), adults given \(\hat p = 0.2\), of whom 40% have diabetes, are not referred for a test, although referring them costs less on average
Calibration is not accuracy. The base rate, \(0.14\) for every adult, is calibrated and separates no one. An increasing transformation keeps a score’s ranking (and AUC), not its calibration


Optimal threshold theorem: with costs \(c_{FP}\) and \(c_{FN}\), the rule that minimizes expected cost at \(x\) predicts \(1\) exactly when \(p(x) > c^\star = c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Reliability diagram
Adults in ten bins by score: each bin’s share with diabetes against its average score. Two scores from nine measurements, on the 4,000 training adults used to fit them









On the diagonal: calibrated. On their own adults, logistic regression is; the boosted trees look too cautious at the top

title: Machine learning
text:
Reliability on fresh adults
The same two scores on 3,000 tuning adults, who played no part in fitting them









Logistic regression (10 coefficients) hardly moves. Boosted trees (100 trees): too confident at the top, the opposite of what their training adults said

title: Machine learning
text:
Recalibration
A map from the old score to a new one, learned on half the tuning adults, checked on the other half: a logistic regression of the label on \(\mathrm{logit}\,\hat p\), giving \(\mathrm{logit}\,\tilde p = a + b\,\mathrm{logit}\,\hat p\)












For \(b > 0\) the map is increasing: the same ranking, new probabilities. \(b = 0.39\): two adults whose boosted log-odds differ by 1 differ by 0.39 after. Log loss on the other half: 0.375 to 0.329

title: Machine learning
text:
Calibration within groups
One score for everyone: the logistic score, with race and ethnicity left out of its inputs. Is it calibrated within each group?









White adults: average score 14.8%, 10.6% with diabetes, a gap of 5.1 standard errors; the other gaps are about 2 standard errors or less

title: Machine learning
text:
Calibration and fairness

A score that is too high for one group and too low for another, cut at one threshold, refers the first group for tests more often, and the second less often, than their risk warrants
The score discriminates, even with race and ethnicity left out of its inputs
Calibration within groups is one fairness criterion among several, and they conflict: with different base rates, no imperfect score is calibrated within groups and also averages the same in each group among adults with diabetes, and among those without (Kleinberg et al. 2017)

title: Machine learning
text:
Multicalibration
Multicalibration (Hébert-Johnson et al. 2018): calibrated in every group named in advance, at every range of scores. In each group and tenth of the scores, shift the scores by the gap; repeat


Learned on the tuning adults, checked on the test adults. Gap in standard errors:

White (1,001 adults): 2.0 to 0.6
Mexican American (317): 0.7 to 2.4












It fixes the gap the data can establish. A gap of 2 or 3 points in a group of a few hundred is within noise, and a shift fitted to it does not carry over

title: Machine learning
text: Part 3: interpreting the model

title: Machine learning
text:
One predictor at a time
How does the model use one specific predictor, \(x_2\), say? For linear regression this is simple: its coefficient. With flexible models the answer changes depending on where you look in the input space










We can change \(x_2\) to see how the predictions vary, but what do we do with the other predictors?

title: Machine learning
section: Partial dependence for any model (not just GAM)
text:
Partial dependence for any model (not just GAM)
Options for the other inputs: hold them fixed (at medians, say: plotmo’s default); average over them (partial dependence, pdp); one curve for each unit (individual conditional expectation, ICE)
Unit \(i\)’s inputs with input \(j\) set to a value \(t\), the others left as they are: \[
\mathrm{ICE}_i(t) = \hat f(x_{i1}, \ldots, t, \ldots, x_{ip}), \qquad
\mathrm{PDP}_j(t) = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \hat f(x_{i1}, \ldots, t, \ldots, x_{ip})
\]
Compute on a grid of \(t\) values and plot the curve(s)
ICE evaluates \(\hat f\) at a modified input, which may correspond to no plausible unit

text:
Does this forest use \(x_1\)?

fit_rf <- randomForest(y ~ x1 + x2, data = df_int, ntree = 300, mtry = 2, nodesize = 50)
ice_x1 <- partial(fit_rf, pred.var = "x1", ice = TRUE, train = df_sub)










The PDP: \(x_1\) set, \(x_2\) at each unit’s value, predictions averaged over 100 units

title: Machine learning
text:
The forest’s ICE curves









Thin: one curve per unit (ICE). Right: solid where \(\cos(\pi x_2/2) > 0\), dashed where it is negative, more opaque the larger \(|\cos(\pi x_2/2)|\). The forest fitted the interaction, PDP hides it, and ICE might show it

title: Machine learning
text:
Every predictor at once

What if we don’t have one specific predictor of interest, but want to know how the model uses all the predictors?



For one prediction: split it among the inputs (Shapley values)
For the whole model: one number for each input (importance)

title: Machine learning
text:
Shapley values
Split a prediction among the inputs, \(\hat f(\mathbf x_i) - v_i(\varnothing) = \phi_{i1} + \dots + \phi_{ip}\); \(v_i(S)\) predicts from the inputs in \(S\) only (usually: the others averaged over the data, as in partial dependence). For two inputs, adding \(x_1\) in either order (for \(p\), all \(p!\) orders): \[
\phi_{i1} = \tfrac12\Big[\big(v_i(\{1\}) - v_i(\varnothing)\big) + \big(v_i(\{1, 2\}) - v_i(\{2\})\big)\Big]
\]
The forest, one unit with \(x_1 = 1.00\) and \(x_2 = 0.06\):









\(v_i(\varnothing)\)
\(v_i(\{1\})\)
\(v_i(\{2\})\)
\(v_i(\{1, 2\}) = \hat f(\mathbf x_i)\)




-0.00
-0.08
0.19
0.92



\(\phi_{i1} = \frac12\big[(-0.08 - -0.00) + (0.92 - 0.19)\big] = 0.325\)
\(\phi_{i2} = \frac12\big[(0.19 - -0.00) + (0.92 - (-0.08))\big] = 0.595\); together 0.92 \(= 0.92 - -0.00 = \hat f(\mathbf x_i) - v_i(\varnothing)\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Shapley values for one adult
We now use the same NHANES adults to predict systolic blood pressure (mm Hg): a forest on nine inputs, fitted on the 4,000 training adults












A waterfall plot (SHAP: Lundberg and Lee 2017). It starts at the average prediction over the background adults, \(v_i(\varnothing)\), adds each input’s \(\phi_{ij}\), largest first, and ends at this adult’s prediction \(\hat f(\mathbf x_i)\)
The adult with the highest prediction of 200 tuning adults

title: Machine learning
text:
Feature/variable “importance”

Which predictors are used most by the model? The forest for systolic blood pressure



Tree-specific importance ■
Sum the RSS decrease of every split on \(x_j\) within a tree, then average over trees
Permutation importance ▲
Permute values of predictor \(x_j\). How much does the accuracy of the model decrease? \[\mathrm{PI}_j = \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}(\hat f, x_j \text{ permuted}) - \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}(\hat f)\]

Leave one covariate out ◆
Refit without input \(j\), with the same settings; score on the same held-out adults (Lei et al. 2018): \[\mathrm{LOCO}_j = \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}\big(\hat f^{(-j)}\big) - \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}(\hat f)\]
No extrapolation from permuting; any method, at the cost of \(p\) refits

title: Machine learning
text:
Part 4: the model and the world
Background: after Loftus, Bynum and Hansen (2024), Figure 5

title: Machine learning
text:
Predictions and outcomes

A partial dependence plot for \(x_1\) leaves \(x_2\) and \(x_3\) at each unit’s value. In the world, they respond to \(x_1\). To let them respond, what do we need besides the fitted model?




A causal model for the inputs. An explanatory causal model (ECM; Loftus, Bynum and Hansen 2024) adds the prediction \(\hat Y = \hat f(X)\), with dashed arrows from the model’s inputs. Here \(x_3\) depends on \(y\), so \(y\) is in it too:
\(x_2 = x_1 + \varepsilon_2\), \(\ y = \tfrac12 x_1 + \tfrac32 \sin x_2 + \varepsilon\), \(\ x_3 = y + x_1 + \varepsilon_3\); \(\hat f\), a forest on \(x_1, x_2, x_3\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Natural direct and total dependence
In the ECM, set \(x_1 = t\) for every unit, predict, average, with \(x_2\) and \(x_3\)

left at each unit’s value: the natural direct dependence plot (NDDP), which is the PDP
recomputed from their equations: the total dependence plot (TDP), \(\mathbb E[\hat f(X) \mid do(x_1 = t)]\)













NDDP falls: with \(x_3\) held fixed, a larger \(x_1\) means a smaller \(y\). TDP follows the effect of setting \(x_1\) (dashed). Grey: Shapley values for \(x_1\)
Causal Shapley values (Heskes et al. 2020) put \(do(\cdot)\) in place of conditioning

title: Machine learning
text:
Partial dependence and causal effects



If the adjustment theorem’s assumptions hold, with the plotted input as \(T\) and the model’s other inputs as \(Z\), and the model fits the true regression function well, then the PDP can show the causal effect of \(T\) on the outcome (Zhao and Hastie 2021)
Whatever the causal structure, the PDP shows the natural direct effect of the plotted input on the predicted outcome \(\hat Y\) (Loftus, Bynum and Hansen 2024)













Adjustment theorem: \(Z\) holds every common cause of \(T\) and \(Y\), and no consequence of \(T\)

title: Machine learning
text:
Conclusion
Uncertainty
The loss decides which number is the best prediction; the pinball loss gives a quantile. Residuals from held-out rows give an interval that covers 90% on average, for any model. Coverage at every \(x\) needs edges fitted near \(x\), enough rows there, and assumptions: no method guarantees it in finite samples without them. Check coverage and calibration on data not used to fit or tune, across the range of the inputs and within groups
Interpretation
Partial dependence, ICE, Shapley values and importance describe \(\hat f\). If the adjustment theorem’s assumptions hold and the model fits well, the PDP can show a causal effect; with a causal model for the inputs, the total dependence plot answers a different question

title: Machine learning
text:
Conformalized quantile regression



Fit \(\hat q_{0.05}\), \(\hat q_{0.95}\) on some training rows; keep \(m\) others, the calibration set
Score how far each \(y_i\) is outside (negative inside): \(E_i = \max\{\hat q_{0.05}(x_i) - y_i,\ y_i - \hat q_{0.95}(x_i)\}\)
\(Q\): the \(\lceil 0.9\,(m + 1) \rceil\)-th smallest score
\(\hat C(x) = \big[\hat q_{0.05}(x) - Q,\ \hat q_{0.95}(x) + Q\big]\)











\(m = 500\), \(Q = 0.21\): 87% to 89%; for \(x\) in 4–6, 92% to 93%


The conformal coverage theorem holds for any quantile fits (Romano et al. 2019): \(P(Y \in \hat C(X)) \ge 0.9\), and \(\le 0.9 + 1/(m + 1)\) for continuous scores. If the fits are consistent, \(Q \to 0\) and coverage at every \(x\) approaches 90% (Sesia and Candès 2020)

title: Machine learning
text:
Exchangeable rows and atoms
These slides state two conditions more simply than the sources do:

Exchangeable rows. The conformal coverage theorem (Lei et al. 2018; Romano et al. 2019, Theorem 1) needs only rows \((X_1, Y_1), \dots, (X_{m+1}, Y_{m+1})\) whose joint distribution is unchanged when they are reordered: exchangeable rows. Independent draws from one distribution are exchangeable; draws without replacement from a finite population are exchangeable but not independent.
Atoms. The impossibility theorem (Barber et al. 2021, Proposition 2.2) is about each \(x\) that is not an atom, a value with positive probability; continuous inputs have no atoms. The upper bound \(1 - \alpha + 1/(m + 1)\) needs only scores that are distinct with probability one
Sesia and Candès (2020) do assume independent rows from one distribution

title: You found the best predictor. Now what?
text:
Most of what machine learning knows about which methods work comes from competitions: a shared dataset, a task, an agreed score, and a hidden evaluation set, with the winner chosen by best score. This note is about what such a win establishes. It follows the lecture: how far a score can be from what it estimates; how reusing a test set can mislead; what happens when the data a model meets differ from the data it was scored on; what a winning score can justify; and what it cannot answer, because the target or the task itself is in question. Each section opens with the works it draws on, and the sections of them it uses; full references are at the end.

# Course palette (theme/st310.scss): viridis for the primary scale, magma for the second.
